items.title: Blue Planet III is keeping the rough edges in the age of AI
items.summary: BBC's Blue Planet III is looking to prove its authenticity by leaving in the less-than-perfect shots. Previous incarnations of the nature series were defined by their gorgeous, crystal-clear footage that seemed almost too good to be real. But one dead giveaway of AI is when things look too polished and seamless. To counter that, Blue Planet III goes warts and all. Executive Producer Elizabeth White told The Guardian in the past, "the amount of plankton and things" floating in the water would have caused them to cut a shot. Or "we might have framed out a boat or a buoy or gone: 'Oh, actually … the water conditions are not really good enough …

items.title: Yama Judges, Chitragupta Keeps the Records: Open-Source AI for Indian Languages
items.summary: Detect and redact Aadhaar, PAN and UPI data in Hindi, Hinglish and 11 more languages, then classify the text with your own labels. Two Apache-2.0 models that run locally. Source: Image by the author. TL;DR Chitragupta (arunp0/chitragupta-pii-indic) is a free, open-source model that finds and masks personal data in Indian text: Aadhaar, PAN, voter ID, GSTIN, UPI ID, IFSC, card and bank numbers, phone numbers, emails, addresses, dates of birth and names, in 13 languages. Yama (arunp0/yama-indic) is its companion: a zero-shot classifier that answers plain-English questions about the same kinds of text ("is this a complaint?", "how urgent?") with labels you choose at run time. Both are Apache-2.0, run on your own CPU or GPU, and send nothing to an API. On my own synthetic test set, built to be hard (a different writer model, unseen ID formats), Chitragupta scores 0.959 exact-span F1 . On two public benchmarks built by others, knowledgator’s GLiNER-PII beats it (0.966 and 0.965 against 0.954 and 0.878), and this post shows exactly where. Two questions every Indian product asks about a message Here is a typical support message in India: “Hi, main Rohit Verma bol raha hoon. Mera Aadhaar XXXX XXXX 5246 hai aur UPI rohit.example@upi, refund isi pe bhej do. Call: 98765 43210” Before this message goes anywhere useful, two things have to happen: Someone has to decide what it is. A refund request? Urgent? Angry? Someone has to protect what is in it. A name, an Aadhaar number, a UPI ID and a phone number, none of which belongs in your logs, your analytics or a prompt sent to a third-party LLM. In Indian tradition, these are two different jobs. Yama is the judge who weighs what is placed before him and gives a verdict. Chitragupta , his record-keeper, writes down the details of every person’s life. I built one open model for each job. My previous article, Before You Invent a New Architecture, Try a Bigger Encoder , covered Yama. This one introduces Chitragupta and shows how the two work together. Mask first, then classify. Both models run locally. Source: Image by the author. Why Indian text needs its own PII model Personal data in Indian text is hard to catch with English tools, for four reasons: Mixed languages and scripts. People write Hindi in Devanagari, in Roman letters, and mixed with English in the same sentence. The same is true for Tamil, Bengali, Marathi and the rest. Native digits and spoken numbers. A phone number can arrive as ९८७६५४३२१०, as ৯৮৭৬৫…, or, in a call-centre transcript, as “nau aath saat chhe…”. Indian identifiers. Aadhaar, PAN, voter ID (EPIC), GSTIN, IFSC and UPI IDs each have their own formats, and people type them with spaces, dashes or dots in unpredictable places. Regulation. India’s Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Rules, notified in November 2025, phase in over 18 months, and minimising the personal data you store is the simplest place to start. Most open PII models are English-first. Of the Indian-focused ones I tested, few cover Indian IDs, 13 languages and a permissive licence in one model. What Chitragupta does Chitragupta tags 18 types of personal data : People: person names, dates of birth Contact: phone numbers, emails, addresses, pincodes Government IDs: Aadhaar, PAN, voter ID, passport, driving licence, vehicle registration Financial: UPI ID, bank account, IFSC, card number, GSTIN Technical: IP addresses It works in Hindi, Hinglish, Bengali, Tamil, Telugu, Marathi, Gujarati, Kannada, Malayalam, Punjabi, Urdu, Odia and Indian English , in native scripts and in Roman letters, including native digits and numbers spoken out as words. One call to redact(). Dummy values: a masked Aadhaar and the common placeholder phone number. Source: Image by the author. Try it in a few lines # pip install torch transformers huggingface_hub import sys from huggingface_hub import snapshot_download path = snapshot_download("arunp0/chitragupta-pii-indic") sys.path.insert(0, path) from chitragupta import Chitragupta m = Chitragupta(path) # uses a GPU if available, otherwise CPU text = ("Hi, main Rohit Verma bol raha hoon. Mera Aadhaar XXXX XXXX 5246 hai aur " "UPI rohit.example@upi, refund isi pe bhej do. Call: 98765 43210") print(m.redact(text)) # Hi, main [PERSON] bol raha hoon. Mera Aadhaar [AADHAAR] hai aur UPI [UPI_ID], refund isi pe bhej do. Call: [PHONE] print(m.detect(text)[1]) # {'label': 'AADHAAR', 'start': 49, 'end': 63, 'text': 'XXXX XXXX 5246'} detect() returns character offsets, so you can mask, hash or tokenise the values however your system needs. Ordinary numbers are left alone: m.detect("Order #4410293 delivered on 12/03/2025 at 10:30. Thanks!") returns nothing. On a multi-core server CPU it takes about 24 ms per short message in batches of 32. You can also try it in the box on the model page. How it works: a tagger plus checksums Chitragupta has two parts. 1. A tagger. XLM-RoBERTa-large (560M parameters) fine-tuned to label every token as the beginning, inside or outside of a personal-data span. 2. A small rule layer. Most Indian IDs carry their own proof of validity: Aadhaar numbers pass the Verhoeff checksum. Card numbers pass the Luhn checksum. GSTINs end in a check character . PAN, IFSC, voter ID, passport, vehicle and phone numbers have fixed formats . When the tagger sees an ID format it has never met, it often splits it into pieces with mixed labels. The rules glue the pieces back together and let the checksum decide the label. They never touch names or addresses, and they never relabel bank account or driving licence numbers, which have no checksum. The effect is large where it matters: Recall on unseen ID formats jumps from 0.793 to 0.959 with the rules. The x-axis starts at 0.7. Source: Image by the author. Exact-span F1: 0.876 for the model alone, 0.959 with the rules. Redaction F1 (were the right characters masked, whatever the label?): 0.984 alone, 0.987 with the rules. “Strict” means separator styles never seen in training. They turned out easier than unseen digit groupings, which is why that slice scores higher. So the rules mostly fix labels , not coverage. The model already finds almost every value; the checksum decides whether it is an Aadhaar or a card number. A small model cannot memorise every way people type a GSTIN, but a few lines of arithmetic can verify one. Training data without anyone’s real data No real personal data, production data or public PII dataset went into training. Every training text is synthetic: An open model wrote the text. Gemma 4 (26B-A4B, Apache-2.0) wrote 114,431 messages in 14 document types: support chats, WhatsApp chats, call-centre transcripts, KYC forms, emails, bank SMS, loan notes, courier instructions, HR onboarding, clinic messages, police complaints, rental agreements, social posts and scam messages. Code filled in the values. Gemma wrote placeholders such as {AADHAAR_1}. Code replaced them with generated values, checksum-valid where the ID has a checksum and rendered in many formats. Because code placed the IDs, contact details and names, those offsets are exact. Addresses are the exception: Gemma wrote and tagged them. A second open model checked the work. Qwen3.6 (Apache-2.0) read every text and flagged personal data that was not labelled; those texts were dropped. The lesson I would pass on: when you generate training data with an LLM, let code produce the labels. LLMs are good at writing realistic text and unreliable at reporting exact character offsets. How I tried not to fool myself A model trained on synthetic data can score well simply by memorising its own generator. I built the test set to make that impossible: A different writer. Test texts were written by Qwen3.6 (a 4-bit AWQ build), not by Gemma. New document types. 10 types never seen in training: matrimonial profiles, admission forms, court notices, sale deeds, voice-note transcripts, cover letters, utility requests, lost-and-found notices, ration and pension applications, ride disputes. New ID formats. 65% of the ID values in the test set (2,386 of 3,650) use shapes no training example uses; 799 of them use separator styles never seen in training at all. New names. Names and addresses were written by the test model itself, not taken from the training name list. Label review. LLM agents reviewed a sample of 300 test texts and found a label error in 2.1% of spans. Re-scoring those 300 texts with corrected labels left their F1 at 0.960, so label noise does not explain the model’s mistakes. (This was an LLM review, not human verification.) The test set has 1,582 texts: 1,289 with personal data (6,123 spans) and 293 without. On the texts with no personal data, Chitragupta raised a false alarm on 2.4% (7 of 293). The benchmark said ship it. My own rule said no. After v1, I trained three v2 variants to fix two weaknesses the public benchmarks exposed: short one-line addresses and look-alike numbers such as timestamps and invoice IDs. On Ylemis, v2b jumped from 0.878 to 0.998. That gain is not independent: I designed v2’s data after reading the benchmark’s errors. Before looking at the results, I had written down a release rule: ship v2 only if it is not significantly worse than v1 on the fresh test set, overall or on driving licences. Paired bootstrap on the fresh test set. Orange intervals exclude zero. Source: Image by the author. Both variants I tested with the bootstrap significantly hurt driving licences (v2b −3.5, v2c −1.6 points), which fails the rule. v2c also lost 3.6 points on voter IDs, and the first v2 had already broken slash-separated IDs. Teaching the model that invoice numbers are not personal data made it more cautious about ID formats it had never seen. A missed voter ID leaks real data; a masked timestamp is only over-redaction. So I shipped v1, and the model card lists short addresses and look-alike numbers as known limits. How Chitragupta compares I ran nine public alternatives on the same texts. To compare models with different label sets, the score is character-level redaction F1 : whatever label a model uses, did it mask the personal-data characters? Redaction F1 on the fresh test set (axis from 0). This test set favours Chitragupta: it shares its label set and synthetic style. Source: Image by the author. Two caveats belong next to this chart: Home advantage. The test set is mine. It shares Chitragupta’s labels and synthetic style. Different designs. Several of these models tag things outside this label set (cities, organisations, dates), and some are meant to run behind a separate regex layer for IDs. Anything they mask outside our labels counts against them here. Where it loses On two public benchmarks built by other people, Chitragupta is not the best model. IndiaPII-Bench (maskflow): knowledgator’s GLiNER-PII leads. The x-axis starts at 0.5. Source: Image by the author. Ylemis India PII: Chitragupta is seventh, held back by short addresses. The x-axis starts at 0.5. Out-of-scope entities are excluded for every model. Source: Image by the author. IndiaPII-Bench (maskflow): Chitragupta finds almost everything (recall 0.998), but its precision is 0.914. It tags chat speaker names the benchmark leaves unannotated, and it flags 48% of the benchmark’s planted look-alikes, such as timestamps and invoice numbers. Ylemis India PII: precision is 0.999, but address recall is only 0.22. Ylemis addresses are short one-line forms like “803 Park Street, Mysuru 486221”, and Chitragupta learned from longer postal addresses. If your text has short addresses, test both models on a sample of your own data before choosing. Benchmarks tell you where to look, not what to deploy. Known limitations Short addresses are often missed, although the pincode next to them is usually caught. Look-alike numbers such as timestamps and order IDs can be flagged as bank accounts, cards or licences. Bank account numbers have no checksum, so they are the weakest ID label (F1 0.879). IP addresses score 1.000, but read that as optimistic: the IP rule was added after the fresh test showed IP as the weakest label. Long documents: on inputs of 450 to 1,400 tokens, F1 drops to 0.93–0.94, against 0.96 for the same texts one by one. Run it per message or paragraph. Synthetic evaluation only. No public human-labelled test set of Indian personal data exists, so real-world accuracy is unknown. Not a compliance tool by itself. Use it as one layer in a privacy process. Using Yama and Chitragupta together The pipeline from the diagram fits in a few lines. Chitragupta masks the personal data; Yama decides what the message is about. Far less personal data reaches your logs or a hosted LLM. import thx01 # pip install thx01 (the open-source library Yama uses) yama = thx01.load("arunp0/yama-indic") safe = m.redact(text) # Chitragupta, from the snippet above out = yama.system_one(safe, { "topic": {"type": "choice", "instructions": "What is the customer writing about?", "criteria": {"refund": "asking for a refund", "failed_payment": "payment failed", "account": "login or account access", "other": None}}, "urgent": {"type": "noul", "instructions": "Does the customer need help urgently?"}, }) # log `safe` and `out`, never `text` Yama is a zero-shot classifier: you write the labels and questions at run time, with no fine-tuning. On 33 tasks it never trained on, across 19 languages, it scores 0.814 accuracy, against 0.770 for the next best zero-shot model I tested. I have not measured Yama’s accuracy on redacted text, so check it on your own data. Two lessons from building both Let code write the labels. Use an LLM for realistic text and generated placeholders for the values, and most offsets come out exact. Write your release rule before you see the results. It is the only thing that stops a good benchmark number from talking you into a worse model. FAQ What is Chitragupta? Chitragupta (arunp0/chitragupta-pii-indic) is an open-source PII detection and redaction model for Indian languages and Hinglish. It finds 18 types of personal data, including Aadhaar, PAN, UPI IDs, phone numbers and names, in 13 languages, and returns their character offsets. How do I mask Aadhaar or PAN numbers in Python? Download the model with snapshot_download("arunp0/chitragupta-pii-indic"), then call Chitragupta(path).redact(text). It replaces each value with its label, such as [AADHAAR] or [PAN]. The full snippet is above. Is it free for commercial use? Yes. The weights and code are Apache-2.0, the base model (XLM-RoBERTa-large) is MIT, and the training data was generated only with open-weights models (Gemma 4 and Qwen3.6, both Apache-2.0). Does it run offline? Yes. It runs locally on CPU or GPU with PyTorch, and no text leaves your machine. How is it different from Microsoft Presidio or regex rules? Regex finds well-formed IDs but misses names, addresses, unusual formats, native digits and spoken numbers. On the fresh test set, Chitragupta masked 99.0% of personal-data characters, against 55.0% for Presidio with its Indian recognisers. Does it make a system DPDP-compliant? No model does that on its own. It helps you keep personal data out of logs, analytics and LLM prompts, as one part of a privacy process. What is Yama? Yama (arunp0/yama-indic) is a companion zero-shot text classifier for the same 13 languages. You describe the labels in plain English, and it returns a calibrated probability for each, without fine-tuning. Try them Chitragupta (PII detection and redaction): huggingface.co/arunp0/chitragupta-pii-indic Yama (zero-shot classification): huggingface.co/arunp0/yama-indic How Yama was built: Before You Invent a New Architecture, Try a Bigger Encoder If you run Chitragupta on real text and it misses something, open a discussion on the model page. Real failure cases are the most useful thing anyone can send me. Chitragupta and Yama are independent personal releases by Arun Prabhakaran, licensed Apache-2.0. Drafted with help from Claude (Anthropic); experiments, numbers and final edits by the author. Yama Judges, Chitragupta Keeps the Records: Open-Source AI for Indian Languages was originally published in Towards AI on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

TL;DR

  • Chitragupta (arunp0/chitragupta-pii-indic) is a free, open-source model that finds and masks personal data in Indian text: Aadhaar, PAN, voter ID, GSTIN, UPI ID, IFSC, card and bank numbers, phone numbers, emails, addresses, dates of birth and names, in 13 languages.
  • Yama (arunp0/yama-indic) is its companion: a zero-shot classifier that answers plain-English questions about the same kinds of text ("is this a complaint?", "how urgent?") with labels you choose at run time.
  • Both are Apache-2.0, run on your own CPU or GPU, and send nothing to an API.
  • On my own synthetic test set, built to be hard (a different writer model, unseen ID formats), Chitragupta scores 0.959 exact-span F1. On two public benchmarks built by others, knowledgator’s GLiNER-PII beats it (0.966 and 0.965 against 0.954 and 0.878), and this post shows exactly where.
Two questions every Indian product asks about a message

Here is a typical support message in India:

“Hi, main Rohit Verma bol raha hoon. Mera Aadhaar XXXX XXXX 5246 hai aur UPI rohit.example@upi, refund isi pe bhej do. Call: 98765 43210”

Before this message goes anywhere useful, two things have to happen:

  1. Someone has to decide what it is. A refund request? Urgent? Angry?
  2. Someone has to protect what is in it. A name, an Aadhaar number, a UPI ID and a phone number, none of which belongs in your logs, your analytics or a prompt sent to a third-party LLM.

In Indian tradition, these are two different jobs. Yama is the judge who weighs what is placed before him and gives a verdict. Chitragupta, his record-keeper, writes down the details of every person’s life.

I built one open model for each job. My previous article, Before You Invent a New Architecture, Try a Bigger Encoder, covered Yama. This one introduces Chitragupta and shows how the two work together.

Mask first, then classify. Both models run locally. Source: Image by the author.Why Indian text needs its own PII model

Personal data in Indian text is hard to catch with English tools, for four reasons:

  • Mixed languages and scripts. People write Hindi in Devanagari, in Roman letters, and mixed with English in the same sentence. The same is true for Tamil, Bengali, Marathi and the rest.
  • Native digits and spoken numbers. A phone number can arrive as ९८७६५४३२१०, as ৯৮৭৬৫…, or, in a call-centre transcript, as “nau aath saat chhe…”.
  • Indian identifiers. Aadhaar, PAN, voter ID (EPIC), GSTIN, IFSC and UPI IDs each have their own formats, and people type them with spaces, dashes or dots in unpredictable places.
  • Regulation. India’s Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Rules, notified in November 2025, phase in over 18 months, and minimising the personal data you store is the simplest place to start.

Most open PII models are English-first. Of the Indian-focused ones I tested, few cover Indian IDs, 13 languages and a permissive licence in one model.

What Chitragupta does

Chitragupta tags 18 types of personal data:

  • People: person names, dates of birth
  • Contact: phone numbers, emails, addresses, pincodes
  • Government IDs: Aadhaar, PAN, voter ID, passport, driving licence, vehicle registration
  • Financial: UPI ID, bank account, IFSC, card number, GSTIN
  • Technical: IP addresses

It works in Hindi, Hinglish, Bengali, Tamil, Telugu, Marathi, Gujarati, Kannada, Malayalam, Punjabi, Urdu, Odia and Indian English, in native scripts and in Roman letters, including native digits and numbers spoken out as words.

One call to redact(). Dummy values: a masked Aadhaar and the common placeholder phone number. Source: Image by the author.Try it in a few lines
# pip install torch transformers huggingface_hub
import sys
from huggingface_hub import snapshot_download
path = snapshot_download("arunp0/chitragupta-pii-indic")
sys.path.insert(0, path)
from chitragupta import Chitragupta
m = Chitragupta(path)   # uses a GPU if available, otherwise CPU
text = ("Hi, main Rohit Verma bol raha hoon. Mera Aadhaar XXXX XXXX 5246 hai aur "
        "UPI rohit.example@upi, refund isi pe bhej do. Call: 98765 43210")
print(m.redact(text))
# Hi, main [PERSON] bol raha hoon. Mera Aadhaar [AADHAAR] hai aur UPI [UPI_ID], refund isi pe bhej do. Call: [PHONE]
print(m.detect(text)[1])
# {'label': 'AADHAAR', 'start': 49, 'end': 63, 'text': 'XXXX XXXX 5246'}

detect() returns character offsets, so you can mask, hash or tokenise the values however your system needs. Ordinary numbers are left alone: m.detect("Order #4410293 delivered on 12/03/2025 at 10:30. Thanks!") returns nothing.

On a multi-core server CPU it takes about 24 ms per short message in batches of 32. You can also try it in the box on the model page.

How it works: a tagger plus checksums

Chitragupta has two parts.

1. A tagger. XLM-RoBERTa-large (560M parameters) fine-tuned to label every token as the beginning, inside or outside of a personal-data span.

2. A small rule layer. Most Indian IDs carry their own proof of validity:

  • Aadhaar numbers pass the Verhoeff checksum.
  • Card numbers pass the Luhn checksum.
  • GSTINs end in a check character.
  • PAN, IFSC, voter ID, passport, vehicle and phone numbers have fixed formats.

When the tagger sees an ID format it has never met, it often splits it into pieces with mixed labels. The rules glue the pieces back together and let the checksum decide the label. They never touch names or addresses, and they never relabel bank account or driving licence numbers, which have no checksum.

The effect is large where it matters:

Recall on unseen ID formats jumps from 0.793 to 0.959 with the rules. The x-axis starts at 0.7. Source: Image by the author.
  • Exact-span F1: 0.876 for the model alone, 0.959 with the rules.
  • Redaction F1 (were the right characters masked, whatever the label?): 0.984 alone, 0.987 with the rules.

“Strict” means separator styles never seen in training. They turned out easier than unseen digit groupings, which is why that slice scores higher.

So the rules mostly fix labels, not coverage. The model already finds almost every value; the checksum decides whether it is an Aadhaar or a card number. A small model cannot memorise every way people type a GSTIN, but a few lines of arithmetic can verify one.

Training data without anyone’s real data

No real personal data, production data or public PII dataset went into training. Every training text is synthetic:

  1. An open model wrote the text. Gemma 4 (26B-A4B, Apache-2.0) wrote 114,431 messages in 14 document types: support chats, WhatsApp chats, call-centre transcripts, KYC forms, emails, bank SMS, loan notes, courier instructions, HR onboarding, clinic messages, police complaints, rental agreements, social posts and scam messages.
  2. Code filled in the values. Gemma wrote placeholders such as {AADHAAR_1}. Code replaced them with generated values, checksum-valid where the ID has a checksum and rendered in many formats. Because code placed the IDs, contact details and names, those offsets are exact. Addresses are the exception: Gemma wrote and tagged them.
  3. A second open model checked the work. Qwen3.6 (Apache-2.0) read every text and flagged personal data that was not labelled; those texts were dropped.

The lesson I would pass on: when you generate training data with an LLM, let code produce the labels. LLMs are good at writing realistic text and unreliable at reporting exact character offsets.

How I tried not to fool myself

A model trained on synthetic data can score well simply by memorising its own generator. I built the test set to make that impossible:

  • A different writer. Test texts were written by Qwen3.6 (a 4-bit AWQ build), not by Gemma.
  • New document types. 10 types never seen in training: matrimonial profiles, admission forms, court notices, sale deeds, voice-note transcripts, cover letters, utility requests, lost-and-found notices, ration and pension applications, ride disputes.
  • New ID formats. 65% of the ID values in the test set (2,386 of 3,650) use shapes no training example uses; 799 of them use separator styles never seen in training at all.
  • New names. Names and addresses were written by the test model itself, not taken from the training name list.
  • Label review. LLM agents reviewed a sample of 300 test texts and found a label error in 2.1% of spans. Re-scoring those 300 texts with corrected labels left their F1 at 0.960, so label noise does not explain the model’s mistakes. (This was an LLM review, not human verification.)

The test set has 1,582 texts: 1,289 with personal data (6,123 spans) and 293 without. On the texts with no personal data, Chitragupta raised a false alarm on 2.4% (7 of 293).

The benchmark said ship it. My own rule said no.

After v1, I trained three v2 variants to fix two weaknesses the public benchmarks exposed: short one-line addresses and look-alike numbers such as timestamps and invoice IDs. On Ylemis, v2b jumped from 0.878 to 0.998. That gain is not independent: I designed v2’s data after reading the benchmark’s errors.

Before looking at the results, I had written down a release rule: ship v2 only if it is not significantly worse than v1 on the fresh test set, overall or on driving licences.

Paired bootstrap on the fresh test set. Orange intervals exclude zero. Source: Image by the author.

Both variants I tested with the bootstrap significantly hurt driving licences (v2b −3.5, v2c −1.6 points), which fails the rule. v2c also lost 3.6 points on voter IDs, and the first v2 had already broken slash-separated IDs. Teaching the model that invoice numbers are not personal data made it more cautious about ID formats it had never seen. A missed voter ID leaks real data; a masked timestamp is only over-redaction. So I shipped v1, and the model card lists short addresses and look-alike numbers as known limits.

How Chitragupta compares

I ran nine public alternatives on the same texts. To compare models with different label sets, the score is character-level redaction F1: whatever label a model uses, did it mask the personal-data characters?

Redaction F1 on the fresh test set (axis from 0). This test set favours Chitragupta: it shares its label set and synthetic style. Source: Image by the author.

Two caveats belong next to this chart:

  • Home advantage. The test set is mine. It shares Chitragupta’s labels and synthetic style.
  • Different designs. Several of these models tag things outside this label set (cities, organisations, dates), and some are meant to run behind a separate regex layer for IDs. Anything they mask outside our labels counts against them here.
Where it loses

On two public benchmarks built by other people, Chitragupta is not the best model.

IndiaPII-Bench (maskflow): knowledgator’s GLiNER-PII leads. The x-axis starts at 0.5. Source: Image by the author.Ylemis India PII: Chitragupta is seventh, held back by short addresses. The x-axis starts at 0.5. Out-of-scope entities are excluded for every model. Source: Image by the author.
  • IndiaPII-Bench (maskflow): Chitragupta finds almost everything (recall 0.998), but its precision is 0.914. It tags chat speaker names the benchmark leaves unannotated, and it flags 48% of the benchmark’s planted look-alikes, such as timestamps and invoice numbers.
  • Ylemis India PII: precision is 0.999, but address recall is only 0.22. Ylemis addresses are short one-line forms like “803 Park Street, Mysuru 486221”, and Chitragupta learned from longer postal addresses.

If your text has short addresses, test both models on a sample of your own data before choosing. Benchmarks tell you where to look, not what to deploy.

Known limitations
  • Short addresses are often missed, although the pincode next to them is usually caught.
  • Look-alike numbers such as timestamps and order IDs can be flagged as bank accounts, cards or licences.
  • Bank account numbers have no checksum, so they are the weakest ID label (F1 0.879).
  • IP addresses score 1.000, but read that as optimistic: the IP rule was added after the fresh test showed IP as the weakest label.
  • Long documents: on inputs of 450 to 1,400 tokens, F1 drops to 0.93–0.94, against 0.96 for the same texts one by one. Run it per message or paragraph.
  • Synthetic evaluation only. No public human-labelled test set of Indian personal data exists, so real-world accuracy is unknown.
  • Not a compliance tool by itself. Use it as one layer in a privacy process.
Using Yama and Chitragupta together

The pipeline from the diagram fits in a few lines. Chitragupta masks the personal data; Yama decides what the message is about. Far less personal data reaches your logs or a hosted LLM.

import thx01   # pip install thx01  (the open-source library Yama uses)
yama = thx01.load("arunp0/yama-indic")
safe = m.redact(text)   # Chitragupta, from the snippet above
out = yama.system_one(safe, {
    "topic":  {"type": "choice", "instructions": "What is the customer writing about?",
               "criteria": {"refund": "asking for a refund", "failed_payment": "payment failed",
                            "account": "login or account access", "other": None}},
    "urgent": {"type": "noul", "instructions": "Does the customer need help urgently?"},
})
# log `safe` and `out`, never `text`

Yama is a zero-shot classifier: you write the labels and questions at run time, with no fine-tuning. On 33 tasks it never trained on, across 19 languages, it scores 0.814 accuracy, against 0.770 for the next best zero-shot model I tested. I have not measured Yama’s accuracy on redacted text, so check it on your own data.

Two lessons from building both
  1. Let code write the labels. Use an LLM for realistic text and generated placeholders for the values, and most offsets come out exact.
  2. Write your release rule before you see the results. It is the only thing that stops a good benchmark number from talking you into a worse model.
FAQ

What is Chitragupta? Chitragupta (arunp0/chitragupta-pii-indic) is an open-source PII detection and redaction model for Indian languages and Hinglish. It finds 18 types of personal data, including Aadhaar, PAN, UPI IDs, phone numbers and names, in 13 languages, and returns their character offsets.

How do I mask Aadhaar or PAN numbers in Python? Download the model with snapshot_download("arunp0/chitragupta-pii-indic"), then call Chitragupta(path).redact(text). It replaces each value with its label, such as [AADHAAR] or [PAN]. The full snippet is above.

Is it free for commercial use? Yes. The weights and code are Apache-2.0, the base model (XLM-RoBERTa-large) is MIT, and the training data was generated only with open-weights models (Gemma 4 and Qwen3.6, both Apache-2.0).

Does it run offline? Yes. It runs locally on CPU or GPU with PyTorch, and no text leaves your machine.

How is it different from Microsoft Presidio or regex rules? Regex finds well-formed IDs but misses names, addresses, unusual formats, native digits and spoken numbers. On the fresh test set, Chitragupta masked 99.0% of personal-data characters, against 55.0% for Presidio with its Indian recognisers.

Does it make a system DPDP-compliant? No model does that on its own. It helps you keep personal data out of logs, analytics and LLM prompts, as one part of a privacy process.

What is Yama? Yama (arunp0/yama-indic) is a companion zero-shot text classifier for the same 13 languages. You describe the labels in plain English, and it returns a calibrated probability for each, without fine-tuning.

Try them
  • Chitragupta (PII detection and redaction): huggingface.co/arunp0/chitragupta-pii-indic
  • Yama (zero-shot classification): huggingface.co/arunp0/yama-indic
  • How Yama was built: Before You Invent a New Architecture, Try a Bigger Encoder

If you run Chitragupta on real text and it misses something, open a discussion on the model page. Real failure cases are the most useful thing anyone can send me.

Chitragupta and Yama are independent personal releases by Arun Prabhakaran, licensed Apache-2.0.

Drafted with help from Claude (Anthropic); experiments, numbers and final edits by the author.

items.title: Imputation of Missing Climate Data and Vulnerability Analysis: A Survey
items.summary: The previous article [65] covered effects of climate change such as global warming and rising sea levels, and investigated time series forecasting models for predicting global temperature anomalies, from statistical models such as ARIMA to large language models (LLMs). Although LLMs have mainly advanced natural language processing, they are gaining importance in time series tasks. Transformer-based foundation models, which form the basis of most LLMs, offer unprecedented capabilities in tasks such as forecasting, classification and trend analysis. Transformer and Patch-Based Time Series Models Time Series Transformer (TST) adapts the standard transformer architecture, using positional encodings tailored to temporal data and an attention mechanism to capture long-term dependencies. TST can be fine-tuned for tasks such as forecasting. PatchTST divides a time series into non-overlapping patches and processes them using a hierarchical attention mechanism. This captures both global and local temporal patterns, making it applicable to multivariate time series (Kottapalli et al. [1], Wen et al. [2], Nie et al. [3]). Patch-based time series models divide the input series into fixed-length windows, or patches, which are handled as separate tokens. This allows the model to understand local temporal patterns within each patch before modeling global dependencies across the whole series. Tiny Time Mixer, a non-transformer model based on the TSMixer architecture (Ekambaram et al. [4]), uses adaptive patching, which lets the model work with different patch lengths and patch counts, along with techniques to widen coverage of different temporal resolutions (Kottapalli et al. [1]). TimesFM also splits the input time series into non-overlapping patches, and Time-LLM breaks multivariate time series down into univariate patches. These architectures differ from models such as Time-MoE, Chronos, Lag-Llama, TimeGPT and LLMTime, which do not rely on patching (Garza et al. [5], Shi et al. [6], Gruver et al. [7]). The applicability of patch-based techniques towards global climate research and forecasting carbon emissions is discussed in Chen et al. [8] and Xiong and Wang [9]. Figure 1 Visualization of temperature anomalies over land and ocean from NASA GISS Surface Temperature Analysis (GISTEMP v4) (GISTEMP Team [10], Lenssen et al. [11]). Figure 1 shows global temperature anomalies over land and ocean, based on data from NASA GISS Surface Temperature Analysis (GISTEMP v4) (GISTEMP Team [10], Lenssen et al. [11]). The dataset was downloaded and subsequently plotted using Claude Code. GISTEMP Team [10] and Lenssen et al. [11] explain that the thin lines in Figure 1 are granular annual values and thick lines correspond to the average (five-year LOWESS smooth), for temperature anomalies (with respect to the 1951–1980 baseline) as a mean over all land areas and the sea surface temperature anomalies (with respect to the 1951–1980 baseline). With this as background, the next section focuses on imputation of missing climate data. Imputation of Missing Climate Data This section investigates techniques for imputing spatiotemporal data, which support accurate analysis and help mitigate risks related to climate change and global warming (Mariappan et al. [12]). Chronologically continuous, accurate and gap-free climate data are hence needed. Replacing missing data with substituted values, known as imputation, is common in domains such as meteorology, climatology and even power systems. In climate change impact studies, weather data with good spatial and temporal granularity are needed for analysis of past climate to support forecasting of parameters such as future temperature (Shtiliyanova et al. [13]). Missing data can pose a challenge, and several published research studies have discussed both conventional and state-of-the-art techniques to impute missing data. Figure 2 Visualization of air temperature anomalies from NASA GISS Surface Temperature Analysis (GISTEMP v4) (GISTEMP Team [10], Lenssen et al. [11]). Climate data consist of parameters such as temperature, precipitation, wind speed and relative humidity, measured by a network of sensors. Sensor data can be prone to instrument or measurement errors (or sensor malfunction), leading to outliers or missing data. In this context, imputation is the process of replacing missing values in a dataset with reasonable estimated values so that the dataset is complete (Palarea-Albaladejo [14]). Using point data requires quality assurance and control, which involves assessing the data for errors after collection. Understanding why data points are missing is important, since missing values can conceal meaningful information. Missing data are a common problem in climatological time series, as reliable statistical analysis is not possible with an incomplete dataset. While some algorithms such as random forest (RF) can handle missing data innately, it is still important to gauge the mechanism of missingness as explained by Teegavarapu [15]. Teegavarapu [15] further describes three mechanisms of missing data: missing at random (MAR), missing completely at random (MCAR) and missing not at random (MNAR). Data on a variable X are MAR if the probability of missing data on X does not depend on X itself after taking into consideration the remaining variables (e.g., Y or Z). Data on variable X are MCAR if the probability of missing data on X is not related to the value of X or any value of the other variables (e.g., Y or Z) in the data. Data are MNAR, also known as not missing at random (NMAR), if the probability of missing data on the variable X does depend on the value of X or any values of the other variables in the data. Beyond understanding why data are missing, reliable spatiotemporal analysis and modeling require complete and sequential data. Data homogeneity should be investigated using the available metadata, and emphasis should be on correcting the outliers and anomalies if needed. Missing data can pose a significant issue. In this regard, gaps in the data can be filled with spatial or temporal imputation. The choice of the imputation technique may depend on the type of variable and the granularity of the data. Imputation thus completes the dataset but may alter some of its underlying characteristics. Imputation replaces an incomplete record with an estimated value. The techniques for imputing missing data broadly include non-geostatistical, geostatistical and combined methods for spatial interpolation, as well as temporal interpolation, universal function approximation and data mining-assisted imputation approaches (Teegavarapu [15]). Overview of Imputation Approaches In spatiotemporal applications, gaps in the data can arise from human error, sensor malfunction or bad weather. Zahmatkesh and Zech [16] describe several approaches for handling the missing data. Removing incomplete records (dropping the null records) leaves the model with complete data, at the cost of losing some information or possibly biasing the results. Prediction-based methods estimate missing data by learning the mapping between past and future observations; they are especially applicable to time series and include ARIMA, Bayesian networks, feedforward neural networks and support vector regression (SVR). Interpolation-based approaches estimate values between the observations, assuming the data change smoothly; examples are linear, polynomial and spline interpolation. The authors [16] emphasize that these suit spatial or time series data that can be reasonably expected to vary smoothly, such as in climatology. Other approaches include statistical learning methods such as Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC), probabilistic principal component analysis (PPCA), hot-deck imputation and linear regression with the expectation-maximization (EM) algorithm. While Lin et al. [17] mention that data quality issues such as measurement inconsistencies or missing data introduce uncertainty during model training and forecasting, Başakın et al. [18] note that the validity of classical imputation techniques may depend on the assumptions about the data distribution and the characteristics of the missing values in the data. They also mention that advanced imputation techniques may give more accurate results due to their ability to handle complex non-linear interactions in the data, suggesting deep learning-based approaches as well as the use of explainable artificial intelligence (such as SHAP and LIME) in imputation. Building on this, Zainuddin et al. [19] mention that advances in data collection have increased the volume of time series data, which, due to many factors (including those mentioned above), may contain missing values and that failing to model and analyze these missing data may affect the results of the forecasting outcome. Conventional preprocessing methods make assumptions about the data generation process that are not always valid. The authors also review several approaches for handling missing data and emphasize that the characteristics of the given time series need to be carefully examined before an appropriate imputation technique is selected, as also noted by Başakın et al. [18]. Focusing on specific techniques, Alejo-Sanchez et al. [20] mention that averages (mean and median), simple and multiple linear regression, interpolation and principal component analysis (PCA) are traditional approaches for filling in the missing data, whereas artificial neural networks (ANN) and generative adversarial networks (GAN) can identify complex patterns when imputing missing climate data. They also note that imputation may simplify the prediction of climate phenomena such as temperature and precipitation, which are the climate variables most often studied. Beyond climate data, a comparable challenge arises in traffic time series, where gaps can lead to analysis errors (Chan et al. [21]); tensor factorization and neural network models are used for imputation, with GANs, graph neural networks (GNNs) and PPCA among the popular techniques. Statistical Imputation Methods Statistical imputation methods are techniques that replace missing or null values with a statistical estimate. Iqbal and Mukherjee [22] handle missing values in raw air quality data using median imputation, where missing values are replaced with the median of that column or variable. This ensures data consistency while being less sensitive to outliers. Similarly, Li et al. [23] point out that with deteriorating air quality and increasing pollution, accurate air quality prediction is becoming increasingly important, and air quality index (AQI) prediction is gaining prominence. While noting that data preprocessing is an essential stage that affects how accurate and reliable the predictions are, and that missing data points occur when equipment fails or outliers are removed, the authors use a statistical imputation approach by checking the hourly data for missing values: hours with no missing values are retained, and missing points are filled with the average of neighboring values, keeping the data continuous and valid. On a similar theme, Shreyas et al. [24] point out that air quality forecasting is essential in developing countries such as India, where climate variability and industrialization may degrade air quality and cause health risks. As part of predicting the AQI, they apply data preprocessing techniques, including handling missing values and outliers. Although an initial check showed the dataset to be largely complete, a specific imputation strategy was used to achieve a complete dataset, and listwise deletion was performed after feature engineering so that the models were trained on real atmospheric conditions instead of synthesized patterns as a result of imputation. In contrast to these single-value approaches, Hayati Rezvan et al. [25] describe multiple imputation as a way to deal with missing data, which, if not handled appropriately, can reduce statistical power and bias the results. Along these lines, Hui et al. [26] note that gaps in the data are a problem in long-term field measurements caused by equipment failures such as those from lightning strikes. Filling these gaps in the data is important for estimating the annual net ecosystem carbon exchange. The authors use multiple imputation, a Monte Carlo method that fills each gap with several simulated values. This leads to several complete datasets that share the observed values and differ only in the imputed ones, so standard statistical analysis may be applied. In a different domain, Krishnamoorthy et al. [27] mention that tracking oceans and coastal areas is key to understanding the impacts of climate change and predicting undesirable outcomes. Satellite imagery-based remote sensing has transformed the collection of large volumes of environmental data with complex spatial and temporal patterns. However, missing data often occur in remote sensing databases due to cloud cover or sensing instrument failures. Simpler techniques such as mean imputation may not suffice, as they cannot account for correlation between parameters, so the authors use multivariate imputation by chained equations (MICE), which uses multiple regression models. Zahmatkesh and Zech [16] also mention the use of MICE (Van Buuren [30]) on maximum temperature data for the Diourbel station in 1985, showing that the imputed values track the time series reasonably. They also describe how spatial imputation methods estimate a station’s missing data from observed data at neighboring stations. Spatial gaps may occur due to cloud cover, as also stated by Krishnamoorthy et al. [27], and kriging is a popular method for imputing them (Zahmatkesh and Zech [16]). Like the previous authors, Costa et al. [28] use the MICE technique to impute missing data for climate variables (precipitation, temperature, humidity, atmospheric pressure, wind speed and insolation) from several stations in Brazil from 1961 to 2014, and apply quality control techniques for validation. For rainfall networks, O’Sullivan and Kelly [29] note that modeling spatiotemporal precipitation data can be computationally expensive because the datasets are high-dimensional. Frequent missing entries can affect data quality, and filling them can help a rainfall network yield more accurate models. They propose a likelihood-based imputation approach to lower computational cost while also investigating DeepKriging, a deep learning approach to spatiotemporal modeling. The authors also compare these techniques with elastic-net chained equations (ENCE) and multiple imputation by chained equations with direct use of regularized regression (MICE DURR), quantifying the imputation accuracy. Williams et al. [31], on the other hand, use Bayesian approaches (Bayesian compressive sensing) to impute environmental temperature data. These methods need data only from the target station and yet perform comparably to or better than a spatiotemporal model that also needs data from nearby stations. Most climate studies require complete time series, so gaps in the data need to be imputed (Afrifa-Yamoah et al. [32]). In this regard, the authors evaluate several imputation approaches, including a structural time series model with Kalman smoothing, ARIMA with Kalman smoothing and multiple linear regression, using complete 12-month portions of hourly temperature, humidity and wind speed records from four coastal locations in Western Australia. Observations were treated as missing at random, and artificial gaps were created and evaluated with five-fold cross-validation, with the proportion of missingness set at 10%. Spatial Interpolation and Geostatistical Methods Raja et al. [33] describe geostatistical imputation techniques for filling missing first floor elevation (FFE) data when assessing how vulnerable the buildings are to floods, including kriging, which fills gaps based on how close the known points are and how they relate in space. Shtiliyanova et al. [13] also use kriging, normally applied across space to estimate missing values using neighboring data in geostatistical datasets, to impute air temperature time series. Xu et al. [34] mention that climate records often have gaps in some locations and periods (as noted earlier), and introduce P-BSHADE, evaluated on an annual temperature dataset for China from 1950 to 2000. The method weights the observations from surrounding stations to derive unbiased estimates of the missing data with minimum error variance. On a similar theme, since missing values in geographic information system (GIS) datasets may result in challenges for spatial analytics and decision making, Hamza and Salem [35] describe a set-based framework that represents each missing entry as a domain-consistent set and imputes it through statistical sampling, evaluation guided by clustering and refinement through local search. Machine Learning Methods Turning to machine learning, Shukur and Lee [36] note that wind speed data may have missing values due to malfunctioning sensing devices, and propose a hybrid technique combining an ANN with an auto-regressive model for imputation. Similarly, Körner et al. [37] suggest a gradient boosting-based machine learning technique for filling in the gaps due to missing or erroneous data in meteorological time series. The method is evaluated on extensive hourly records of temperature, wind speed and relative humidity from 1951 to 2015. In a related direction, Zhang et al. [38] point out that clustering analysis is affected by datasets with partially missing values. In this regard, they propose a hybrid algorithm based on fuzzy clustering and particle swarm optimization (PSO) and treat the missing data as intervals. A neighbor interval reconstruction (NIR) method pre-classifies the data and then estimates the interval of a missing attribute from its nearest neighbors. Returning to climate data, Diouf et al. [39] evaluate k-nearest neighbors (KNN), PPCA, MICE, missForest (Stekhoven and Bühlmann [40]) and imputeTS for imputation on a Senegalese meteorological dataset, finding missForest better for imputing temperature and imputeTS better for precipitation. Along similar lines, Qaraghuli et al. [41] note that monitoring climate change depends on complete climate records but these datasets often have gaps that need to be imputed for data integrity. The authors evaluate six univariate and multivariate imputation techniques for temperature, precipitation and relative humidity by comparing root mean square error (RMSE) and Kling-Gupta Efficiency (KGE). The evaluation showed KNN was better at imputing precipitation, MICE was optimal at imputing temperature data and missForest for relative humidity. While Qaraghuli et al. [41] focus on temperature, precipitation and relative humidity, Başakın et al. [42] compare various techniques for filling in the gaps in solar radiation data, a key variable for understanding climate dynamics. An XGBoost-differential evolution model built with measurements from neighboring stations performed better at gap sizes of 5%, 10% and 30%, while RF gave the highest accuracy at 20%, based on Nash-Sutcliffe Efficiency (NSE) and KGE. For rainfall, Pinthong et al. [43] address missing rainfall data in climate research and examine machine learning approaches, including multiple linear regression, M5 model tree, RF, SVR, multilayer perceptron (MLP) and genetic programming, as well as spatial interpolation techniques, namely arithmetic average, inverse distance weighting (IDW), correlation coefficient weighted and normal ratio. They mention that selection of the neighboring stations may be required for spatial approaches, whereas machine learning techniques imputed the monthly rainfall data better, as quantified by NSE, Pearson’s correlation coefficient R and the overall index (OI). At a finer time scale, Boukdire et al. [44] describe the need for sub-hourly datasets for accurate rainfall forecasting. Gaps in such data may be common due to malfunctioning sensors (as pointed out earlier), and filling them at finer granularity can be difficult. The authors compare approaches using machine learning (MLP and RF) and interpolation (ordinary kriging and IDW) to impute missing 10-minute rainfall data. Outside climate data, Kim et al. [45] also point out that due to the increase in spatial data, concerns about missing observations that may lead to biased conclusions continue to grow. Recent studies suggest that machine learning techniques applied to environmental data may address these issues more efficiently than standard interpolation methods like IDW or kriging. To test their efficacy in socioeconomic applications, the authors compare neural networks, RF, IDW and kriging-based techniques to fill in the missing data. Returning to environmental data, Hu et al. [46] examine missing data in air quality prediction caused by software and hardware malfunctions, and suggest filling in the gaps from the spatial and temporal structure of the data. Simple approaches include removing missing values (dropping the null values), which may leave some time steps unavailable, and statistical methods such as averaging over a two-hour or six-hour window. Machine learning methods, by contrast, learn the complex patterns of how air quality changes and use them to estimate the missing values. Other approaches referenced by the authors apply correlations across space and time to fill missing data from multiple views or use singular value thresholding (SVT) to reconstruct gaps in the air quality matrix. Deep Learning Methods Figure 3 Architecture of a simple MLP Turning to neural networks, Coulibaly and Evora [47] note that accurately filling in missing daily precipitation values can be hard, and compare ANNs such as the MLP (shown in Figure 3) and its variants, time-lagged feedforward networks (TLFN), generalized radial basis function (RBF) networks and recurrent neural networks (RNN) and their variants (such as the time-delay recurrent neural network (TDRNN)), along with different optimization methods, for filling in gaps in total precipitation records and extreme temperature time series at daily granularity. Moving beyond daily weather records, Eum and Yoo [48] propose a two-step, multi-scale neural network-based imputation method. A word2vec model (continuous bag-of-words) first converts daily time-activity sequences into a low-dimensional embedding, and a multi-scale residual convolutional neural network (CNN)-stacked long short-term memory (LSTM) network then learns multi-scale temporal patterns from past observations to predict missing values. The authors note that even as time-activity data become more widely available and spatially detailed, long gaps in such records still limit their use in human mobility research. Similarly, Galdelli et al. [49] mention that spatial time series are fundamental to physical processes that need continuous monitoring and forecasting (e.g., object tracking). However, malfunctioning sensors or missing data may result in time series that cause classification bias. The authors propose a deep learning technique based on sequential bidirectional LSTM (BiLSTM) to fill in the missing trajectories in spatiotemporal data. While Galdelli et al. [49] focus on trajectories, Boujoudar et al. [50] use an MLP, LSTM and CNN to accurately impute missing temperature data recorded over two years at a meteorological station at the Green Energy Park facility in Morocco. Measurements of precipitation, humidity, direct normal irradiation, global horizontal irradiation, and wind speed and direction were recorded every minute. On a broader scale, Wang et al. [51] note that missing data are common in multivariate time series and make it difficult to perform accurate analysis. In recent years, deep learning models have been used for imputation because they can handle complex temporal dependencies and learn the distribution of the data. The authors review deep learning-based techniques for multivariate time series imputation and group them by imputation uncertainty and neural network architecture. They also list tools such as imputeTS and mice (R packages), and Impyute and Autoimpute (Python packages). Impyute offers simpler techniques such as a moving average window, whereas Autoimpute offers polynomial and spline interpolation. GluonTS (Python) provides naive methods such as dummy value and causal mean imputation, sktime (Python) supports machine learning-based imputation, and ImputeBench (R) (Richter et al. [52]) supports deep learning-based imputation. As future work, Wang et al. [51] suggest that LLMs are a promising direction for time series imputation research. In a related review, Sun et al. [53] present a comprehensive evaluation of statistical, machine learning and deep learning models for imputation, suggesting that conventional methods such as MICE and missForest may outperform deep learning methods for tabular data with fewer than 30,000 samples, whereas advanced techniques such as generative adversarial imputation networks (GAIN) may perform well in the MCAR scenario. Variational auto-encoders (VAEs) are also discussed in Sun et al. [53]. Yoon et al. [54] introduce GAIN, which adapts GANs to missing data imputation: the generator observes some parts of a data vector, fills in the missing parts based on what is observed and produces a complete vector. Turning to graph-based models, Shen et al. [55] propose the graph attention recurrent neural network (GARNN) for spatiotemporal traffic data imputation, which uses both temporal and spatial information. This matters because unexpected disruptions during data collection and storage leave gaps that can affect downstream tasks. In this technique, observations and missingness are modeled separately via LSTMs, treating missing information as distinct from observations. A decay mechanism models dependencies across time steps, and a graph attention network (GAT) learns the spatial correlations. For time series imputation specifically, Jin et al. [56] discuss GNNs, which can capture complex spatial and temporal dependencies, whereas statistical methods such as mean imputation cannot adequately capture non-linear relationships. The authors group GNN-based imputation into deterministic and probabilistic methods: the former gives a best estimate for missing values, whereas the latter accounts for uncertainty by providing a distribution over possible values. Other Techniques and Imputation Quality Taking a wider view, Hameed and Ali [57] compare seventeen missing value imputation techniques, including some mentioned above: EM, median imputation, hot-deck (cold-deck) imputation, regression imputation, MICE, support vector machine (SVM) imputation, single center imputation from multiple chained equation (SICE) (Khan and Hoque [58]), which combines single and multiple imputation methods, non-parametric iterative imputation algorithms and MLPs. Whichever method is used, Shadbahr et al. [59] note that imputation quality must be considered, since it directly affects the downstream task that uses the imputed data. Applications of Machine Learning in Climate Change and Vulnerability Analysis: Some Relevant Case Studies Coastal regions face growing risk from climate change, rising sea levels and severe weather events such as hurricanes. These areas are often important to the economy, but they come under strain from both natural and human-related activity. To evaluate this vulnerability, Mondal et al. [60] describe a coastal vulnerability index, which draws on elevation, water depth, coastal shape, sea level rise, population density and other factors over a 30-year period, and assess coastal vulnerability using machine learning techniques including ANN, KNN, SVM and RF. The ANN model in Mondal et al. [60] consisted of an input layer, two hidden layers with 10 neurons each and an output layer; the hidden layers model complex non-linear relationships between the input features and coastal vulnerability. KNN assigned a vulnerability class based on the closest data points, SVM by finding the optimal hyperplane that best separates the classes, and RF, an ensemble that combines predictions from many decision trees, was chosen for its accuracy in regression and classification. The RF model (shown in Figure 4) captured how the variables interact and how important each feature is (Mondal et al. [60]). For evaluation, the data were stratified and split into training and test sets. A low RMSE showed that the predictions were reliable and that the model measured the coastal exposure well. The coastline was then grouped into exposure levels from very low to very high. Figure 4 Flow diagram of the RF algorithm On a similar theme, Forzieri et al. [61] use RF regression [66–67] to identify drivers of temporal autocorrelation when studying how climate change affects forest resilience. Vegetation and climate variables were used as predictors, the latter including monthly averaged precipitation, air temperature at 2 m and evapotranspiration deficit from the ERA5-Land reanalysis dataset. Moving from forests to cities, Cano Pecharroman et al. [62] use gradient-boosted decision trees to rank which climate vulnerability indicators matter most in cities such as Buenos Aires, London, Seoul and Johannesburg. Gradient-boosted decision trees were chosen over RF because they offer higher accuracy and are trained sequentially, rather than independently, to reduce errors. Taking a geospatial view, Sultana et al. [63] point out that combining remote sensing and GIS can help turn geospatial data into useful knowledge. Remote sensing records the Earth’s surface using sensors on satellites, whereas GIS is software for storing, analyzing and mapping location-based data. Analytics plays a vital role in Earth resource management, and Sultana et al. [63] assess drought vulnerability (drought forecasting) by modeling precipitation and temperature with an ANN. Turning to agriculture, Jian et al. [64] examine how global warming affects rice yield by studying exposure to high temperature and quantifying the uncertainty through Monte Carlo simulations. Key Takeaways Among the imputation techniques reviewed, MICE, missForest and kriging are commonly applied to fill gaps in geospatial data, which will form the basis for accurate analysis in the context of climate change. Deep learning-based techniques have also been discussed as approaches to impute missing data, with LLMs noted as a direction for future research.
