The previous article [65] covered effects of climate change such as global warming and rising sea levels, and investigated time series forecasting models for predicting global temperature anomalies, from statistical models such as ARIMA to large language models (LLMs). Although LLMs have mainly advanced natural language processing, they are gaining importance in time series tasks. Transformer-based foundation models, which form the basis of most LLMs, offer unprecedented capabilities in tasks such as forecasting, classification and trend analysis.

Transformer and Patch-Based Time Series Models

Time Series Transformer (TST) adapts the standard transformer architecture, using positional encodings tailored to temporal data and an attention mechanism to capture long-term dependencies. TST can be fine-tuned for tasks such as forecasting. PatchTST divides a time series into non-overlapping patches and processes them using a hierarchical attention mechanism. This captures both global and local temporal patterns, making it applicable to multivariate time series (Kottapalli et al. [1], Wen et al. [2], Nie et al. [3]).

Patch-based time series models divide the input series into fixed-length windows, or patches, which are handled as separate tokens. This allows the model to understand local temporal patterns within each patch before modeling global dependencies across the whole series. Tiny Time Mixer, a non-transformer model based on the TSMixer architecture (Ekambaram et al. [4]), uses adaptive patching, which lets the model work with different patch lengths and patch counts, along with techniques to widen coverage of different temporal resolutions (Kottapalli et al. [1]). TimesFM also splits the input time series into non-overlapping patches, and Time-LLM breaks multivariate time series down into univariate patches. These architectures differ from models such as Time-MoE, Chronos, Lag-Llama, TimeGPT and LLMTime, which do not rely on patching (Garza et al. [5], Shi et al. [6], Gruver et al. [7]). The applicability of patch-based techniques towards global climate research and forecasting carbon emissions is discussed in Chen et al. [8] and Xiong and Wang [9].

Figure 1 Visualization of temperature anomalies over land and ocean from NASA GISS Surface Temperature Analysis (GISTEMP v4) (GISTEMP Team [10], Lenssen et al. [11]).

Figure 1 shows global temperature anomalies over land and ocean, based on data from NASA GISS Surface Temperature Analysis (GISTEMP v4) (GISTEMP Team [10], Lenssen et al. [11]). The dataset was downloaded and subsequently plotted using Claude Code. GISTEMP Team [10] and Lenssen et al. [11] explain that the thin lines in Figure 1 are granular annual values and thick lines correspond to the average (five-year LOWESS smooth), for temperature anomalies (with respect to the 1951–1980 baseline) as a mean over all land areas and the sea surface temperature anomalies (with respect to the 1951–1980 baseline). With this as background, the next section focuses on imputation of missing climate data.

Imputation of Missing Climate Data

This section investigates techniques for imputing spatiotemporal data, which support accurate analysis and help mitigate risks related to climate change and global warming (Mariappan et al. [12]). Chronologically continuous, accurate and gap-free climate data are hence needed. Replacing missing data with substituted values, known as imputation, is common in domains such as meteorology, climatology and even power systems. In climate change impact studies, weather data with good spatial and temporal granularity are needed for analysis of past climate to support forecasting of parameters such as future temperature (Shtiliyanova et al. [13]). Missing data can pose a challenge, and several published research studies have discussed both conventional and state-of-the-art techniques to impute missing data.

Figure 2 Visualization of air temperature anomalies from NASA GISS Surface Temperature Analysis (GISTEMP v4) (GISTEMP Team [10], Lenssen et al. [11]).

Climate data consist of parameters such as temperature, precipitation, wind speed and relative humidity, measured by a network of sensors. Sensor data can be prone to instrument or measurement errors (or sensor malfunction), leading to outliers or missing data. In this context, imputation is the process of replacing missing values in a dataset with reasonable estimated values so that the dataset is complete (Palarea-Albaladejo [14]).

Using point data requires quality assurance and control, which involves assessing the data for errors after collection. Understanding why data points are missing is important, since missing values can conceal meaningful information. Missing data are a common problem in climatological time series, as reliable statistical analysis is not possible with an incomplete dataset. While some algorithms such as random forest (RF) can handle missing data innately, it is still important to gauge the mechanism of missingness as explained by Teegavarapu [15].

Teegavarapu [15] further describes three mechanisms of missing data: missing at random (MAR), missing completely at random (MCAR) and missing not at random (MNAR). Data on a variable X are MAR if the probability of missing data on X does not depend on X itself after taking into consideration the remaining variables (e.g., Y or Z). Data on variable X are MCAR if the probability of missing data on X is not related to the value of X or any value of the other variables (e.g., Y or Z) in the data. Data are MNAR, also known as not missing at random (NMAR), if the probability of missing data on the variable X does depend on the value of X or any values of the other variables in the data.

Beyond understanding why data are missing, reliable spatiotemporal analysis and modeling require complete and sequential data. Data homogeneity should be investigated using the available metadata, and emphasis should be on correcting the outliers and anomalies if needed. Missing data can pose a significant issue. In this regard, gaps in the data can be filled with spatial or temporal imputation. The choice of the imputation technique may depend on the type of variable and the granularity of the data. Imputation thus completes the dataset but may alter some of its underlying characteristics.

Imputation replaces an incomplete record with an estimated value. The techniques for imputing missing data broadly include non-geostatistical, geostatistical and combined methods for spatial interpolation, as well as temporal interpolation, universal function approximation and data mining-assisted imputation approaches (Teegavarapu [15]).

Overview of Imputation Approaches

In spatiotemporal applications, gaps in the data can arise from human error, sensor malfunction or bad weather. Zahmatkesh and Zech [16] describe several approaches for handling the missing data. Removing incomplete records (dropping the null records) leaves the model with complete data, at the cost of losing some information or possibly biasing the results. Prediction-based methods estimate missing data by learning the mapping between past and future observations; they are especially applicable to time series and include ARIMA, Bayesian networks, feedforward neural networks and support vector regression (SVR). Interpolation-based approaches estimate values between the observations, assuming the data change smoothly; examples are linear, polynomial and spline interpolation. The authors [16] emphasize that these suit spatial or time series data that can be reasonably expected to vary smoothly, such as in climatology. Other approaches include statistical learning methods such as Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC), probabilistic principal component analysis (PPCA), hot-deck imputation and linear regression with the expectation-maximization (EM) algorithm.

While Lin et al. [17] mention that data quality issues such as measurement inconsistencies or missing data introduce uncertainty during model training and forecasting, Başakın et al. [18] note that the validity of classical imputation techniques may depend on the assumptions about the data distribution and the characteristics of the missing values in the data. They also mention that advanced imputation techniques may give more accurate results due to their ability to handle complex non-linear interactions in the data, suggesting deep learning-based approaches as well as the use of explainable artificial intelligence (such as SHAP and LIME) in imputation.

Building on this, Zainuddin et al. [19] mention that advances in data collection have increased the volume of time series data, which, due to many factors (including those mentioned above), may contain missing values and that failing to model and analyze these missing data may affect the results of the forecasting outcome. Conventional preprocessing methods make assumptions about the data generation process that are not always valid. The authors also review several approaches for handling missing data and emphasize that the characteristics of the given time series need to be carefully examined before an appropriate imputation technique is selected, as also noted by Başakın et al. [18].

Focusing on specific techniques, Alejo-Sanchez et al. [20] mention that averages (mean and median), simple and multiple linear regression, interpolation and principal component analysis (PCA) are traditional approaches for filling in the missing data, whereas artificial neural networks (ANN) and generative adversarial networks (GAN) can identify complex patterns when imputing missing climate data. They also note that imputation may simplify the prediction of climate phenomena such as temperature and precipitation, which are the climate variables most often studied.

Beyond climate data, a comparable challenge arises in traffic time series, where gaps can lead to analysis errors (Chan et al. [21]); tensor factorization and neural network models are used for imputation, with GANs, graph neural networks (GNNs) and PPCA among the popular techniques.

Statistical Imputation Methods

Statistical imputation methods are techniques that replace missing or null values with a statistical estimate. Iqbal and Mukherjee [22] handle missing values in raw air quality data using median imputation, where missing values are replaced with the median of that column or variable. This ensures data consistency while being less sensitive to outliers.

Similarly, Li et al. [23] point out that with deteriorating air quality and increasing pollution, accurate air quality prediction is becoming increasingly important, and air quality index (AQI) prediction is gaining prominence. While noting that data preprocessing is an essential stage that affects how accurate and reliable the predictions are, and that missing data points occur when equipment fails or outliers are removed, the authors use a statistical imputation approach by checking the hourly data for missing values: hours with no missing values are retained, and missing points are filled with the average of neighboring values, keeping the data continuous and valid.

On a similar theme, Shreyas et al. [24] point out that air quality forecasting is essential in developing countries such as India, where climate variability and industrialization may degrade air quality and cause health risks. As part of predicting the AQI, they apply data preprocessing techniques, including handling missing values and outliers. Although an initial check showed the dataset to be largely complete, a specific imputation strategy was used to achieve a complete dataset, and listwise deletion was performed after feature engineering so that the models were trained on real atmospheric conditions instead of synthesized patterns as a result of imputation.

In contrast to these single-value approaches, Hayati Rezvan et al. [25] describe multiple imputation as a way to deal with missing data, which, if not handled appropriately, can reduce statistical power and bias the results. Along these lines, Hui et al. [26] note that gaps in the data are a problem in long-term field measurements caused by equipment failures such as those from lightning strikes. Filling these gaps in the data is important for estimating the annual net ecosystem carbon exchange. The authors use multiple imputation, a Monte Carlo method that fills each gap with several simulated values. This leads to several complete datasets that share the observed values and differ only in the imputed ones, so standard statistical analysis may be applied.

In a different domain, Krishnamoorthy et al. [27] mention that tracking oceans and coastal areas is key to understanding the impacts of climate change and predicting undesirable outcomes. Satellite imagery-based remote sensing has transformed the collection of large volumes of environmental data with complex spatial and temporal patterns. However, missing data often occur in remote sensing databases due to cloud cover or sensing instrument failures. Simpler techniques such as mean imputation may not suffice, as they cannot account for correlation between parameters, so the authors use multivariate imputation by chained equations (MICE), which uses multiple regression models.

Zahmatkesh and Zech [16] also mention the use of MICE (Van Buuren [30]) on maximum temperature data for the Diourbel station in 1985, showing that the imputed values track the time series reasonably. They also describe how spatial imputation methods estimate a station’s missing data from observed data at neighboring stations. Spatial gaps may occur due to cloud cover, as also stated by Krishnamoorthy et al. [27], and kriging is a popular method for imputing them (Zahmatkesh and Zech [16]).

Like the previous authors, Costa et al. [28] use the MICE technique to impute missing data for climate variables (precipitation, temperature, humidity, atmospheric pressure, wind speed and insolation) from several stations in Brazil from 1961 to 2014, and apply quality control techniques for validation.

For rainfall networks, O’Sullivan and Kelly [29] note that modeling spatiotemporal precipitation data can be computationally expensive because the datasets are high-dimensional. Frequent missing entries can affect data quality, and filling them can help a rainfall network yield more accurate models. They propose a likelihood-based imputation approach to lower computational cost while also investigating DeepKriging, a deep learning approach to spatiotemporal modeling. The authors also compare these techniques with elastic-net chained equations (ENCE) and multiple imputation by chained equations with direct use of regularized regression (MICE DURR), quantifying the imputation accuracy.

Williams et al. [31], on the other hand, use Bayesian approaches (Bayesian compressive sensing) to impute environmental temperature data. These methods need data only from the target station and yet perform comparably to or better than a spatiotemporal model that also needs data from nearby stations.

Most climate studies require complete time series, so gaps in the data need to be imputed (Afrifa-Yamoah et al. [32]). In this regard, the authors evaluate several imputation approaches, including a structural time series model with Kalman smoothing, ARIMA with Kalman smoothing and multiple linear regression, using complete 12-month portions of hourly temperature, humidity and wind speed records from four coastal locations in Western Australia. Observations were treated as missing at random, and artificial gaps were created and evaluated with five-fold cross-validation, with the proportion of missingness set at 10%.

Spatial Interpolation and Geostatistical Methods

Raja et al. [33] describe geostatistical imputation techniques for filling missing first floor elevation (FFE) data when assessing how vulnerable the buildings are to floods, including kriging, which fills gaps based on how close the known points are and how they relate in space.

Shtiliyanova et al. [13] also use kriging, normally applied across space to estimate missing values using neighboring data in geostatistical datasets, to impute air temperature time series.

Xu et al. [34] mention that climate records often have gaps in some locations and periods (as noted earlier), and introduce P-BSHADE, evaluated on an annual temperature dataset for China from 1950 to 2000. The method weights the observations from surrounding stations to derive unbiased estimates of the missing data with minimum error variance. On a similar theme, since missing values in geographic information system (GIS) datasets may result in challenges for spatial analytics and decision making, Hamza and Salem [35] describe a set-based framework that represents each missing entry as a domain-consistent set and imputes it through statistical sampling, evaluation guided by clustering and refinement through local search.

Machine Learning Methods

Turning to machine learning, Shukur and Lee [36] note that wind speed data may have missing values due to malfunctioning sensing devices, and propose a hybrid technique combining an ANN with an auto-regressive model for imputation. Similarly, Körner et al. [37] suggest a gradient boosting-based machine learning technique for filling in the gaps due to missing or erroneous data in meteorological time series. The method is evaluated on extensive hourly records of temperature, wind speed and relative humidity from 1951 to 2015.

In a related direction, Zhang et al. [38] point out that clustering analysis is affected by datasets with partially missing values. In this regard, they propose a hybrid algorithm based on fuzzy clustering and particle swarm optimization (PSO) and treat the missing data as intervals. A neighbor interval reconstruction (NIR) method pre-classifies the data and then estimates the interval of a missing attribute from its nearest neighbors.

Returning to climate data, Diouf et al. [39] evaluate k-nearest neighbors (KNN), PPCA, MICE, missForest (Stekhoven and Bühlmann [40]) and imputeTS for imputation on a Senegalese meteorological dataset, finding missForest better for imputing temperature and imputeTS better for precipitation.

Along similar lines, Qaraghuli et al. [41] note that monitoring climate change depends on complete climate records but these datasets often have gaps that need to be imputed for data integrity. The authors evaluate six univariate and multivariate imputation techniques for temperature, precipitation and relative humidity by comparing root mean square error (RMSE) and Kling-Gupta Efficiency (KGE). The evaluation showed KNN was better at imputing precipitation, MICE was optimal at imputing temperature data and missForest for relative humidity.

While Qaraghuli et al. [41] focus on temperature, precipitation and relative humidity, Başakın et al. [42] compare various techniques for filling in the gaps in solar radiation data, a key variable for understanding climate dynamics. An XGBoost-differential evolution model built with measurements from neighboring stations performed better at gap sizes of 5%, 10% and 30%, while RF gave the highest accuracy at 20%, based on Nash-Sutcliffe Efficiency (NSE) and KGE.

For rainfall, Pinthong et al. [43] address missing rainfall data in climate research and examine machine learning approaches, including multiple linear regression, M5 model tree, RF, SVR, multilayer perceptron (MLP) and genetic programming, as well as spatial interpolation techniques, namely arithmetic average, inverse distance weighting (IDW), correlation coefficient weighted and normal ratio. They mention that selection of the neighboring stations may be required for spatial approaches, whereas machine learning techniques imputed the monthly rainfall data better, as quantified by NSE, Pearson’s correlation coefficient R and the overall index (OI).

At a finer time scale, Boukdire et al. [44] describe the need for sub-hourly datasets for accurate rainfall forecasting. Gaps in such data may be common due to malfunctioning sensors (as pointed out earlier), and filling them at finer granularity can be difficult. The authors compare approaches using machine learning (MLP and RF) and interpolation (ordinary kriging and IDW) to impute missing 10-minute rainfall data.

Outside climate data, Kim et al. [45] also point out that due to the increase in spatial data, concerns about missing observations that may lead to biased conclusions continue to grow. Recent studies suggest that machine learning techniques applied to environmental data may address these issues more efficiently than standard interpolation methods like IDW or kriging. To test their efficacy in socioeconomic applications, the authors compare neural networks, RF, IDW and kriging-based techniques to fill in the missing data.

Returning to environmental data, Hu et al. [46] examine missing data in air quality prediction caused by software and hardware malfunctions, and suggest filling in the gaps from the spatial and temporal structure of the data. Simple approaches include removing missing values (dropping the null values), which may leave some time steps unavailable, and statistical methods such as averaging over a two-hour or six-hour window. Machine learning methods, by contrast, learn the complex patterns of how air quality changes and use them to estimate the missing values. Other approaches referenced by the authors apply correlations across space and time to fill missing data from multiple views or use singular value thresholding (SVT) to reconstruct gaps in the air quality matrix.

Deep Learning MethodsFigure 3 Architecture of a simple MLP

Turning to neural networks, Coulibaly and Evora [47] note that accurately filling in missing daily precipitation values can be hard, and compare ANNs such as the MLP (shown in Figure 3) and its variants, time-lagged feedforward networks (TLFN), generalized radial basis function (RBF) networks and recurrent neural networks (RNN) and their variants (such as the time-delay recurrent neural network (TDRNN)), along with different optimization methods, for filling in gaps in total precipitation records and extreme temperature time series at daily granularity.

Moving beyond daily weather records, Eum and Yoo [48] propose a two-step, multi-scale neural network-based imputation method. A word2vec model (continuous bag-of-words) first converts daily time-activity sequences into a low-dimensional embedding, and a multi-scale residual convolutional neural network (CNN)-stacked long short-term memory (LSTM) network then learns multi-scale temporal patterns from past observations to predict missing values. The authors note that even as time-activity data become more widely available and spatially detailed, long gaps in such records still limit their use in human mobility research.

Similarly, Galdelli et al. [49] mention that spatial time series are fundamental to physical processes that need continuous monitoring and forecasting (e.g., object tracking). However, malfunctioning sensors or missing data may result in time series that cause classification bias. The authors propose a deep learning technique based on sequential bidirectional LSTM (BiLSTM) to fill in the missing trajectories in spatiotemporal data.

While Galdelli et al. [49] focus on trajectories, Boujoudar et al. [50] use an MLP, LSTM and CNN to accurately impute missing temperature data recorded over two years at a meteorological station at the Green Energy Park facility in Morocco. Measurements of precipitation, humidity, direct normal irradiation, global horizontal irradiation, and wind speed and direction were recorded every minute.

On a broader scale, Wang et al. [51] note that missing data are common in multivariate time series and make it difficult to perform accurate analysis. In recent years, deep learning models have been used for imputation because they can handle complex temporal dependencies and learn the distribution of the data. The authors review deep learning-based techniques for multivariate time series imputation and group them by imputation uncertainty and neural network architecture. They also list tools such as imputeTS and mice (R packages), and Impyute and Autoimpute (Python packages). Impyute offers simpler techniques such as a moving average window, whereas Autoimpute offers polynomial and spline interpolation. GluonTS (Python) provides naive methods such as dummy value and causal mean imputation, sktime (Python) supports machine learning-based imputation, and ImputeBench (R) (Richter et al. [52]) supports deep learning-based imputation. As future work, Wang et al. [51] suggest that LLMs are a promising direction for time series imputation research.

In a related review, Sun et al. [53] present a comprehensive evaluation of statistical, machine learning and deep learning models for imputation, suggesting that conventional methods such as MICE and missForest may outperform deep learning methods for tabular data with fewer than 30,000 samples, whereas advanced techniques such as generative adversarial imputation networks (GAIN) may perform well in the MCAR scenario. Variational auto-encoders (VAEs) are also discussed in Sun et al. [53]. Yoon et al. [54] introduce GAIN, which adapts GANs to missing data imputation: the generator observes some parts of a data vector, fills in the missing parts based on what is observed and produces a complete vector.

Turning to graph-based models, Shen et al. [55] propose the graph attention recurrent neural network (GARNN) for spatiotemporal traffic data imputation, which uses both temporal and spatial information. This matters because unexpected disruptions during data collection and storage leave gaps that can affect downstream tasks. In this technique, observations and missingness are modeled separately via LSTMs, treating missing information as distinct from observations. A decay mechanism models dependencies across time steps, and a graph attention network (GAT) learns the spatial correlations.

For time series imputation specifically, Jin et al. [56] discuss GNNs, which can capture complex spatial and temporal dependencies, whereas statistical methods such as mean imputation cannot adequately capture non-linear relationships. The authors group GNN-based imputation into deterministic and probabilistic methods: the former gives a best estimate for missing values, whereas the latter accounts for uncertainty by providing a distribution over possible values.

Other Techniques and Imputation Quality

Taking a wider view, Hameed and Ali [57] compare seventeen missing value imputation techniques, including some mentioned above: EM, median imputation, hot-deck (cold-deck) imputation, regression imputation, MICE, support vector machine (SVM) imputation, single center imputation from multiple chained equation (SICE) (Khan and Hoque [58]), which combines single and multiple imputation methods, non-parametric iterative imputation algorithms and MLPs. Whichever method is used, Shadbahr et al. [59] note that imputation quality must be considered, since it directly affects the downstream task that uses the imputed data.

Applications of Machine Learning in Climate Change and Vulnerability Analysis: Some Relevant Case Studies

Coastal regions face growing risk from climate change, rising sea levels and severe weather events such as hurricanes. These areas are often important to the economy, but they come under strain from both natural and human-related activity. To evaluate this vulnerability, Mondal et al. [60] describe a coastal vulnerability index, which draws on elevation, water depth, coastal shape, sea level rise, population density and other factors over a 30-year period, and assess coastal vulnerability using machine learning techniques including ANN, KNN, SVM and RF. The ANN model in Mondal et al. [60] consisted of an input layer, two hidden layers with 10 neurons each and an output layer; the hidden layers model complex non-linear relationships between the input features and coastal vulnerability. KNN assigned a vulnerability class based on the closest data points, SVM by finding the optimal hyperplane that best separates the classes, and RF, an ensemble that combines predictions from many decision trees, was chosen for its accuracy in regression and classification. The RF model (shown in Figure 4) captured how the variables interact and how important each feature is (Mondal et al. [60]). For evaluation, the data were stratified and split into training and test sets. A low RMSE showed that the predictions were reliable and that the model measured the coastal exposure well. The coastline was then grouped into exposure levels from very low to very high.

Figure 4 Flow diagram of the RF algorithm

On a similar theme, Forzieri et al. [61] use RF regression [66–67] to identify drivers of temporal autocorrelation when studying how climate change affects forest resilience. Vegetation and climate variables were used as predictors, the latter including monthly averaged precipitation, air temperature at 2 m and evapotranspiration deficit from the ERA5-Land reanalysis dataset.

Moving from forests to cities, Cano Pecharroman et al. [62] use gradient-boosted decision trees to rank which climate vulnerability indicators matter most in cities such as Buenos Aires, London, Seoul and Johannesburg. Gradient-boosted decision trees were chosen over RF because they offer higher accuracy and are trained sequentially, rather than independently, to reduce errors. Taking a geospatial view, Sultana et al. [63] point out that combining remote sensing and GIS can help turn geospatial data into useful knowledge. Remote sensing records the Earth’s surface using sensors on satellites, whereas GIS is software for storing, analyzing and mapping location-based data. Analytics plays a vital role in Earth resource management, and Sultana et al. [63] assess drought vulnerability (drought forecasting) by modeling precipitation and temperature with an ANN. Turning to agriculture, Jian et al. [64] examine how global warming affects rice yield by studying exposure to high temperature and quantifying the uncertainty through Monte Carlo simulations.

Key Takeaways

Among the imputation techniques reviewed, MICE, missForest and kriging are commonly applied to fill gaps in geospatial data, which will form the basis for accurate analysis in the context of climate change. Deep learning-based techniques have also been discussed as approaches to impute missing data, with LLMs noted as a direction for future research.

items.title: Peter Thiel says Apple has done 'nothing new' after Steve Jobs
items.summary: Peter Thiel said that after Steve Jobs died in 2011, Apple hasn't innovated. Justin Sullivan/Getty Images Peter Thiel said Apple hasn't innovated since the iPhone. Thiel said Tim Cook hasn't taken the company in new directions. The billionaire venture capitalist said eccentric CEOs like Elon Musk "are way better for society." Peter Thiel, evidently, isn't a fan of the iPhone Duo . In fact, the billionaire PayPal cofounder and tech investor said he hasn't been very impressed with much of anything that Apple has done since its eccentric founder, Steve Jobs, died of cancer in 2011. "In my telling, it did nothing new after Jobs," Thiel said of the iPhone maker in a September interview with author Walter Isaacson for the "Builder's Podcast," which was released on Thursday. "It turned out, yeah, the mobile phone was this giant invention — there was not that much more to do," he said. "Then it was just scaling and branding and building it out over 15 years or whatever." Indeed, Apple has faced criticism for failing to innovate beyond the mobile phone and tablet, especially in the age of AI, where its "Siri" product is not as advanced as rivals from ChatGPT or Anthropic. Jobs unveiled the first iPhone back in 2007 at a conference in San Francisco. Nearly 20 years later, Apple released the 18th iteration this week, with one slight caveat: This one folds. That said, MacBooks are the de facto laptops for many an AI-nerd and normie alike. iPhones are ubiquitous, and the sleek AirPods design took hold when they were released in 2016. Though Thiel told Maureen Dowd of The New York Times in 2017 that Apple's era was over, the company's stock price has grown steadily since then. Thiel didn't pooh-pooh Apple entirely. He called it a "pure, well-run value stock," but lamented what he described as the loss of vision after Jobs' death. "I would still say somehow Elon or Steve Jobs are way better for society than Tim Cook," he said. Apple didn't immediately respond to a request for comment sent on Saturday. Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: The Two AI Cutout Failures No Setting Can Fix After the Shoot
items.summary: Every AI background remover is sold as a fix-it-in-post button, and for two very common failure modes that promise is exactly backwards. One of them can be largely repaired after the fact with three commands. The other cannot be repaired at all — no tolerance slider, no better model, no second attempt — because the information the tool needs was never in the file. Knowing which failure you have, before you spend an evening re-running the same clip, is worth more than any tool switch. Both cases here were measured on a real test clip in October 2026, with the numbers read back from rendered frames rather than eyeballed. Case one: the underexposed clip (repairable) Dim footage kills cutouts for a reason that has nothing to do with AI. Brightness in 8-bit video is stored on a non-linear curve with the fewest distinguishable codes reserved for the dark end — roughly luma 0 through 16. Underexpose a shot and you are not making the subject harder to see; you are deleting the code values the edge is made of. A segmentation model can only trace a boundary that exists in the data. The measurement makes this concrete. On a 640x360 H.264 test clip, a 140x120 textured patch at normal exposure held 150 distinct luma values, range 0 to 185, mean 89.8, with nothing below 16. After a modest dim — a third of a stop equivalent, applied as an ffmpeg eq filter — the same patch held 63 distinct values with a mean of 8.1, and 81% of its pixels sat below luma 16. Frame-wide, 48% of pixels fell into that crushed band. Nothing about the model changed between those two numbers. The information it needs to segment simply stopped being stored. The repair works because most of the signal is still there, just compressed. Brightening the dimmed patch back up returns the mean to 78.5 and clears the crushed band entirely — but only 100 of the original 150 distinct levels come back, and the range tops out at 156 instead of 185. That is banding by definition: smooth gradation redistributed into a few wide steps. Against a plain wall it is invisible. Against a textured background it is the difference between a matte that tracks the subject and one that crawls. Order of operations matters more than the filters themselves. Grain is not the enemy here — adding heavy grain to the normal-exposure clip left the patch with 147 distinct levels instead of 150, and raised frame-to-frame luma change from 2.19 to 2.70, while the dim alone dropped that temporal figure to 1.69. Darkness removes signal; grain adds it. So denoise first, then lift: on a dim, grainy copy, lifting alone left the temporal figure at 2.51, denoising first brought it to 1.93 at the same brightness. The one-command check before you start: run a luma mask at 16 through signalstats and read the printed average. Divide by 255 and you have the share of pixels no repair can ever recover — that number is the ceiling on the whole salvage. Case two: the clashing colors (not repairable) A color keyer — and the segmenter underneath most one-click removers — works from measurable distance between two colors. Tolerance is the only dial, and it has enormous headroom when the colors are actually far apart: keying a red background with a blue subject in frame, every similarity setting from 0.005 to 0.30 removed the background completely while the subject stayed at full opacity. Slide the subject toward the background color and that window closes fast. With a subject only a few percent redder than the background, the same setting that keys the background drops the subject's opacity to 216 out of 255, then 177, then 126, then 24, gone by 0.15. Nudge the subject one step closer — a red barely distinguishable from the background — and at the lowest tolerance that does anything, the subject sits at 100 while the background is still at 5. There is no setting between those states. A distance threshold cannot separate things that are not distant. AI segmentation fails here for a related reason: with color gone as a cue, it leans on shape and motion, which is why the damage shows up as missing arms and chunks of background riding along on the subject. The failure reports as a question rather than a bug — footage of red models against a red painted wall is the classic. The fix lives entirely before the shoot: change the light, change the wardrobe, or hang a screen. Post has no dial for this one. Budgeting for rotoscope is the honest fallback, and it is why the comparison always comes back to lighting rather than software. One nuance saves part of this case: dimming hurts luma far more than chroma. On a saturated area of the same test clip, dropping brightness by 0.35 left the chroma planes untouched — U average 90, V average 240, before and after. So a dim green screen is not the same problem as a dim room: the separation still exists, only darker, and a key will still find it. The home-studio version that does break is spill and uneven lighting, not darkness itself. Evenly lit but dim: key it. Patchy: no tolerance saves it. The two-minute triage Before re-running anything: measure the crushed-pixel share; if it is high, denoise, lift, and retry — that failure is on your side. If colors are close, stop re-rolling and change the inputs; that failure is not. And if the clip survives all of this but you need it smaller afterward, a browser-based video compressor runs the same measured approach locally in a tab. Disclosure: that last link is to this site's own tool page, not an affiliate link.

items.title: From Ancient Epigraphy to 3D Proteins: Building Plugins, Skills & MCP Sidecars in Google Antigravity
items.summary:
What happens when you ask an AI coding agent to score a non-coding human genomic variant with AlphaGenome , map a missense mutation onto an AlphaFold 3D protein structure , screen ChEMBL for nanomolar small-molecule inhibitors , or restore a damaged 2,000-year-old Roman inscription using Google DeepMind's Aeneas model ? If you try to stuff 33 scientific APIs, rate limiters, clinical safety guardrails, and 3D WebGL visualizers into a single mega-prompt, the agent collapses under context bloat and hallucinated parameters. Google Antigravity solves this at the runtime level with its Plugin & Customization Architecture —combining Progressive-Disclosure Skills ( SKILL.md ) , Always-On Rules ( AGENTS.md ) , Lifecycle Hooks ( hooks.json ) , Zero-Leak Credential Protocols , and Dual-Process 3D MCP Sidecars ( mcp_config.json + sidecar.json ) . Instead of just reading the docs, I reverse-engineered the newly released Google Antigravity Science Plugin ( v1.3.1 ) and built the open-source Antigravity Science Plugin Cookbook & Interactive 3D Studio —complete with a live browser-based 3D Biomolecular & Variant WebGL Sandbox , a zero-dependency PEP 723 3D protein + PAE generator , and a production bio-structural-qc custom plugin . Try the Live 3D Biomolecular & MCP Sidecar Studio in Your Browser Launch the Interactive 3D Biomolecular & Variant WebGL Studio ( index.html ) Explore 3D C-alpha backbones & non-covalent contact networks for **TP53 ( AF-P04637 ) , **Crambin ( 1CRN ) , and **EGFR Kinase + Gefitinib ( CHEMBL203 ) . Five Production Engineering Patterns Inside the Science Plugin While inspecting the source files across all 33 skills, five engineering patterns stood out that every agent builder should steal. Pattern 1: Always-On Behavioral Routing via rules/AGENTS.md When an agent has access to Matplotlib, headless PyMOL, and an interactive 3D Mol* sidecar, how do you guarantee it prioritizes the interactive 3D viewer and never forgets to surface the clickable UI pill? You place a compact, always-on rule in rules/AGENTS.md : # Science Visualization Priority Rules For any science visualization task, **prefer the interactive sidecar viewers** (e.g. Biomolecular Structure Viewer) over static image generation, Generative UI, or text-based representations. The sidecars provide an interactive experience that the user can explore directly. ## Key Rules - Only fall back to other visualization skills (e.g. `pymol` ) when no viewer sidecar can do what the user needs. - **Always surface a sidecar link.** Whenever the agent loads or updates a visualization in a sidecar (e.g. by calling its MCP tools), it **MUST** include that viewer's `sidecar://` pill link in the chat response so the user can open the viewer panel with one click. Copy the exact link given in the viewer's skill; don't read sidecar files to build it. Pattern 2: Zero-Pollution Python Micro-Environments ( uv + PEP 723 + Sliding-Window PAE Math) Running global pip install inside a user's repository breaks virtual environments. Instead, every Science skill uses uv run with PEP 723 inline script metadata ( # /// script ) and enforces rate limits and mathematical heuristics inside deterministic Python scripts. For example, in skills/alphafold_database_fetch_and_analyze/scripts/ : fetch_structure.py uses polite-http with a hard qps=1.0 rate limit ( CLIENT = http_client.HttpClient("https://alphafold.ebi.ac.uk", qps=1.0) ) and automatically falls back to the longest isoform for massive proteins ( > 2,700 amino acids like Dystrophin). analyze_pae.py forbids the LLM from guessing domain boundaries by running a 20-residue sliding-window Predicted Aligned Error (PAE) clustering algorithm ( distance_cutoff=7.0 Å , min_domain_size=40 , merge_cutoff=15.0 Å ): """ Analyzes Predicted Aligned Error (PAE) and detects domain boundaries. """ # /// script # requires-python = ">=3.10" # dependencies = [] # /// def find_sub_domains ( pae_matrix , distance_cutoff = 7.0 , min_domain_size = 40 ): """ Identifies structurally independent sub-domains based on the PAE matrix. """ n_res = len ( pae_matrix ) domains , current_domain = [], [] for i in range ( n_res ): if not current_domain : current_domain . append ( i ) continue window_size = min ( 20 , len ( current_domain )) recent_res = current_domain [ - window_size :] pae_sum = sum ( pae_matrix [ r ][ i ] + pae_matrix [ i ][ r ] for r in recent_res ) avg_pae = pae_sum / ( 2.0 * window_size ) if avg_pae < distance_cutoff : current_domain . append ( i ) else : if len ( current_domain ) >= min_domain_size : domains . append ( current_domain ) current_domain = [ i ] if len ( current_domain ) >= min_domain_size : domains . append ( current_domain ) return [[ comp [ 0 ] + 1 , comp [ - 1 ] + 1 ] for comp in domains ] Pattern 3: The Zero-Leak Credential Protocol ( skills/credentials/SKILL.md ) Genomic and literature APIs like AlphaGenome ( ALPHAGENOME_API_KEY ) require secret keys. If an agent asks a user to paste their API key into the chat—or runs cat ~/.env —that secret is permanently recorded in the conversation transcript and model context. The credentials skill solves this with a strict Zero-Leak Protocol : Silent Exit-Code Verification: The agent checks whether the variable exists in ~/.env using grep -sq (quiet + suppress errors), reading only the 0 vs. non-zero exit code: grep -sq "^ALPHAGENOME_API_KEY=" ~/.env Hidden Terminal Prompting ( read -s ): If missing, the agent stops immediately and outputs a terminal command for the user to run locally where keystrokes are hidden ( read -s ): printf "Enter ALPHAGENOME_API_KEY (typing hidden): " && read -s val && echo && echo "ALPHAGENOME_API_KEY= $val " >> " $HOME /.env" && echo "Saved." Internal dotenv Ingestion: Helper scripts load ~/.env internally via dotenv , so the key never appears in command-line flags or stdout. It pairs an MCP Server ( dist/mcp_entry.cjs , launched via agy-node ) with an Auxiliary Pane Web UI Sidecar ( dist/server.cjs + ui.html , powered by PDBe Mol* v3.12.0 and Lit v3.1.2 ): sequenceDiagram } Pattern 5: Domain-Specific Guardrails — From Clinical Genetics ( AlphaGenome ) to Ancient Epigraphy ( Aeneas & Ithaca ) Two of the most fascinating skills in the bundle demonstrate how SKILL.md enforces domain-specific scientific rigor: alphagenome-variant-impact-score (Strict Molecular Framing + Context-Overflow Protection): Clinical Safety Gate: Explicitly forbids extrapolating high AlphaGenome Variant Impact (AVI) scores into clinical diagnoses or patient prognosis, restricting outputs to molecular mechanisms (splicing disruption, chromatin accessibility, TF binding, or GENCODE v46 transcript coordinates). Stdout Overflow Guard: Warns the agent that --include_track_info --format json emits ~3.9 KB per variant, requiring direct file redirection ( -o query_results.json ) whenever querying > 3 variants so stdout never floods the context window. predictingthepast (Ancient Latin & Greek Epigraphy with DeepMind's Aeneas & Ithaca): Restores damaged ancient inscriptions, attributes geographical province + chronological date ranges, and finds parallel inscriptions using special gap syntax ( ? for a single missing character, # for an unknown-length damaged gap): uv run scripts/preprocess.py --language = latin --input = "imp caesar divi f ???????? cos xi" Enforces a Self-Contained Epigraphy Rule : forbids the agent from using web search to "cheat" or override the neural restoration probabilities returned by Aeneas/Ithaca. 4. Five End-to-End Multi-Skill Use Cases Across the 33 Science Skills Because all 33 skills share the conversation's artifact directory, Antigravity can chain multiple domain-specific CLI scripts and MCP sidecars in a single research session. I included a runnable benchmark suite in examples/multi_domain_science_use_cases.py ( uv run examples/multi_domain_science_use_cases.py ) that executes and scores all five multi-skill pipelines below: Use Case 1: Precision Oncology & 3D Pocket Triage ( ClinVar → gnomAD → AlphaFold → ChEMBL → 3D Mol* Sidecar ) Scenario: A translational oncology team wants to evaluate an EGFR L858R ( rs121434568 , chr7:55191822:T>G ) driver mutation, verify gene loss-of-function constraint, inspect 3D active-site confidence, rank nanomolar kinase inhibitors, and highlight the pocket in 3D. # 1. Check allele rarity & gene constraint (pLI / LOEUF) in gnomAD uv run ~/.gemini/config/plugins/science/skills/gnomad_database/scripts/get_gene_constraint.py \ --gene EGFR --output ./artifacts/egfr_constraint.json # 2. Fetch AlphaFold 3D structure (P00533) & audit pLDDT + PAE domains uv run ~/.gemini/config/plugins/science/skills/alphafold_database_fetch_and_analyze/scripts/fetch_structure.py \ P00533 -o ./artifacts/P00533/ uv run ~/.gemini/config/plugins/science/skills/alphafold_database_fetch_and_analyze/scripts/analyze_pae.py \ ./artifacts/P00533/AF-P00533-F1-predicted_aligned_error_v6.json # 3. Screen ChEMBL for EGFR (CHEMBL203) bioactivities & download 3D SDF ligands uv run ~/.gemini/config/plugins/science/skills/chembl_database/scripts/chembl_api.py \ activity --search "EGFR" --limit 10 --output ./artifacts/egfr_chembl_ic50.json uv run ~/.gemini/config/plugins/science/skills/chembl_database/scripts/chembl_api.py \ molecule --id CHEMBL939 --dl_format sdf --output ./artifacts/gefitinib.sdf Finally, the agent invokes science_biomolecular_structure_viewer_mcp ( load_structure + highlight_region(chain="A", start_residue=855, end_residue=862, color="#FF1744") ) and surfaces [Biomolecular Structure Viewer](sidecar://science/biomolecular_structure_viewer/ui.html) : Use Case 2: Non-Coding GWAS Enhancer Variant Triage ( AlphaGenome → UCSC phyloP → ENCODE cCRE → JASPAR → GTEx ) Scenario: Over 90% of GWAS risk loci fall in non-coding DNA. Suppose you are investigating chr1:109274968:G>T ( rs12740374 at the SORT1 1p13 locus) and want to know how it alters gene regulation across human tissues without hallucinating clinical diagnoses: # 1. Score variant impact across 18 biological modalities + GENCODE v46 coordinates uv run ~/.gemini/config/plugins/science/skills/alphagenome_variant_impact_score/scripts/alphagenome_atlas_avi.py \ query "chr1:109274968:G>T" --include_track_info --format json -o ./artifacts/sort1_avi.json # 2. Check 100-vertebrate evolutionary constraint (phyloP100way & phastCons100way) uv run ~/.gemini/config/plugins/science/skills/ucsc_conservation_and_tfbs/scripts/get_conservation.py \ --coordinates "chr1:109274968" --output ./artifacts/sort1_phylop.json # 3. Fetch Transcription Factor Position Weight Matrices (PWMs) from JASPAR (CEBPA) uv run ~/.gemini/config/plugins/science/skills/jaspar_database/scripts/jaspar_cli.py \ search --query "CEBPA" --output ./artifacts/cebpa_jaspar.json Engineering Guardrail in Action: The alphagenome-variant-impact-score skill enforces that --include_track_info outputs ( ~3.9 KB/variant ) are redirected via -o and framed strictly in terms of molecular mechanisms ( CEBPA binding site creation + liver RNA-seq eQTL shift): Use Case 3: Dark-Proteome Enzyme Discovery ( AlphaFold → Foldseek 3D Search → InterPro → Clustal Omega MSA → Headless PyMOL ) Scenario: A protein engineering group wants to discover novel thermostable plastic-degrading PETase homologs hidden in environmental metagenomes where sequence identity is below 25% (the "twilight zone" where BLAST fails, but 3D fold geometry is conserved): # 1. Search the 3D coordinate file against Foldseek's metagenomic & AlphaFold databases uv run ~/.gemini/config/plugins/science/skills/foldseek_structural_search/scripts/search.py \ ./artifacts/PETase_AF.cif \ --databases afdb50,mgnify_esm30,pdb100,cath50 \ -o ./artifacts/petase_foldseek.json > ./artifacts/petase_foldseek_summary.md # 2. Align the top structural hits with EBI Clustal Omega to verify the Ser-Asp-His catalytic triad uv run ~/.gemini/config/plugins/science/skills/protein_sequence_msa/scripts/clustalo.py \ --input ./artifacts/petase_homologs.fasta --output ./artifacts/petase_msa.aln Engineering Guardrail in Action: Look at foldseek-structural-search/SKILL.md : Strict Input Gate: If the user only gives a gene name or sequence without a .pdb / .cif file, the skill halts immediately and instructs the agent to fetch the 3D structure first. Database Allowlist: Enforces validation against the exact 9 supported Foldseek databases ( afdb50 , afdb-swissprot , pdb100 , BFVD , mgnify_esm30 , cath50 , gmgcl_id , bfmd , afdb-proteome ). Headless OSMesa PyMOL Superposition ( pymol skill): When generating static publication figures alongside .pse session files, the pymol skill runs headless via PYOPENGL_PLATFORM=osmesa and automatically checks cmd.count_atoms("name CA") == cmd.count_atoms("all") so C-alpha-only traces still render as smooth cartoons! Use Case 4: Clinical Trial Intelligence & Pharmacovigilance Audit ( OpenTargets → ClinicalTrials.gov → openFDA → OpenAlex ) Scenario: A clinical data science team wants to map all recruiting Phase 3 trials for a target indication, inspect inclusion/exclusion criteria without overflowing the LLM context window, and audit real-world post-market adverse events across 28 FDA end

What happens when you ask an AI coding agent to score a non-coding human genomic variant with AlphaGenome, map a missense mutation onto an AlphaFold 3D protein structure, screen ChEMBL for nanomolar small-molecule inhibitors, or restore a damaged 2,000-year-old Roman inscription using Google DeepMind's Aeneas model?

If you try to stuff 33 scientific APIs, rate limiters, clinical safety guardrails, and 3D WebGL visualizers into a single mega-prompt, the agent collapses under context bloat and hallucinated parameters.

Google Antigravity solves this at the runtime level with its Plugin & Customization Architecture—combining Progressive-Disclosure Skills (SKILL.md), Always-On Rules (AGENTS.md), Lifecycle Hooks (hooks.json), Zero-Leak Credential Protocols, and Dual-Process 3D MCP Sidecars (mcp_config.json + sidecar.json).

Instead of just reading the docs, I reverse-engineered the newly released Google Antigravity Science Plugin (v1.3.1) and built the open-source Antigravity Science Plugin Cookbook & Interactive 3D Studio—complete with a live browser-based 3D Biomolecular & Variant WebGL Sandbox, a zero-dependency PEP 723 3D protein + PAE generator, and a production bio-structural-qc custom plugin.

Pattern 2: Zero-Pollution Python Micro-Environments (uv + PEP 723 + Sliding-Window PAE Math)

Running global pip install inside a user's repository breaks virtual environments. Instead, every Science skill uses uv run with PEP 723 inline script metadata (# /// script) and enforces rate limits and mathematical heuristics inside deterministic Python scripts.

For example, in skills/alphafold_database_fetch_and_analyze/scripts/:

  • fetch_structure.py uses polite-http with a hard qps=1.0 rate limit (CLIENT = http_client.HttpClient("https://alphafold.ebi.ac.uk", qps=1.0)) and automatically falls back to the longest isoform for massive proteins (> 2,700 amino acids like Dystrophin).
  • analyze_pae.py forbids the LLM from guessing domain boundaries by running a 20-residue sliding-window Predicted Aligned Error (PAE) clustering algorithm (distance_cutoff=7.0 Å, min_domain_size=40, merge_cutoff=15.0 Å): 
"""Analyzes Predicted Aligned Error (PAE) and detects domain boundaries."""

# /// script
# requires-python = ">=3.10"
# dependencies = []
# ///

def find_sub_domains(pae_matrix, distance_cutoff=7.0, min_domain_size=40):
    """Identifies structurally independent sub-domains based on the PAE matrix."""
    n_res = len(pae_matrix)
    domains, current_domain = [], []

    for i in range(n_res):
        if not current_domain:
            current_domain.append(i)
            continue

        window_size = min(20, len(current_domain))
        recent_res = current_domain[-window_size:]
        pae_sum = sum(pae_matrix[r][i] + pae_matrix[i][r] for r in recent_res)
        avg_pae = pae_sum / (2.0 * window_size)

        if avg_pae < distance_cutoff:
            current_domain.append(i)
        else:
            if len(current_domain) >= min_domain_size:
                domains.append(current_domain)
            current_domain = [i]

    if len(current_domain) >= min_domain_size:
        domains.append(current_domain)
    return [[comp[0] + 1, comp[-1] + 1] for comp in domains]
Pattern 3: The Zero-Leak Credential Protocol (skills/credentials/SKILL.md)

Genomic and literature APIs like AlphaGenome (ALPHAGENOME_API_KEY) require secret keys. If an agent asks a user to paste their API key into the chat—or runs cat ~/.env—that secret is permanently recorded in the conversation transcript and model context.

The credentials skill solves this with a strict Zero-Leak Protocol:

  1. Silent Exit-Code Verification: The agent checks whether the variable exists in ~/.env using grep -sq (quiet + suppress errors), reading only the 0 vs. non-zero exit code: 
   grep -sq "^ALPHAGENOME_API_KEY=" ~/.env
  1. Hidden Terminal Prompting (read -s): If missing, the agent stops immediately and outputs a terminal command for the user to run locally where keystrokes are hidden (read -s): 
   printf "Enter ALPHAGENOME_API_KEY (typing hidden): " && read -s val && echo && echo "ALPHAGENOME_API_KEY=$val" >> "$HOME/.env" && echo "Saved."
  1. Internal dotenv Ingestion: Helper scripts load ~/.env internally via dotenv, so the key never appears in command-line flags or stdout.

Whenever a workflow downloads or modifies a 3D coordinate file (`.pdb`, `.cif`, or `.mmcif`) for downstream structural analysis, homology search, or variant mapping:

2. The Zero-Dependency PEP 723 Structure Auditor (audit_structure.py) 
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Audits PDB and mmCIF coordinate files for chain completeness and B-factor/pLDDT distribution."""

# /// script
# requires-python = ">=3.10"
# dependencies = []
# ///

import argparse, json, statistics
from pathlib import Path

def parse_ca_bfactors(filepath: Path) -> dict:
    chains: dict[str, list[tuple[int, float]]] = {}
    ext = filepath.suffix.lower()
    with filepath.open("r", encoding="utf-8", errors="replace") as f:
        for line in f:
            if ext == ".pdb" and line.startswith("ATOM  ") and line[12:16].strip() == "CA":
                chain_id = line[21].strip() or "A"
                chains.setdefault(chain_id, []).append((int(line[22:26]), float(line[60:66])))
            elif ext in {".cif", ".mmcif"} and line.startswith("ATOM "):
                parts = line.split()
                if len(parts) >= 15 and parts[3] == "CA":
                    chains.setdefault(parts[6], []).append((int(parts[8]), float(parts[14])))
    return chains

uv run plugins/genomics-variant-mcp/mcp/variant_mcp_server.py --self-test
C. Starter Plugin #3: plugins/epigraphy-citation-kit (Ancient Epigraphy Validator + PreToolUse Hook)

The third starter plugin, plugins/epigraphy-citation-kit, pairs a PreToolUse lifecycle hook (hooks.json) with a PEP 723 Leiden bracket normalizer (validate_epigraphy.py) that automatically converts standard Leiden epigraphic brackets ([---] and [...]) into DeepMind Aeneas/Ithaca # and ? tokens, checks for forbidden ## or ?# sequences, and pads short inscriptions to the 25-character minimum:

uv run plugins/epigraphy-citation-kit/skills/epigraphy-gap-validator/scripts/validate_epigraphy.py \
  --text "IMP CAESAR DIVI F [---] COS [...] III" --language latin
7. Bonus: Distilling Live Chat Sessions into Skills & Language Server RPC Debugging A. Automatic Skill Distillation with workflow-skill-creator

Don't want to write SKILL.md files from scratch? After completing any multi-step scientific workflow in chat, trigger the Science plugin's workflow-skill-creator skill:

"Package the workflow we just ran into a reusable skill."

It walks you through a mandatory 4-round brainstorming protocol (confirming inputs/outputs, error-handling rigidity, composing existing Science skills without duplicating code, and generating a CLI helper script) before writing the new skill to ~/.gemini/config/skills//.

B. Querying & Toggling Plugins via the Language Server Connect RPC

Antigravity manages plugins live through its local Connect RPC server (ANTIGRAVITY_LS_ADDRESS).

  • Golden Rule #1: Always key mutations on the install directory (dir), never plugin.json's name.
  • Golden Rule #2: Never read GetAllPlugins unfiltered—it inlines the full text of every SKILL.md across all installed plugins! Pipe it through jq (see examples/inspect_plugins_rpc.sh): 
: "${ANTIGRAVITY_LS_ADDRESS:=localhost:5387}"
curl -sS -X POST \
  "http://${ANTIGRAVITY_LS_ADDRESS}/exa.language_server_pb.LanguageServerService/GetAllPlugins" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "x-codeium-csrf-token: ${ANTIGRAVITY_CSRF_TOKEN}" \
  -d '{}' | jq '[.plugins[] | {
    name,
    dir: (.path | split("/") | last),
    disabled: (.disabled // false),
    skills: (.skills | length),
    mcp: [.mcpServers[]?.name]
  }]'
C. Fixing Windows unlinkat Sidecar Locks During Plugin Upgrades

If you upgrade or reinstall a plugin with an active sidecar ("restart_policy": "always") on Windows and hit:

Failed to install marketplace customization "science": failed to remove existing plugin:
unlinkat ...\science\sidecars\biomolecular_structure_viewer: The process cannot access the file because it is being used by another process.

Simply close the sidecar pane, quit Antigravity completely (checking the system tray so the directory handle is released), run Remove-Item -Recurse -Force "$HOME\.gemini\config\plugins\science" in PowerShell, and click Install in the Marketplace tab.

What Custom Plugin Are You Building First?
  • Play with the Live 3D Biomolecular & Variant WebGL Studio
  • Star & Fork the Cookbook Repository on GitHub (RobinaMirbahar/antigravity-science-plugin-cookbook)

Let me know in the comments what domain you're packaging into an Antigravity plugin next—whether it's 3D structural biology, genomic variant scoring, ancient epigraphy, or autonomous cloud SRE!

Slothly - The Overnight Agent That Works While You Sleep

Theme: Slow and Steady (International Sloth Day, Oct 20)

Most AI agents are built to move fast — a firehose of notifications, always-on cloud calls, per-token billing, data leaving your device. This week, I built the sloth edition.

What I built

Slothly is a fully local, overnight AI agent.

  • You drop a voice note or written note into inbox/ before bed
  • Overnight, Slothly transcribes (with faster-whisper) and summarizes (with llama3.2 via Ollama) into a crisp two-line morning report
  • It writes the report to reports/YYYY-MM-DD.md, archives the source file, and even adds a calming sloth-themed haiku
  • Runs on a schedule via Windows Task Scheduler
The Stack (All Open Source)
  • Agent harness: OpenAI Agents SDK (open source)
  • LLM inference: Ollama + open-weight model llama3.2
  • Transcription: faster-whisper (open source)
  • Runtime: 100% local, CPU-only
Why open innovation matters
  • Runs on a laptop with no internet — After the one-time model download, everything runs locally. No cloud APIs required.
  • Keeps data off servers you don't control — Notes, voice memos, and summaries never leave your device.
  • Fine-tune, swap models, or change agent behavior — Being able to swap open-weight models or tweak the agent logic is a first-class feature, not a locked-down API.
  • Cost nothing to run — Local inference means zero API spend.
Where the open approach worked better than a closed one

A closed stack would have meant cloud transcription + cloud LLM + API keys + per-run cost + third-party data flow. With Slothly, the entire loop — transcribe, summarize, report — runs offline, on-device, for free. The open pieces made this simple lazy automation possible in a way that would be impractical (and expensive) with closed APIs.

The Sloth Philosophy

The agent moves slow and steady, conserves energy, and does the work so you don't have to. You sleep; the agent works. You wake to a two-line report — and maybe a sloth haiku.

Repo: https://github.com/MAXxDEVIL/Slothly

items.title: Protocol Upgrade Compatibility Review: Lido
items.summary: Protocol Upgrade Compatibility Review: Lido Target Protocol : Lido (TVL: $22447.3M) Lido – Protocol Upgrade Compatibility Review Prepared by: Senior DeFi Security Researcher Date: 24 Oct 2026 1. Executive Summary Lido Finance is the market‑leading liquid‑staking solution on Ethereum and several L2s, managing ≈ $22.4 B in total value locked (TVL). Its core architecture consists of a set of upgradeable proxy contracts (BeaconProxy & Transparent Proxy) that mediate interactions between stakers, node operators, and the Lido DAO. The protocol’s upgrade path is governed by the Lido DAO (via the LDO token) and a multi‑sig treasury (Lido Multisig). Our Upgrade Compatibility Review focuses on the ability of the system to safely evolve (new features, bug‑fixes, parameter changes) without compromising existing state, user funds, or the economic guarantees of the staking pool. Key Findings Area Overall Assessment Critical Issues Comments Proxy & Storage Layout Generally sound – uses OpenZeppelin’s UUPS and BeaconProxy patterns with well‑documented storage slots. 1️⃣ Potential storage‑slot collision when adding new state variables to StakingRouter and StETH contracts without explicit gap padding. The existing gaps (e.g., uint256[50] private __gap; ) are insufficient for the planned expansion roadmap (estimated > 70 new variables). Governance & Upgrade Execution DAO‑centric, multi‑sig enforced, with a timelock (48 h) on proposals. 2️⃣ Insufficient timelock for emergency upgrades – the same 48 h delay applies to both benign and critical patches, exposing the protocol to prolonged oracle or validator attacks. A separate “emergency” timelock (e.g., 6 h) is recommended. Upgrade Validation & Testing CI pipeline includes Foundry + Hardhat, with fuzzing on core functions. 3️⃣ Lack of automated storage‑layout diff checks in CI; manual review is required for each PR. This increases human error risk. Cross‑Chain & L2 Deployments Beacon proxies deployed on Arbitrum, Optimism, Base, and zkSync. 4️⃣ Inconsistent implementation of initialize across L2s – some L2 proxies skip the initializeV2 step, leading to uninitialized storage that can be hijacked. Upgrade Governance Transparency Public proposal repository, but upgrade artefacts (bytecode hashes) are not published on‑chain. 5️⃣ Missing on‑chain bytecode hash verification – users cannot independently verify that the implementation deployed matches the DAO‑approved code. Overall, Lido’s upgrade framework is robust but not fully hardened against sophisticated upgrade‑related attacks. The most pressing gaps are storage‑layout safety, emergency upgrade latency, and verification of on‑chain bytecode. 2. Identified Attack Vectors # Vector Description Potential Impact Exploitability 1 Storage‑Slot Collision on Future Upgrades Adding new state variables without preserving the reserved gap can overwrite existing storage (e.g., totalSupply , paused ). Theft of stETH, loss of staking rewards, protocol freeze. Medium – requires a malicious upgrade proposal accepted by DAO. 2 Timelock Abuse for Governance Capture An attacker who gains > 50 % of LDO can push a malicious upgrade through the standard 48 h timelock, then front‑run the execution to drain funds. Full protocol takeover. Low–Medium – depends on LDO concentration; currently ~ 15 % held by top 10 addresses. 3 Uninitialized Proxy on L2 If a new L2 proxy is deployed without calling initializeV2 , the storage slot for admin remains zero, allowing anyone to become the admin via upgradeTo . Unauthorized upgrade of L2 implementation, potential fund lock or drain. High – observed in testnet deployments; could be replicated on mainnet if a new L2 is added. 4 Upgrade Bytecode Mismatch (Code Substitution) DAO approves ImplementationV3 but the transaction submitted to the proxy points to a different bytecode (e.g., attacker‑controlled contract). Malicious logic execution, fund exfiltration. Medium – mitigated by off‑chain verification but not enforced on‑chain. 5 Replay of Old Implementation via Beacon Proxy Beacon proxy points to a beacon contract that can be upgraded. An attacker could downgrade the beacon to a previously audited but vulnerable version (e.g., StakingRouterV1 ) if the DAO does not enforce monotonic versioning. Re‑introduction of known bugs (re‑entrancy, integer overflow). Low – requires DAO approval but possible if governance is rushed. 6 Cross‑Chain State Inconsistency Upgrades on Ethereum may not be mirrored on L2s, leading to divergent logic (e.g., fee calculation). Economic arbitrage, loss of user confidence. Medium – operational risk. 7 Upgrade‑Induced Re‑entrancy New functions added to StETH that call external contracts (e.g., price oracles) before updating internal balances. Draining of stETH via re‑entrancy loops. Low – would be caught in static analysis but could slip through if not audited. 3. Prioritized Technical Recommendations Priority Recommendation Rationale Implementation Steps Critical (P1) Enforce a formal storage‑layout verification step in CI (e.g., openzeppelin-upgrades storageLayout diff). Prevents accidental slot collisions that could corrupt state. 1. Integrate forge build --sizes + openzeppelin test-upgrade . 2. Fail CI if any existing slot is overwritten. Critical (P1) Introduce a dual‑timelock model – 48 h for regular upgrades, 6 h for emergency patches (e.g., oracle compromise). Reduces exposure window for critical fixes while preserving governance safety. 1. Deploy a new EmergencyTimelock contract. 2. Update DAO governance scripts to route emergency proposals there. High (P2) Add explicit on‑chain bytecode hash storage (e.g., bytes32 public implementationHash ) for each implementation contract, and require DAO proposals to include the hash. Enables users and auditors to verify that the deployed bytecode matches the approved code. 1. Extend ProxyAdmin to store hash on upgradeTo . 2. Emit ImplementationHashUpdated(hash) event. High (P2) Standardize L2 proxy initialization – create a library L2ProxyInitializer that enforces initializeV2 call and reverts if admin is zero. Eliminates the uninitialized‑proxy attack surface on any new L2 deployment. 1. Refactor L2 deployment scripts to import the library. 2. Add a unit test that deploys a proxy without init and expects revert. Medium (P3) Implement monotonic versioning in the Beacon contract – each upgrade must increase a uint256 version and cannot downgrade. Prevents accidental or malicious rollback to vulnerable code. 1. Add uint256 public version; to beacon. 2. In upgradeTo , require newVersion > version . Medium (P3) Publish a signed off‑chain “Upgrade Manifest” (JSON) containing implementation addresses, hashes, and a DAO‑signed digest. Improves transparency for the community and third‑party monitoring services. 1. Create a CI step that generates the manifest. 2. Sign with DAO multisig and post to IPFS + link on docs. Low (P4) Run a full‑suite of fuzz tests on any new external calls introduced in upgrades (e.g., oracle callbacks). Mitigates re‑entrancy and unexpected revert scenarios. 1. Extend existing Foundry fuzz harnesses. 2. Add coverage thresholds (≥ 90 %). Low (P4) Periodic cross‑chain state audit – compare fee rates, totalSupply, and paused flags across all L2s after each upgrade. Detects divergence early before it can be exploited. 1. Deploy a monitoring script (e.g., using TheGraph). 2. Alert on mismatches > 0.01 %. 4. Risk Score Metric Score (1 = Negligible, 10 = Critical) Upgrade‑Related Technical Risk 6 / 10 Governance / Timelock Risk 5 / 10 Cross‑Chain Consistency Risk 4 / 10 Overall Protocol Upgrade Compatibility Risk 5.5 → Rounded to 6 Interpretation : Lido’s upgrade framework is moderately risky . The primary concerns are storage‑layout safety and the lack of an emergency upgrade path. With the recommended mitigations, the risk can be reduced to ≤ 3 (low). 5. Conclusion Lido’s liquid‑staking infrastructure has proven resilient at scale, but the upgrade surface remains a critical vector for both accidental failures and targeted attacks. The current design—while leveraging industry‑standard proxy patterns—exposes the protocol to: Storage‑slot collisions as the codebase expands, Delayed emergency response due to a uniform timelock, Potential governance‑level code substitution without on‑chain verification, and Inconsistent initialization across its L2 deployments. By institutionalizing automated storage‑layout checks , splitting timelocks , recording implementation hashes on‑chain , and hardening L2 proxy deployment , Lido can substantially lower its upgrade‑related risk profile while preserving the decentralized governance model that underpins its ecosystem. Implementing the prioritized recommendations will: Safeguard the $22 B+ TVL from inadvertent state corruption, Enable rapid response to critical security incidents, Provide transparent, verifiable upgrade artefacts for the community, and Ensure uniform behavior across all supported chains. We recommend that Lido’s core development and DAO teams adopt the above roadmap within the next 3‑6 months and schedule a follow‑up audit after the first set of mitigations is live. Continuous monitoring and periodic re‑assessment will be essential as the protocol evolves and new features (e.g., restaking, cross‑chain liquidity) are introduced. Lido – Protocol Upgrade Compatibility Review

Prepared by: Senior DeFi Security Researcher

Date: 24 Oct 2026

1. Executive Summary

Lido Finance is the market‑leading liquid‑staking solution on Ethereum and several L2s, managing ≈ $22.4 B in total value locked (TVL). Medium – requires a malicious upgrade proposal accepted by DAO. 2 Timelock Abuse for Governance Capture An attacker who gains > 50 % of LDO can push a malicious upgrade through the standard 48 h timelock, then front‑run the execution to drain funds. High – observed in testnet deployments; could be replicated on mainnet if a new L2 is added. 4 Upgrade Bytecode Mismatch (Code Substitution) DAO approves ImplementationV3 but the transaction submitted to the proxy points to a different bytecode (e.g., attacker‑controlled contract). Malicious logic execution, fund exfiltration. Medium – mitigated by off‑chain verification but not enforced on‑chain. 5 Replay of Old Implementation via Beacon Proxy Beacon proxy points to a beacon contract that can be upgraded. An attacker could downgrade the beacon to a previously audited but vulnerable version (e.g., StakingRouterV1) if the DAO does not enforce monotonic versioning. Re‑introduction of known bugs (re‑entrancy, integer overflow). Low – requires DAO approval but possible if governance is rushed. 6 Cross‑Chain State Inconsistency Upgrades on Ethereum may not be mirrored on L2s, leading to divergent logic (e.g., fee calculation). Economic arbitrage, loss of user confidence. Medium – operational risk. 7 Upgrade‑Induced Re‑entrancy New functions added to StETH that call external contracts (e.g., price oracles) before updating internal balances. Draining of stETH via re‑entrancy loops. Low – would be caught in static analysis but could slip through if not audited.
3. Prioritized Technical Recommendations
Priority Recommendation Rationale Implementation Steps Critical (P1) Enforce a formal storage‑layout verification step in CI (e.g., openzeppelin-upgrades storageLayout diff). Prevents accidental slot collisions that could corrupt state. 1. Integrate forge build --sizes + openzeppelin test-upgrade.
2. Fail CI if any existing slot is overwritten. Critical (P1) Introduce a dual‑timelock model – 48 h for regular upgrades, 6 h for emergency patches (e.g., oracle compromise). Reduces exposure window for critical fixes while preserving governance safety. 1. Deploy a new EmergencyTimelock contract.
2. Update DAO governance scripts to route emergency proposals there. High (P2) Add explicit on‑chain bytecode hash storage (e.g., bytes32 public implementationHash) for each implementation contract, and require DAO proposals to include the hash. Enables users and auditors to verify that the deployed bytecode matches the approved code. 1. Extend ProxyAdmin to store hash on upgradeTo.
2. Emit ImplementationHashUpdated(hash) event. High (P2) Standardize L2 proxy initialization – create a library L2ProxyInitializer that enforces initializeV2 call and reverts if admin is zero. Eliminates the uninitialized‑proxy attack surface on any new L2 deployment. 1. Refactor L2 deployment scripts to import the library.
2. Add a unit test that deploys a proxy without init and expects revert. Medium (P3) Implement monotonic versioning in the Beacon contract – each upgrade must increase a uint256 version and cannot downgrade. Prevents accidental or malicious rollback to vulnerable code. 1. Add uint256 public version; to beacon.
2. In upgradeTo, require newVersion > version. Medium (P3) Publish a signed off‑chain “Upgrade Manifest” (JSON) containing implementation addresses, hashes, and a DAO‑signed digest. Improves transparency for the community and third‑party monitoring services. 1. Create a CI step that generates the manifest.
2. Sign with DAO multisig and post to IPFS + link on docs. Low (P4) Run a full‑suite of fuzz tests on any new external calls introduced in upgrades (e.g., oracle callbacks). Mitigates re‑entrancy and unexpected revert scenarios. 1. Extend existing Foundry fuzz harnesses.

2. Alert on mismatches > 0.01 %.
4. Risk Score
Metric Score (1 = Negligible, 10 = Critical) Upgrade‑Related Technical Risk 6 / 10 Governance / Timelock Risk 5 / 10 Cross‑Chain Consistency Risk 4 / 10 Overall Protocol Upgrade Compatibility Risk 5.5 → Rounded to 6

Lido’s liquid‑staking infrastructure has proven resilient at scale, but the upgrade surface remains a critical vector for both accidental failures and targeted attacks. The current design—while leveraging industry‑standard proxy patterns—exposes the protocol to:

  • Storage‑slot collisions as the codebase expands,
  • Delayed emergency response due to a uniform timelock,
  • Potential governance‑level code substitution without on‑chain verification, and
  • Inconsistent initialization across its L2 deployments.

By institutionalizing automated storage‑layout checks, splitting timelocks, recording implementation hashes on‑chain, and hardening L2 proxy deployment, Lido can substantially lower its upgrade‑related risk profile while preserving the decentralized governance model that underpins its ecosystem.

Implementing the prioritized recommendations will:

  • Safeguard the $22 B+ TVL from inadvertent state corruption,
  • Enable rapid response to critical security incidents,
  • Provide transparent, verifiable upgrade artefacts for the community, and
  • Ensure uniform behavior across all supported chains.

items.title: CADCraft: an open-source Rust 2D CAD workflow for automation
items.summary: When a project needs precise technical drawings and a workflow that can be scripted, CADCraft is a free, open-source 2D CAD application built in Rust. It is designed for architects, engineers, students, educators, makers, and technical designers who want a familiar drafting workflow without a subscription or account requirement. A practical drafting core CADCraft includes command-line tools for common drafting operations such as LINE, PLINE, CIRCLE, ARC, RECTANG, OFFSET, TRIM, FILLET, HATCH, and DIMLINEAR. Users can work with absolute or relative coordinates, distances, and angles. Object snaps, polar tracking, orthographic drawing, autocomplete, command history, aliases, and repeated commands help keep repetitive drafting work precise. Drawings can be organized with layers and extended with associative dimensions, multileaders, tables, hatches, paper-space layouts, and plotting features. The application supports DWG and DXF workflows and can export designs to PDF, SVG, and PNG. Built for automation The interesting part for developer workflows is the built-in automation surface. CADCraft exposes MCP, JSON control, and a headless CLI so users and agents can create drawings, inspect entities, render screenshots, convert files, and verify results. That makes it possible to keep technical drawing steps closer to scripts, repeatable build jobs, and agent-assisted workflows instead of relying only on manual UI actions. CADCraft runs on Windows, macOS, Linux, FreeBSD, and the web through WebAssembly. It is released under the MIT or Apache-2.0 licenses and is still in active development, so it is a project to evaluate, inspect, and contribute to as it evolves. For anyone exploring open-source CAD with a programmable edge, the CADCraft project is worth a look.
