items.title: Building an Internal Company Agent: 5 Things We Got Right and 5 I Would Do Differently
items.summary: In my recent AI engineering setup article , I briefly explained how an observability project at Bold.org turned into an internal company agent. The short version is that back in January 2026, Bold.org had structured backend events in ClickHouse, engineers could investigate them with SQL, and I wanted to see whether an agent could do the same. It worked, so I kept connecting more company systems. Within weeks, people across Bold.org were using it. It eventually became useful across engineering, product, support, operations, marketing, and growth. That summary makes the path sound much cleaner than it was. Several decisions helped the agent spread quickly. I also spent time solving problems I did not really have, left some important problems too late, and assumed things were obvious when they definitely were not. This is not a universal guide to building agents. It is a practical retrospective from building one inside a real company: five things we got right and five I would approach differently today. What this looked like in practice The first workflow was straightforward: I gave the agent read-only access to structured backend events in ClickHouse so it could investigate production questions. I then connected more of the systems where people already worked, including Slack, Linear, PostHog, and Grafana. The practical effect is bigger than a faster way to write SQL. Support can investigate many customer reports autonomously , without waiting for engineering or another team to provide context. For the workflows we target, investigations that previously took multiple hours and required finding the right access through three or four people can usually be completed in zero to one hour . The agent also automates parts of dashboard setup and analysis in PostHog and Grafana without requiring engineering to step in. The system consumes billions of tokens per month . That makes usage analytics and cost awareness important, but it is also a useful signal that the tool is part of how people work rather than a demo that is occasionally opened. I made one security boundary deliberately simple. The agent is gated behind Google sign-in for our company domain, and all of its remote access is read-only. Rather than relying on the model to be smart about when a change is safe, I did not give it permissions to write to remote systems in the first place. What worked 1. Make usage visible early By "visible," I mean visible inside the company. It is tempting to build an internal tool privately, make it feel complete, write an announcement, and then ask everyone to use it. We did almost the opposite. The agent was used in shared Slack channels and connected to Linear, where people were already working and could see what it did. This mattered more than any launch document. Most people do not immediately know what an agent can do. A blank chat box does not explain its capabilities. Even a good list of examples still requires someone to translate those examples into their own work. Seeing real usage solves that problem. Someone asks a question in Slack, the agent investigates it, and ten other people see both the result and the way the question was asked. A product manager notices that it can inspect a user flow. Somebody in support realizes it can help investigate a report. An engineer sees it gather context they were about to collect manually. Each visible interaction becomes a small product demo based on an actual company problem. Slack and Linear were important for another reason: they did not require people to adopt a new destination. Another internal web application would have asked everyone to remember that the tool existed, open it, and decide when to use it. In Slack and Linear, the agent appears where the question or task already exists. The web interface is still useful, especially for private or longer work. But shared usage is what taught the company what was possible. 2. Connect the tools the company already uses When I started this in January, MCP was still emerging and many of the systems we needed did not have useful servers. I closed the gap with small CLI tools, mostly thin wrappers around OpenAPI endpoints or existing SDKs, exposing only the operations needed for our workflows. They were intentionally boring: structured results, narrow permissions, proper error handling, and credentials kept away from the model. The value was not just another action the agent could take. More access meant more company context : production data, tickets, analytics, dashboards, and operational information could be considered together. That gave the agent better evidence for its reasoning and made its answers more useful than anything it could infer from a single system. 3. Track how people actually use it Usage analytics went in early. Not to create a leaderboard or measure who was "doing AI" correctly, but to understand what had been built. Tool calls, token spend, recurring workflows, and broad usage patterns showed which tools were valuable, where requests were becoming expensive, and what capabilities people kept trying to use. That made it possible to improve the product based on behavior rather than guesses: unexpected usage suggested a workflow needed simplifying, while unused tools pointed to poor discoverability, descriptions, or limited value. Aggregate operational metrics were more useful than ranking individuals and kept the analytics focused on improving the tool rather than monitoring employees. 4. Close the feedback loop People will try things you did not anticipate. They will also hit confusing behavior that feels obvious to the person who built the system. Feedback was easy to share, and the agent was adjusted as people used it. This sounds basic, but it created a useful loop: somebody tried a workflow, reported where it failed, and could often try the improved version shortly afterwards. That responsiveness encouraged more experimentation. People are much more willing to explore a new tool when they know a failure is not the end of the conversation. Some basic documentation also helped. It did not need to explain every tool or become a complete AI training course. A short explanation of what the agent could access, examples of good requests, known limitations, and how to share feedback gave people enough confidence to start. The combination matters. Documentation without feedback becomes stale. Feedback without documentation means answering the same introductory questions forever. 5. Design for the whole company The agent started from an engineering and observability problem, so keeping it focused on engineers would have been the obvious path. That would have been a mistake. Some of the most interesting usage came from product, support, operations, marketing, and growth. These teams often need information spread across several systems but do not have a convenient way to query or combine it. An agent with the right company context can remove a lot of that navigation. Support can be especially powerful here: people can investigate many reports themselves instead of waiting for engineering to gather the context. Engineers can actually be harder to convince. They already have coding agents, terminal workflows, preferred models, custom instructions, and strong opinions about harnesses. Asking them to move into a shared company interface can feel like asking them to give up a setup they spent months refining. I understand the resistance because I have the same opinions about my own tools. Other departments may have fewer existing agent workflows to replace. Once they see a relevant example and trust the access model, the value can be more immediate. Treating the agent as company infrastructure rather than an engineering experiment changed both its adoption and the features that mattered most. Five things I would do differently 1. Design local access earlier The biggest missing piece is making company tools available safely from local agent harnesses. The shared web, Slack, and Linear interfaces are useful, but local agents have context that a company agent does not. They can work with a person's files, notes, project memory, terminal, and current repository. Engineers in particular do not want to abandon that context every time they need company information. The ideal setup is not forcing everyone into one harness. It is allowing approved local harnesses to use company tools without exposing credentials or bypassing permissions. That is a much harder problem than adding another interface. Authentication needs to represent the person making the request. Secrets cannot be handed to the local model. Tool access should remain scoped and auditable. A compromised or badly configured local environment should not gain broad company access. 2. Spend less time chasing the perfect architecture Agent tooling changes constantly. Frameworks appear, models improve, MCP conventions evolve, and every week there is a new opinion about what AI should be, how it should be built, and which patterns or use cases are right or wrong. It is very easy to keep redesigning the system around what everyone is discussing online. I spent too much time considering whether I should rebuild parts of the agent around the latest approach. Most of that thinking had a short expiry date: a tool or pattern that looked essential one month could be irrelevant a few months later. Today I would pick one simple architecture that supports the immediate use case and move forward. Keep connectors small, keep boundaries clear, avoid coupling everything to one model or framework, and replace pieces only when there is a real reason rather than because a new diagram is popular on social media. Internal tools have an advantage here: they do not need to become a generic platform for every possible customer. They need to solve the company's actual problems. 3. Make contribution paths obvious The agent improved quickly, but too much of that improvement depended on a small number of people. It was not obvious who could write a skill, add a connector, improve instructions, or contribute code. Even when the repository was available, people were understandably hesitant. Agent systems combine code, prompts, permissions, and unfamiliar conventions. Nobody wants to break a tool used across the company or accidentally expose something sensitive. I have not solved this yet. People are welcome to use the agent, but it is not obvious how to contribute safely . The repository is available, but writing a skill, adding a connector, or changing instructions requires understanding code, prompts, permissions, and unfamiliar conventions. A short contribution guide with examples, ownership, review requirements, and a safe test path would make this easier. Until then, too much of the improvement depends on a small number of people. 4. Build fewer evals and less tracing infrastructure I spent too much time on evals, detailed traces, and comparing model behavior. Some visibility is essential: enough tracing to debug failures, usage analytics to control spend, and tests for critical tools and permissions. But this is not a frontier lab or a product with a dedicated evaluation team. It is an internal tool, and I cannot devote all my time to building infrastructure around hypothetical failures. The goal is to make it simple, make it work, and keep it maintainable . A few representative workflows and permission tests are enough until recurring failures justify more. The evaluation system should grow from real problems rather than from the fear of not measuring enough. 5. Assume less prior AI knowledge The largest mistake was probably assuming that capabilities obvious to me would be obvious to everyone else. AI adoption varies enormously across departments and individuals. Some people work with agents all day. Others have only used the basic ChatGPT interface. Terms such as tools, memory, connectors, context, or skills may mean nothing to them, and there is no reason they should. From the builder's perspective, the benefit seems clear: the agent can search several company systems, combine what it finds, and act on the result. From somebody else's perspective, it may look like another chat box. Why use this instead of ChatGPT? What does it know? What can it do? What is safe to ask? Will it make a change without permission? I have not solved this completely either. What helps most is turning abstract capabilities into visible functionality. Do not announce that the agent has a new connector. Show that it can prepare a specific report, investigate a known type of issue, or automate a repetitive workflow. Give people something relevant they can try immediately. Adoption does not happen because the architecture is impressive. It happens when somebody sees the agent solve a problem they recognize. The main lessons These are the main lessons and mistakes from the first six months: make the agent visible early, connect it to the systems where context lives, keep access safe, and optimize for something simple enough to maintain . The best decision was letting people see the agent being used before it felt finished. The recurring lesson is that what feels obvious to the builder is rarely obvious to everyone else . I am interested in hearing how other teams are adopting AI in practice, what is working, and where workflows are still awkward or blocked by access, context, or trust. If you are working through similar questions or facing challenges introducing AI-native workflows in your team or company, I would love to hear more and see whether I can help . I'm Orestis, VP of Technology at Bold.org . On the side I build clssrm , simple booking software for small studios. More of my writing is on oioannou.com .
items.summary_html:
In my recent AI engineering setup article, I briefly explained how an observability project at Bold.org turned into an internal company agent.

The short version is that back in January 2026, Bold.org had structured backend events in ClickHouse, engineers could investigate them with SQL, and I wanted to see whether an agent could do the same. It worked, so I kept connecting more company systems. Within weeks, people across Bold.org were using it. It eventually became useful across engineering, product, support, operations, marketing, and growth.

That summary makes the path sound much cleaner than it was.

Several decisions helped the agent spread quickly. I also spent time solving problems I did not really have, left some important problems too late, and assumed things were obvious when they definitely were not.

This is not a universal guide to building agents. It is a practical retrospective from building one inside a real company: five things we got right and five I would approach differently today.

What this looked like in practice

The first workflow was straightforward: I gave the agent read-only access to structured backend events in ClickHouse so it could investigate production questions. I then connected more of the systems where people already worked, including Slack, Linear, PostHog, and Grafana.

The practical effect is bigger than a faster way to write SQL. Support can investigate many customer reports autonomously, without waiting for engineering or another team to provide context. For the workflows we target, investigations that previously took multiple hours and required finding the right access through three or four people can usually be completed in zero to one hour. The agent also automates parts of dashboard setup and analysis in PostHog and Grafana without requiring engineering to step in.

The system consumes billions of tokens per month. That makes usage analytics and cost awareness important, but it is also a useful signal that the tool is part of how people work rather than a demo that is occasionally opened.

I made one security boundary deliberately simple. The agent is gated behind Google sign-in for our company domain, and all of its remote access is read-only. Rather than relying on the model to be smart about when a change is safe, I did not give it permissions to write to remote systems in the first place.

What worked 1. Make usage visible early

By "visible," I mean visible inside the company.

It is tempting to build an internal tool privately, make it feel complete, write an announcement, and then ask everyone to use it. We did almost the opposite. The agent was used in shared Slack channels and connected to Linear, where people were already working and could see what it did.

This mattered more than any launch document.

Most people do not immediately know what an agent can do. A blank chat box does not explain its capabilities. Even a good list of examples still requires someone to translate those examples into their own work.

Seeing real usage solves that problem. Someone asks a question in Slack, the agent investigates it, and ten other people see both the result and the way the question was asked. A product manager notices that it can inspect a user flow. Somebody in support realizes it can help investigate a report. An engineer sees it gather context they were about to collect manually.

Each visible interaction becomes a small product demo based on an actual company problem.

Slack and Linear were important for another reason: they did not require people to adopt a new destination. Another internal web application would have asked everyone to remember that the tool existed, open it, and decide when to use it. In Slack and Linear, the agent appears where the question or task already exists.

The web interface is still useful, especially for private or longer work. But shared usage is what taught the company what was possible.

2. Connect the tools the company already uses

When I started this in January, MCP was still emerging and many of the systems we needed did not have useful servers. I closed the gap with small CLI tools, mostly thin wrappers around OpenAPI endpoints or existing SDKs, exposing only the operations needed for our workflows. They were intentionally boring: structured results, narrow permissions, proper error handling, and credentials kept away from the model.

The value was not just another action the agent could take. More access meant more company context: production data, tickets, analytics, dashboards, and operational information could be considered together. That gave the agent better evidence for its reasoning and made its answers more useful than anything it could infer from a single system.

3. Track how people actually use it

Usage analytics went in early. Not to create a leaderboard or measure who was "doing AI" correctly, but to understand what had been built.

Tool calls, token spend, recurring workflows, and broad usage patterns showed which tools were valuable, where requests were becoming expensive, and what capabilities people kept trying to use. That made it possible to improve the product based on behavior rather than guesses: unexpected usage suggested a workflow needed simplifying, while unused tools pointed to poor discoverability, descriptions, or limited value. Aggregate operational metrics were more useful than ranking individuals and kept the analytics focused on improving the tool rather than monitoring employees.

4. Close the feedback loop

People will try things you did not anticipate. They will also hit confusing behavior that feels obvious to the person who built the system.

Feedback was easy to share, and the agent was adjusted as people used it. This sounds basic, but it created a useful loop: somebody tried a workflow, reported where it failed, and could often try the improved version shortly afterwards.

That responsiveness encouraged more experimentation. People are much more willing to explore a new tool when they know a failure is not the end of the conversation.

Some basic documentation also helped. It did not need to explain every tool or become a complete AI training course. A short explanation of what the agent could access, examples of good requests, known limitations, and how to share feedback gave people enough confidence to start.

The combination matters. Documentation without feedback becomes stale. Feedback without documentation means answering the same introductory questions forever.

5. Design for the whole company

The agent started from an engineering and observability problem, so keeping it focused on engineers would have been the obvious path. That would have been a mistake.

Some of the most interesting usage came from product, support, operations, marketing, and growth. These teams often need information spread across several systems but do not have a convenient way to query or combine it. An agent with the right company context can remove a lot of that navigation. Support can be especially powerful here: people can investigate many reports themselves instead of waiting for engineering to gather the context.

Engineers can actually be harder to convince.

They already have coding agents, terminal workflows, preferred models, custom instructions, and strong opinions about harnesses. Asking them to move into a shared company interface can feel like asking them to give up a setup they spent months refining. I understand the resistance because I have the same opinions about my own tools.

Other departments may have fewer existing agent workflows to replace. Once they see a relevant example and trust the access model, the value can be more immediate.

Treating the agent as company infrastructure rather than an engineering experiment changed both its adoption and the features that mattered most.

Five things I would do differently 1. Design local access earlier

The biggest missing piece is making company tools available safely from local agent harnesses.

The shared web, Slack, and Linear interfaces are useful, but local agents have context that a company agent does not. They can work with a person's files, notes, project memory, terminal, and current repository. Engineers in particular do not want to abandon that context every time they need company information.

The ideal setup is not forcing everyone into one harness. It is allowing approved local harnesses to use company tools without exposing credentials or bypassing permissions.

That is a much harder problem than adding another interface. Authentication needs to represent the person making the request. Secrets cannot be handed to the local model. Tool access should remain scoped and auditable. A compromised or badly configured local environment should not gain broad company access.

2. Spend less time chasing the perfect architecture

Agent tooling changes constantly. Frameworks appear, models improve, MCP conventions evolve, and every week there is a new opinion about what AI should be, how it should be built, and which patterns or use cases are right or wrong.

It is very easy to keep redesigning the system around what everyone is discussing online.

I spent too much time considering whether I should rebuild parts of the agent around the latest approach. Most of that thinking had a short expiry date: a tool or pattern that looked essential one month could be irrelevant a few months later. Today I would pick one simple architecture that supports the immediate use case and move forward. Keep connectors small, keep boundaries clear, avoid coupling everything to one model or framework, and replace pieces only when there is a real reason rather than because a new diagram is popular on social media.

Internal tools have an advantage here: they do not need to become a generic platform for every possible customer. They need to solve the company's actual problems.

3. Make contribution paths obvious

The agent improved quickly, but too much of that improvement depended on a small number of people.

It was not obvious who could write a skill, add a connector, improve instructions, or contribute code. Even when the repository was available, people were understandably hesitant. Agent systems combine code, prompts, permissions, and unfamiliar conventions. Nobody wants to break a tool used across the company or accidentally expose something sensitive.

I have not solved this yet. People are welcome to use the agent, but it is not obvious how to contribute safely. The repository is available, but writing a skill, adding a connector, or changing instructions requires understanding code, prompts, permissions, and unfamiliar conventions.

A short contribution guide with examples, ownership, review requirements, and a safe test path would make this easier. Until then, too much of the improvement depends on a small number of people.

4. Build fewer evals and less tracing infrastructure

I spent too much time on evals, detailed traces, and comparing model behavior. Some visibility is essential: enough tracing to debug failures, usage analytics to control spend, and tests for critical tools and permissions. But this is not a frontier lab or a product with a dedicated evaluation team. It is an internal tool, and I cannot devote all my time to building infrastructure around hypothetical failures.

The goal is to make it simple, make it work, and keep it maintainable. A few representative workflows and permission tests are enough until recurring failures justify more. The evaluation system should grow from real problems rather than from the fear of not measuring enough.

5. Assume less prior AI knowledge

The largest mistake was probably assuming that capabilities obvious to me would be obvious to everyone else.

AI adoption varies enormously across departments and individuals. Some people work with agents all day. Others have only used the basic ChatGPT interface. Terms such as tools, memory, connectors, context, or skills may mean nothing to them, and there is no reason they should.

From the builder's perspective, the benefit seems clear: the agent can search several company systems, combine what it finds, and act on the result. From somebody else's perspective, it may look like another chat box. Why use this instead of ChatGPT? What does it know? What can it do? What is safe to ask? Will it make a change without permission?

I have not solved this completely either.

What helps most is turning abstract capabilities into visible functionality. Do not announce that the agent has a new connector. Show that it can prepare a specific report, investigate a known type of issue, or automate a repetitive workflow. Give people something relevant they can try immediately.

Adoption does not happen because the architecture is impressive. It happens when somebody sees the agent solve a problem they recognize.

The main lessons

These are the main lessons and mistakes from the first six months: make the agent visible early, connect it to the systems where context lives, keep access safe, and optimize for something simple enough to maintain.

The best decision was letting people see the agent being used before it felt finished. The recurring lesson is that what feels obvious to the builder is rarely obvious to everyone else.

I am interested in hearing how other teams are adopting AI in practice, what is working, and where workflows are still awkward or blocked by access, context, or trust. items.title: Pennsylvania will require labels on AI-generated ads
items.summary: On Thursday, Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro signed the Artificial Intelligence Deceptive Advertising Act into law, requiring disclosures on AI-generated ads. The law requires any ad - whether it's a still image, video, audio, or text - that "has been significantly modified or generated by artificial intelligence" to include a label in the same format as the ad itself. That applies to TV commercials from multi-billion-dollar companies , as well as restaurants' ugly, crowded flyers about their wing specials. Pennsylvania is one of the first states to require disclosures on AI content. And it requires those labels regardless of where an ad …

items.title: Building Neumathway: Marrying GNNs with Symbolic Engines for Zero Hallucinations
items.summary: Building Neumathway: Neuro-Symbolic Math with Zero Hallucinations Made by Christopher Alberto Hamonangan *Neumathway is an experimental, open-source project, and contributions from the community are welcome. GitHub: https://github.com/christopherhamonangan/Neumathway Hugging Face: https://huggingface.co/BhinnekaAI/neumathwork-v1 *Research paper in progress. A formal paper documenting the architecture, methodology, and experimental evaluation of Neumathway is currently under development. Introduction Artificial Intelligence (AI) has become a major force in modern technological development, encompassing fields such as Machine Learning (ML), Computer Vision (CV), and Natural Language Processing (NLP). Within this landscape, Large Language Models (LLMs) have emerged as a significant advancement in the ability of machines to process and generate human language. A major milestone was the introduction of GPT-1 by OpenAI in 2018, which demonstrated the potential of generative pre-training using Transformer-based neural networks. Subsequent developments accelerated the adoption of generative AI, transforming language models from research systems into widely accessible tools for education, software development, scientific research, and other practical applications. However, this progress was not the result of a single model, but rather a series of advances in neural architectures, training methods, computational resources, and data availability. The evolution of modern LLMs has been shaped by several important milestones. The Transformer architecture, introduced in 2017, established attention mechanisms as a foundation for many contemporary language models. GPT-1 and BERT followed in 2018, while GPT-2 and T5 advanced text generation and language understanding in 2019. In 2020, GPT-3 demonstrated the capabilities of large-scale language modeling with 175 billion parameters. The public release of ChatGPT in 2022 expanded access to conversational AI, followed by systems such as GPT-4, Claude, and Gemini in subsequent years. Developments in 2024 and 2025 further emphasized multimodal processing, reasoning capabilities, and more efficient training approaches. Despite their differences, these systems share a common foundation in learning representations from data and using those representations to perform language-related tasks. History of Large Language Models (LLM). Source: https://www.scribbledata.io/ At the technical level, an LLM typically processes text through a sequence of numerical transformations. A tokenizer first divides input text into tokens, which are mapped to numerical identifiers and subsequently converted into embedding vectors. Positional information is incorporated to represent token order. These representations are then processed by neural network layers, commonly using a decoder-only Transformer architecture in autoregressive language models. Within each Transformer block, self-attention uses Query, Key, and Value representations to determine how information from preceding tokens contributes to the contextual representation of each position. Feed-forward networks, residual connections, and normalization layers further transform these representations. By stacking multiple blocks, the model learns increasingly complex contextual patterns that support the generation of coherent sequences. Implementation techniques such as Grouped-Query Attention, FlashAttention, and mixed-precision computation can also improve computational or memory efficiency. Internal Architecture of a Transformer. Source: https://deeprevision.github.io/posts/001-transformer/#ref-vaswani2017attention The capabilities of an LLM are developed through training, during which model parameters are optimized using large datasets. Generative models commonly employ a next-token prediction objective, learning to estimate the probability distribution of the next token given the preceding context. The resulting loss is used to update model parameters through backpropagation and optimization algorithms such as AdamW. Depending on the model, additional stages may include supervised fine-tuning, preference optimization, or reinforcement learning to improve instruction following and task performance. During inference, the model generates an output by repeatedly predicting and selecting subsequent tokens according to a decoding strategy. This process enables flexible language generation, but it also means that the model’s output depends on learned statistical representations rather than automatically following explicit computational rules. Model architecture, training data, optimization methods, and inference settings all contribute to its resulting capabilities. LLM Training and Pipeline. Source: https://livephysics.com/infographics/cs-how-llms-trained/ Today, LLMs support a wide range of applications, including educational assistance, code generation, scientific literature analysis, document processing, and conversational interfaces. Multimodal systems have further extended these capabilities to inputs such as images, audio, and video, while tool integration allows certain models to interact with external software and computational systems. These developments demonstrate the versatility of neural language models and their growing role in modern AI. Understanding their architectures, training procedures, and inference mechanisms provides an important foundation for investigating other computational approaches and specialized AI systems. This broader context establishes the technical background for examining how different model architectures can be designed and evaluated for specific problem domains. Motivation Mathematical reasoning is an essential capability in artificial intelligence because it requires more than recognizing patterns or generating plausible sequences of text. Mathematical tasks involve structured expressions, well-defined operators, algebraic relationships, and rules that constrain which transformations are valid. From elementary arithmetic to linear algebra and calculus, a solver must interpret an input, identify the appropriate operation or strategy, and produce a result consistent with mathematical rules. These capabilities are relevant to scientific computing, engineering, education, and automated problem-solving. Consequently, mathematical computation provides an important domain for investigating how AI systems can combine learned representations with structured operations to solve problems reliably. Despite substantial progress in Large Language Models (LLMs), mathematical reasoning remains an active research area. LLMs can solve many mathematical problems through learned patterns, multi-step generation, and tool-assisted reasoning, but their performance does not guarantee consistent correctness across different problem formulations. The GSM-Symbolic study by Mirzadeh et al. (2025), for example, found that model performance could vary when numerical values were changed and could deteriorate when irrelevant clauses were introduced into problems. These findings illustrate why benchmark accuracy alone may not fully characterize the robustness of mathematical reasoning. Moreover, generating a plausible solution and executing a mathematically valid computation are not necessarily equivalent processes. Although external calculators, computer algebra systems, and other tools can improve reliability, they introduce additional design questions concerning tool selection, intermediate representations, and the coordination between learned reasoning and exact computation. ( Mirzadeh et al., 2025 ). Illustration of robustness challenges in language-model-based mathematical reasoning. One potential direction is to combine neural learning with symbolic computation. Neural networks can learn representations from examples, recognize structural patterns, and predict useful operations or strategies without requiring every decision to be manually specified. General-purpose LLMs are trained to support a broad range of language tasks, whereas a mathematical solver can be designed around structured numerical and symbolic inputs. Such specialization makes it possible to investigate alternative representations, task-specific prediction mechanisms, and computational pathways without requiring every stage to operate through natural-language generation. A model may, for instance, represent an expression as a structured graph, predict the operator or strategy required at a given step, and delegate supported calculations to an explicit symbolic engine. Nevertheless, specialization should not be assumed to guarantee better performance or lower resource consumption. Its value must be evaluated against appropriate alternatives using consistent datasets, comparable task coverage, and measurements of accuracy, latency, memory consumption, and generalization. This makes computational efficiency and mathematical reliability measurable research objectives rather than presumed advantages. The central research question is therefore not simply whether neural networks and symbolic computation can be combined, since neuro-symbolic systems have already been investigated across multiple domains. Instead, the question is how their components can be organized to support a dedicated mathematical solver across several categories of operations while balancing predictive flexibility, computational correctness, and resource requirements. In particular, it is worth investigating whether structured expression representations, learned operator prediction, strategy selection, and symbolic execution can work together within a unified processing pipeline. A meaningful evaluation must determine where this combination is effective, which types of operations remain difficult, and whether any improvements persist on unseen examples rather than only on familiar training patterns. Establishing this research gap requires comparison with existing mathematical solvers and relevant neural or neuro-symbolic baselines, rather than assuming that the proposed combination is inherently novel. The objective is to identify and test a specific architectural approach whose behavior can be measured and reproduced. Motivated by these questions, this research investigates Neumathway (NMN) , a specialized neuro-symbolic system designed to process mathematical expressions and operations. NMN explores the integration of structured expression representations, a relation-aware graph neural network, a recurrent controller, neural operator prediction, a neural matrix computation component, and a symbolic engine for supported calculations. Its design also incorporates strategy selection and a memory mechanism intended to reuse previously established solutions where applicable. Rather than treating the entire problem-solving process as unrestricted text generation, NMN investigates how neural components can help select computational actions while symbolic procedures handle operations covered by their explicit rules. The system is evaluated across multiple mathematical categories, including arithmetic, linear equations, systems of equations, quadratic equations, differentiation, integration, limits, matrix operations, and specialized discrete functions. The experiments examine mathematical accuracy, operator prediction, generalization, inference latency, and memory usage. Through this investigation, NMN aims to provide an empirical case study of how neural learning and symbolic computation can be coordinated in a resource-conscious mathematical solver, with its contributions determined by reproducible results and comparisons against relevant baselines. Conceptual architecture of Neumathway, illustrating the coordination between neural prediction and symbolic computation. Introducing Neumathway (NMN) 1. What Is Neumathway? Neumathway (NMN) is an experimental neuro-symbolic AI system designed to explore a different approach to mathematical computation. Instead of treating mathematical problem-solving primarily as a process of generating text, NMN organizes the task around structured mathematical representations, learned computational decisions, and explicit symbolic operations. The central idea is to investigate how neural networks and symbolic computation can work together within a specialized system that processes mathematical expressions. The motivation behind NMN is not simply to build another calculator or reproduce the general capabilities of a large language model. Conventional calculators already perform many numerical operations efficiently, while general-purpose language models can address mathematical questions alongside numerous other tasks. NMN explores a different design question: can a dedicated computational architecture coordinate learned predictions and explicit mathematical procedures across multiple categories of mathematical operations? To investigate this question, NMN combines several components, including a graph-based representation of mathematical expressions, a relation-aware graph neural network, a recurrent controller, neural operator prediction, neural matrix computation, strategy selection, and a symbolic engine for supported operations. These components have different responsibilities, allowing the system to investigate how structural representations, learned decisions, and rule-based computation can be coordinated. NMN should therefore be understood as an ongoing experimental system rather than an established replacement for existing mathematical tools. Its value depends on what its architecture can demonstrate through reproducible experiments, how well it generalizes beyond familiar training examples, and whether its design offers measurable advantages under clearly defined evaluation conditions. 2. How Does Neumathway Work? At a conceptual level, NMN processes mathematical expressions through a sequence of structured representations and computational decisions. Consider the expression 12 + 8 × 2. Neural Matrix Computation (NMC) provides a learned numerical computation pathway, while the symbolic engine executes operations covered by its explicitly implemented rules. Result Generation. Neural networks and symbolic systems offer different computational properties. Neural networks can learn patterns from examples and use those patterns to make predictions in situations that may not have been explicitly programmed. However, a learned prediction is not automatically equivalent to a mathematically valid operation. A neural component may select an inappropriate operator, produce an inaccurate numerical estimate, or fail when an input differs substantially from the examples encountered during training. Symbolic computation takes a different approach. It manipulates mathematical expressions according to explicit rules. For supported operations, a symbolic engine can perform defined transformations without having to learn those rules from numerical examples. This can provide a more controlled computational pathway, although its reliability still depends on implementation correctness, input parsing, domain restrictions, and the operations it actually supports. NMN explores how these complementary properties can be coordinated. Its neural components are intended to help interpret mathematical structure, predict operations, and select strategies, while the symbolic engine executes supported mathematical procedures. In principle, this arrangement could reduce reliance on unconstrained numerical prediction for operations that can be handled explicitly. However, the benefits depend on whether the neural decisions are appropriate and whether the symbolic engine can execute the selected operations correctly. The combination also introduces its own challenges. Neural predictions and symbolic operations must use compatible representations, and errors at the interface between them can propagate through the computation. Some mathematical problems may require operations outside the symbolic engine’s supported scope, while learned components may behave differently on unseen expressions. Consequently, neuro-symbolic integration is not automatically more accurate or efficient than either approach in isolation. It is an architectural hypothesis that requires careful implementation and empirical evaluation. Conceptual comparison of neural learning and symbolic computation in NMN. 4. What Makes NMN Different from a Conventional Calculator or an LLM? NMN explores a specialized approach to mathematical computation. To understand its intended role, it helps to compare its design with conventional calculators and general-purpose large language models (LLMs). This comparison describes general design characteristics rather than universal properties of every system in each category. The main distinction is that NMN investigates how learned decisions can be organized around structured mathematical expressions and coordinated with explicit symbolic operations. Unlike a conventional calculator, it incorporates neural components for predicting operations and computational strategies. Unlike a general-purpose LLM, its architecture is specifically organized around mathematical computation rather than unrestricted language generation. However, these differences do not establish that NMN is more accurate, faster, or more resource-efficient. Such conclusions require controlled comparisons using relevant baselines, equivalent tasks, and clearly documented evaluation conditions. 5. What Happens Inside NMN? At a conceptual level, Neumathway organizes mathematical problem-solving around three complementary functions: Structural representation: The input expression is transformed into a structured representation that captures the relationships between mathematical symbols and operations. Neural decision-making: Neural components learn to identify relevant operations, predict computational actions, and guide the problem-solving process. Symbolic computation: A symbolic component executes supported mathematical operations according to explicit rules, helping maintain computational consistency. These functions are intended to work together rather than operate as isolated components. Neural learning provides flexibility in selecting and organizing computational steps, while symbolic computation provides a rule-based mechanism for executing supported operations. Illustration of structured mathematical expression representation in Neumathway. 6. What Is NMN Designed to Solve? Neumathway is designed to investigate whether a specialized computational model can solve mathematical expressions through a combination of learned decision-making and explicit mathematical operations. Its intended scope extends beyond basic arithmetic to several categories of mathematical problems, including: Arithmetic: Evaluating expressions involving multiple operations and nested parentheses. Algebra: Solving linear and quadratic equations, as well as systems of equations. Calculus: Handling selected differentiation, integration, and limit problems. Linear algebra: Working with matrices and related operations. Discrete and specialized functions: Evaluating mathematical functions defined by particular rules or conditions. This scope represents the system’s intended problem domains, not a claim that every problem within these categories has been solved reliably. Actual performance depends on the supported operations, training data, implementation, and evaluation procedure. 7. What Do We Want to Find Out? The central question behind NMN is whether neural prediction and symbolic computation can be coordinated effectively within a specialized mathematical solver. The investigation considers not only whether the system produces correct answers, but also how its internal computational decisions contribute to those outcomes. Operator prediction, strategy selection, numerical computation, and symbolic execution represent different stages of the process, and each may introduce distinct sources of error. A second question concerns generalization. A model may learn recurring patterns in its training data without developing a reliable approach to unfamiliar expressions. Evaluating NMN therefore requires examining performance on data that was not used to train the model and determining whether the evaluation examples meaningfully differ from the training examples. Category-level results and error analysis can help reveal whether the system handles a broad range of operations or relies heavily on particular patterns. Computational efficiency is another important consideration. A specialized system may be useful in resource-constrained environments if it can provide acceptable mathematical reliability while keeping inference latency and memory consumption manageable. However, these properties must be measured under documented hardware and software conditions. Comparisons are meaningful only when the tested workloads and measurement procedures are sufficiently consistent. Ultimately, NMN is an investigation into a particular architectural approach, not a claim that neuro-symbolic computation has already solved the challenges of mathematical reasoning. Its significance depends on reproducible implementation details, transparent evaluation, and an honest account of both successful results and remaining limitations. With these questions established, the next chapter moves from the conceptual overview to the technical details of NMN’s architecture, training process, and experimental evaluation. However, these results must be interpreted in the context of the evaluation size, class distribution, data-splitting methodology, and potential overlap with training samples. Its interpretation depends on whether the error is calculated in the original numerical domain or the signed-log-transformed domain. Additional metrics, such as mean absolute error and category-level error distributions, would provide a more complete assessment of numerical accuracy. The reported mean inference latency of 0.0183 milliseconds per step and throughput of 19,459 operations per second also require clearly defined measurement conditions. In particular, the evaluation should specify what constitutes an operation or computational step, the hardware and software configuration, and whether timing includes parsing, neural inference, symbolic execution, and Strategy Memory retrieval. These factors can substantially affect the reported performance. Finally, the symbolic contract pass rate of 96.55%, reasoning-turn reduction of 57.5%, Strategy Memory speedup of 38.5×-85×, and peak RAM usage of 893 MB should each be supported by explicit metric definitions and appropriate baselines. Success: {success_cases:,} | Failures: {failure_cases:,}") Include the actual evaluation loop, metric calculations, timing procedure, and resource-measurement logic. The code should show how predictions are compared with reference results and how failed or unsupported cases are counted. For stronger evidence, future experiments should compare NMN against appropriate baselines on identical held-out expressions. These may include a conventional calculator for supported arithmetic, a symbolic mathematics engine for applicable symbolic operations, and a neural baseline for learned action prediction. Each comparison should use equivalent inputs, clearly defined success criteria, and comparable measurement conditions. Ablation experiments should separately evaluate the contributions of the graph encoder, neural controller, symbolic engine, strategy router, and Strategy Memory where technically feasible. Taken together, the reported results provide an initial profile of NMN’s predictive behavior, numerical error, execution characteristics, and resource consumption. They do not, by themselves, establish superiority over existing mathematical systems or reliable generalization across all intended domains. Such conclusions require reproducible benchmarks, held-out evaluation, and clearly documented baselines. These findings and methodological constraints provide the foundation for the limitations and future directions discussed in Section 4.4. 4. Limitations and Future Directions Despite its initial results, Neumathway remains an experimental system with several limitations that must be addressed before its capabilities can be fully established. Its current performance metrics provide an initial perspective on neural prediction, symbolic execution, and computational efficiency, but further experiments are necessary to determine how reliably the system generalizes to unfamiliar mathematical problems. 4.1 Generalization and Dataset Coverage NMN was trained on approximately 8.27 million generated mathematical samples across nine categories. However, dataset size alone does not guarantee that a model can solve previously unseen expressions or unfamiliar combinations of operations. Similar structures may occur across training and evaluation samples, potentially making some predictions easier than genuinely novel problems. Future experiments should evaluate NMN on structurally distinct expressions, more complex combinations of operations, and carefully separated test sets. Performance should also be reported by mathematical category rather than relying exclusively on aggregate metrics. This would help establish whether NMN learns reusable computational patterns or primarily recognizes structures similar to those encountered during training. 4.2 Numerical Representation and Precision In its current form, NMN may convert decimal values and mathematical constants, such as π, into their nearest integer representations during processing. This conversion can discard important numerical information, reducing accuracy in calculations that require decimal precision or the preservation of mathematical constants. Consequently, the system’s current capabilities should not be interpreted as covering all forms of numerical computation. Future development should investigate support for decimal values, rational numbers, and symbolic constants, allowing the system to preserve numerical information throughout the computation pipeline and apply rounding only when explicitly required. 4.3 Neural Prediction and Symbolic Reliability High operator-prediction accuracy does not necessarily guarantee that an entire expression will be solved correctly. Errors in parsing, action selection, numerical prediction, or symbolic execution can propagate through subsequent computational steps. Furthermore, the symbolic engine can only reliably execute operations covered by its implemented rules. Future versions should strengthen result verification, improve the handling of unsupported expressions, and evaluate complete problem-solving success rather than measuring individual components in isolation. An explicit failure-handling mechanism would also help prevent uncertain or unsupported results from being presented as verified answers. 4.4 Computational Efficiency and Benchmarking The reported latency, throughput, memory consumption, and Strategy Memory speedup should be evaluated under clearly documented conditions. Comparisons with conventional calculators, symbolic mathematics engines, and relevant neural baselines would help establish where NMN offers practical advantages and where existing approaches remain more appropriate. Such comparisons should use equivalent workloads and transparent measurement procedures. Ablation studies could additionally isolate the contributions of the graph encoder, neural controller, numerical prediction component, symbolic engine, strategy router, and Strategy Memory. This would help determine whether each component provides a measurable benefit or introduces unnecessary computational overhead. 4.5 Future Research Directions The limitations identified above suggest four priorities for subsequent research: Generalization testing: Evaluate NMN on unseen mathematical structures and independently held-out test sets. Numerical precision: Extend numerical representation to support decimal values, rational numbers, and symbolic constants without unnecessary information loss. Architectural ablation: Measure the individual and combined contributions of NMN’s neural and symbolic components. Reproducible benchmarking: Establish transparent comparisons with appropriate baselines using consistent evaluation protocols. Together, these experiments would provide stronger evidence regarding NMN’s reliability, computational efficiency, and practical value. Neumathway should be viewed as an ongoing exploration of how neural prediction and symbolic computation can be coordinated within a specialized mathematical system. Its contribution will depend not only on the reported metrics but also on its ability to demonstrate reliable generalization, numerical accuracy, and measurable advantages under controlled evaluation. Addressing these limitations will provide a stronger foundation for determining NMN’s practical value and its potential contribution to research in neural-symbolic computation.
