items.title: Pixels, Not Boxes: How a Detection Transformer Paints a Street
items.summary: 100 questions, four answers, each painted pixel by pixel. The hatched area is what a box would have counted as the object.* Left of the line, a box counts everything inside it, including the road. Right of the line, a mask keeps only the object’s own pixels. Eight animated steps, one street: how RF-DETR finds every object and paints its exact pixels, and where it struggles. Look at a photo of a street. A cyclist rides across a zebra crossing. One car waits before the crossing, another drives away, and a dog sits on the pavement. Ask a computer where the objects are, and most systems answer with boxes. Now look closely at those boxes. Step 1. A box is a rough answer. In our drawing, only 20% of the cyclist’s box is cyclist; the cars and the dog fill about half of theirs. In our drawing, only a fifth of the cyclist’s box is cyclist. The rest is road, crossing stripes, and the empty space inside the bicycle wheels. Each car fills about half of its box, and so does the dog. A box tells you where to look. It does not tell you which pixels belong to the object. Answering that question, one yes-or-no for every pixel and a separate answer for every object, is called instance segmentation . You need it to cut out a product photo, measure the area of a lake in a satellite image, or figure out how much of a field is covered by weeds. This post explains how one real-time model, RF-DETR, does it. Itis presented in eight steps, and each step has its own animation. If you only scroll through the animations, you should still get the main idea; the text adds the why and the numbers. No prior knowledge of transformers is needed. Scope. RF-DETR 1.11.2 from PyPI , the RFDETRSeg* instance-segmentation models. Mechanism details come from the RF-DETR source code and the RF-DETR paper ; accuracy and latency numbers come from the RF-DETR benchmarks page . Heat maps and channel maps in the animations are illustrative, built from the true outlines of our drawing, not taken from a trained model. Disclosure: I maintain RF-DETR at Roboflow. The photo becomes a grid of patches A neural network does not see a street. It sees numbers. RF-DETR-Seg Small, the size we use in this post, first resizes the photo to 384 × 384 pixels and cuts it into small 12 × 12-pixel squares called patches. That creates a 32 × 32 grid of 1,024 patches. Step 2. The photo becomes a grid of patches. Each patch becomes a list of numbers; a pretrained backbone refines it into memory, 256 numbers per patch. Each patch becomes a list of numbers called a token. The tokens then pass through the backbone, a vision transformer initialized from DINOv2 . Meta trained DINOv2 on a curated set of 142 million images without any labels, so before RF-DETR has seen a single annotated street, its backbone already tells fur from metal and wheels from asphalt. Inside the backbone, tokens can compare themselves, so a patch on the car’s bonnet can take the rest of the car into account. At the end, a small module called the projector packs everything into one grid of 32 × 32 descriptions, 256 numbers per patch. RF-DETR calls this grid the memory. Every later step reads from it. A model never sees the street, only a grid of descriptions… A hundred questions find the objects Now the model has to find the objects. Many detectors guess a box at every position in the image, then delete duplicates afterward. RF-DETR asks questions instead. It maintains a fixed set of learned queries: 100 in Segmentation Small. Think of each query as a question: “Is there an object I should be responsible for? If so, what is it, and where?” Every query answers exactly once, either with a class and a box, or with “nothing here”, written ∅. Step 3. 100 questions: find the objects. Four queries claim the four objects; the other 96 answer “nothing here”. The queries work through a short stack of decoder layers, four in Seg Small. In each layer, every query reads evidence from the memory, compares notes with the other queries, and updates its answer, including a fresh guess of its box from the same starting point. The last layer’s answer counts. Pause and ponder. Several queries can see the dog. What stops two of them from both answering “dog”? Training does. For every training image, each real object is paired with exactly one query. The pairs are chosen by the Hungarian algorithm so that the total fit over all objects is as good as possible. (Training actually runs 13 groups of 100 queries side by side and pairs each group on its own, which gives the model more practice; only one group is kept for use.) Every other query is taught that the right answer was “nothing here”. A second query that also says “dog” is penalized, so the model learns not to repeat itself. That is why RF-DETR needs no NMS (non-maximum suppression), the clean-up step that many detectors use to delete overlapping duplicate boxes. So far, this is exactly how RF-DETR detects objects. If you want more depth on that side, I covered it in an earlier post . Segmentation adds one thing on top: every query will also paint a mask. Queries trained not to repeat each other leave nothing to clean up. Every pixel gets a description To paint a mask, the model needs something at pixel level. The memory is too coarse for that: each cell covers 12 × 12 pixels of the input. Step 4. Every pixel gets a description. The memory is enlarged three times on each side and refined into a pixel map with 256 channels. Four channels are drawn for illustration. So the segmentation branch first enlarges the memory with bilinear interpolation , the same smooth resizing a photo editor uses. Seg Small goes from 32 × 32 to 96 × 96. The paper states the rule: “segmentation features are always upsampled to 1/4 of the input image resolution” . The enlarged map then passes through a few light convolution blocks. Each block is a 3 × 3 depthwise convolution, LayerNorm, a linear layer, and a GELU activation, with a shortcut around them: a slimmed-down ConvNeXt block. Each decoder layer has one block, so Segmentation Small has four. A final 1 × 1 convolution and a linear layer applied at every pixel then produce the pixel map: 256 numbers for each of the 96 × 96 = 9,216 pixels. It computes this once and shares it across all queries. The design is borrowed from Mask DINO , which, in its authors’ words, “makes use of the query embeddings from DINO to dot-product a high-resolution pixel embedding map to predict a set of binary masks” . RF-DETR keeps it lighter: “Unlike MaskDINO (Li et al., 2023), we do not incorporate multi-scale backbone features in our segmentation head to minimize latency.” Remember that choice; it comes back in step 8. Each query mixes its own mask On the query side, a small MLP (multi-layer perceptron) and a linear layer turn each query's decoder output into 256 numbers. Now every query and every pixel are described by lists of the same length. The mask comes from a dot product : multiply the two lists element-wise and sum them, plus one learned offset. That gives one score per pixel. A positive score means “this pixel is mine”, a negative one means “not mine”. For Seg Small, that is 9,216 scores per query. Pause and ponder. The pixel map is computed once, before any query. It does not know which query will ask. How can the same map give the dog’s query a dog mask and a car’s query a car mask? The answer is easiest to see if you read the dot product the other way round. Think of the 256 channels of the pixel map as 256 images stacked on top of each other. The dot product is then a weighted sum of those images, and the query’s 256 numbers are the weights. Step 5. Each query mixes its own mask. The dog’s query weights the animal-like channel up and the others down. The two cars share the vehicle-like channel, and a left↔right channel separates them. Illustrative. In this illustration, one channel responds to anything vehicle-like, one to animals, one to people, and one simply grows from left to right. The dog’s query gives the animal channel a large positive weight and the others negative weights, so the sum is positive only on the dog. The two cars show why this works for individual objects, not just for categories. Both car queries weight the vehicle channel up. Car 1’s query also weights the left↔right channel down, while car 2’s query weights it up, so each sum stays positive only on its own car. Real learned channels are not this tidy, but the arithmetic is exactly this. The paper puts it the same way: “Interestingly, we can interpret these pixel embeddings as segmentation prototypes” , citing YOLACT , which “produce[s] instance masks by linearly combining the prototypes with the mask coefficients” . The Ultralytics YOLO segmentation models use that recipe with 32 prototypes and 32 weights per detected object. RF-DETR uses 256 channels, and its weights come from the queries, one per object. A mask is not drawn; it is a weighted sum each query chooses. Masks sharpen layer by layer The model does not wait for its last decoder layer to paint. In the paper’s words, it dots “all projected query token embeddings (at the output of each decoder layer transformed by a FFN)” with the pixel map. Decoder layer 1 uses the pixel map after conv block 1, layer 2 the map after block 2, and so on. Step 6. Masks sharpen layer by layer. Each decoder layer paints a mask from one more conv block, and each is trained against the true outline. Illustrative. Each mask is trained against the true outline, so later layers can refine what earlier ones sketched, and the last layer’s mask is the one kept. A useful side effect: if you need more speed, later layers can be dropped at inference, and the earlier ones still give usable masks. Dropping a decoder layer also drops a conv block, so, as the paper notes, “truncating the decoder also shrinks the size of the segmentation branch” . Training checks a few hundred points Training extends the pairing from step 3. When the model decides which query belongs to which object, it now compares masks too, not only classes and boxes. It uses two scores for that: a binary cross-entropy , which checks each pixel’s yes-or-no, and a Dice score, which checks how well the two shapes overlap as a whole. After pairing, the same two scores become the mask losses, each weighted 5.0 by default. Pause and ponder. Segmentation Small paints 9,216 mask pixels per query, and during training it compares 13 groups of 100 queries against every object in every image. Do we really need every pixel to tell a good mask from a bad one? RF-DETR does not compare every pixel. It compares masks at sampled points, an idea from PointRend . The number of points is a sixteenth of the mask: 9,216 ÷ 16 = 576 points for Seg Small. Step 7. Training checks a few hundred points. Pairing uses the same 576 random points for every query; the loss puts 75% of its points where the model is least sure, here around the cyclist, and 25% at random. The two use sampling differently. Pairing draws one set of uniform random points and scores every query against every object at those same points, which keeps the comparison fair. The loss is computed only for the paired queries, so it can be smarter. It draws three times as many random candidates and keeps the 75% of its points where the predicted score is closest to zero, the pixels the model is least sure about. The remaining 25% are random. Points where the model is already confident are mostly skipped; points near its predicted outline get most of the attention. Before it ever sees COCO, the standard benchmark dataset, RF-DETR-Seg is also pretrained on Objects365 , with instance masks generated automatically by SAM 2 , so the detection and segmentation parts learn from the same data. Most pixels are easy; training focuses on the hard ones. Thin parts are the hardest The quarter-resolution pixel map sets a limit. In Seg Small, one mask cell covers 4 × 4 input pixels. Pause and ponder. Our dog spans about 8 × 7 mask cells. Its legs and ears are about one cell wide. What happens to them? Step 8. Thin parts are the hardest. A simple ideal mask, built from how much of each 96 × 96 cell the dog covers and then enlarged and cut at zero the same way, overlaps the drawn dog with an IoU of 0.87. Legs and ears go first. To see the limit, I built a simple ideal mask on the 96 × 96 grid: each cell’s score comes from how much of it the dog covers, then the map is enlarged and cut at zero the same way the model does it. Its IoU (intersection over union, the overlap divided by the combined area) with the drawn dog is 0.87, not 1.0. The body is fine; it loses on the thin legs and the ear tip. Tweaking how the cells are filled moves the score by about a point; it does not get near 1.0. Mask DINO also paints on a quarter-resolution grid, so both share that limit. What RF-DETR gives up is the high-resolution backbone detail that helps fill that grid on fine structures; in exchange, it stays fast. The remedy is a larger model: RF-DETR-Seg 2XL works at 768 pixels with a 192 × 192 mask grid. A mask cannot be sharper than the grid it is painted on. Reading the answer At the end, RF-DETR keeps the highest-scoring query-class pairs. Each kept query brings its own mask from the last decoder layer. The mask scores are enlarged to the size of the original photo, and every pixel with a score above zero and a sigmoid probability above 50% belongs to the mask. Box, class, and mask all come from the same query, so there is no clean-up step. One query can still appear twice if it is confident about two classes, with the same mask both times. from rfdetr import RFDETRSegSmall model = RFDETRSegSmall() detections = model.predict( "https://media.roboflow.com/dog.jpg", threshold=0.5, ) masks = detections.mask # one boolean H × W mask per object The result is a supervision Detections object with boxes, classes, confidences, and a mask array. An exported model returns per-query boxes, class scores, and mask scores at the quarter-resolution grid; picking the top answers, enlarging, and thresholding run after the model. One recipe, several sizes RF-DETR-Seg comes in six sizes, all built on the same DINOv2-S backbone. They differ mainly in input resolution and decoder depth. Configurations as shipped in rfdetr 1.11.2. The paper’s Table 8 lists 300 queries for L; the released config uses 200. Compared with the detection-only models, the segmentation models have deeper decoders and fewer queries: Seg Nano has 4 decoder layers where detection Nano has 2, and Seg Small has 4 where detection Small has 3. The paper suggests this “likely reflects a minimum viable segmentation head depth” , and explains the trade: “to offset its latency, RF-DETR-Seg reduces its total number of queries, yielding a thin, deep decoder” . The parameter count barely moves across sizes, from 33.6 million for N to 38.6 million for 2XL, because every size shares the same backbone. How it compares Here are the reported instance-segmentation numbers next to YOLO26-Seg, a recent Ultralytics generation, size for size. AP50:95 is COCO’s standard accuracy score: average precision, averaged over overlap thresholds from 0.50 to 0.95. Latency is measured on an NVIDIA T4 GPU with TensorRT at half precision (FP16), one image at a time. RF-DETR-Seg is more accurate at every size. YOLO26-Seg is faster at four of five sizes and smaller at four of five. RF-DETR-Seg is more accurate at every size, but the lead varies: 5.6 AP50:95 points at N, 1.3 at M, 2.0 at XL against X. YOLO26-Seg is faster at N, S, L, and X; RF-DETR-Seg is faster at M, 5.9 ms against 6.32 ms. YOLO26-Seg has fewer parameters up to L, while at the top RF-DETR-Seg XL has 38.1 million against 62.8 million for YOLO26-X-Seg. Against the previous generation the gap is wider. The paper reports that “RF-DETR-Seg (nano) outperforms YOLOv11-Seg (x-large) on COCO while running 4 × as fast” : 40.3 against 40.1 AP50:95, at 3.4 ms against 13.7 ms. Three caveats. First, these numbers were measured by the team that builds RF-DETR; treat them as a starting point for your own test. Second, the YOLO26-Seg rows come from the RF-DETR benchmarks page, not the paper. Third, the paper notes that “our latencies for YOLOs also include the conversion of protos into masks” , a step some published YOLO timings leave out, so compare latencies only when you know whether that step is included. Accuracy per millisecond is the claim; your masks on your data are the test. The whole story in eight steps Strip away the details, and RF-DETR-Seg does two things at once. It finds each object with one question, and it paints that object’s pixels by mixing a shared pixel map with the question’s own weights. Here is the path from photo to mask, one step per animation: A box is a rough answer; a mask marks exactly which pixels belong to each object. The photo is cut into patches, and a pretrained backbone turns them into the memory, a grid of descriptions. A hundred learned questions each try to claim one object, and are trained not to repeat each other, so no clean-up step is needed. The memory is enlarged to a quarter of the input and refined into a pixel map, 256 numbers per pixel. Each query’s 256 weights mix the pixel map’s channels into its own mask. Every decoder layer paints a mask, each trained against the true outline; the last one is kept. Training compares masks at a few hundred points, most of them where the model is unsure. Thin parts of small objects are the hardest, because the grid is a quarter of the input. RF-DETR-Seg end-to-end. Photo → patches → memory → four answers → pixel map → four score maps → four masks. The decoder's answers are carried along until the mix step uses them. If your objects have complicated shapes, like bicycles, people, or animals, a box wastes most of its area on them, and this is the cheapest way to get the pixels right. If they are tiny, pick a larger size for a finer grid. If every millisecond counts, YOLO26-Seg is faster at most sizes; RF-DETR-Seg trades a little time for accuracy. And whatever you pick, test it on your own data. The next post takes the same street and the same queries and adds key

To paint a mask, the model needs something at pixel level. The memory is too coarse for that: each cell covers 12 × 12 pixels of the input.

Step 4. Every pixel gets a description. The memory is enlarged three times on each side and refined into a pixel map with 256 channels. Four channels are drawn for illustration.

So the segmentation branch first enlarges the memory with bilinear interpolation, the same smooth resizing a photo editor uses. Seg Small goes from 32 × 32 to 96 × 96. The paper states the rule: “segmentation features are always upsampled to 1/4 of the input image resolution”.

The enlarged map then passes through a few light convolution blocks. Each block is a 3 × 3 depthwise convolution, LayerNorm, a linear layer, and a GELU activation, with a shortcut around them: a slimmed-down ConvNeXt block. Each decoder layer has one block, so Segmentation Small has four. A final 1 × 1 convolution and a linear layer applied at every pixel then produce the pixel map: 256 numbers for each of the 96 × 96 = 9,216 pixels. It computes this once and shares it across all queries.

The design is borrowed from Mask DINO, which, in its authors’ words, “makes use of the query embeddings from DINO to dot-product a high-resolution pixel embedding map to predict a set of binary masks”. RF-DETR keeps it lighter: “Unlike MaskDINO (Li et al., 2023), we do not incorporate multi-scale backbone features in our segmentation head to minimize latency.” Remember that choice; it comes back in step 8.

Each query mixes its own mask

On the query side, a small MLP (multi-layer perceptron) and a linear layer turn each query's decoder output into 256 numbers. Now every query and every pixel are described by lists of the same length.

The mask comes from a dot product: multiply the two lists element-wise and sum them, plus one learned offset. That gives one score per pixel. A positive score means “this pixel is mine”, a negative one means “not mine”. For Seg Small, that is 9,216 scores per query.

Pause and ponder. The pixel map is computed once, before any query. It does not know which query will ask. How can the same map give the dog’s query a dog mask and a car’s query a car mask?

The answer is easiest to see if you read the dot product the other way round. Think of the 256 channels of the pixel map as 256 images stacked on top of each other. The dot product is then a weighted sum of those images, and the query’s 256 numbers are the weights.

Step 5. Each query mixes its own mask. The dog’s query weights the animal-like channel up and the others down. The two cars share the vehicle-like channel, and a left↔right channel separates them. Illustrative.

In this illustration, one channel responds to anything vehicle-like, one to animals, one to people, and one simply grows from left to right. The dog’s query gives the animal channel a large positive weight and the others negative weights, so the sum is positive only on the dog.

The two cars show why this works for individual objects, not just for categories. Both car queries weight the vehicle channel up. Car 1’s query also weights the left↔right channel down, while car 2’s query weights it up, so each sum stays positive only on its own car. Real learned channels are not this tidy, but the arithmetic is exactly this.

The paper puts it the same way: “Interestingly, we can interpret these pixel embeddings as segmentation prototypes”, citing YOLACT, which “produce[s] instance masks by linearly combining the prototypes with the mask coefficients”. The Ultralytics YOLO segmentation models use that recipe with 32 prototypes and 32 weights per detected object. RF-DETR uses 256 channels, and its weights come from the queries, one per object.

A mask is not drawn; it is a weighted sum each query chooses.
Masks sharpen layer by layer

The model does not wait for its last decoder layer to paint. In the paper’s words, it dots “all projected query token embeddings (at the output of each decoder layer transformed by a FFN)” with the pixel map. Decoder layer 1 uses the pixel map after conv block 1, layer 2 the map after block 2, and so on.

Step 6. Masks sharpen layer by layer. Each decoder layer paints a mask from one more conv block, and each is trained against the true outline. Illustrative.

Each mask is trained against the true outline, so later layers can refine what earlier ones sketched, and the last layer’s mask is the one kept. A useful side effect: if you need more speed, later layers can be dropped at inference, and the earlier ones still give usable masks. Dropping a decoder layer also drops a conv block, so, as the paper notes, “truncating the decoder also shrinks the size of the segmentation branch”.

Training checks a few hundred points

Training extends the pairing from step 3. When the model decides which query belongs to which object, it now compares masks too, not only classes and boxes. It uses two scores for that: a binary cross-entropy, which checks each pixel’s yes-or-no, and a Dice score, which checks how well the two shapes overlap as a whole. After pairing, the same two scores become the mask losses, each weighted 5.0 by default.

Pause and ponder. Segmentation Small paints 9,216 mask pixels per query, and during training it compares 13 groups of 100 queries against every object in every image. Do we really need every pixel to tell a good mask from a bad one?

RF-DETR does not compare every pixel. It compares masks at sampled points, an idea from PointRend. The number of points is a sixteenth of the mask: 9,216 ÷ 16 = 576 points for Seg Small.

Step 7. Training checks a few hundred points. Pairing uses the same 576 random points for every query; the loss puts 75% of its points where the model is least sure, here around the cyclist, and 25% at random.

The two use sampling differently. Pairing draws one set of uniform random points and scores every query against every object at those same points, which keeps the comparison fair. The loss is computed only for the paired queries, so it can be smarter. It draws three times as many random candidates and keeps the 75% of its points where the predicted score is closest to zero, the pixels the model is least sure about. The remaining 25% are random. Points where the model is already confident are mostly skipped; points near its predicted outline get most of the attention.

Before it ever sees COCO, the standard benchmark dataset, RF-DETR-Seg is also pretrained on Objects365, with instance masks generated automatically by SAM 2, so the detection and segmentation parts learn from the same data.

Most pixels are easy; training focuses on the hard ones.
Thin parts are the hardest

The quarter-resolution pixel map sets a limit. In Seg Small, one mask cell covers 4 × 4 input pixels.

Pause and ponder. Our dog spans about 8 × 7 mask cells. Its legs and ears are about one cell wide. What happens to them?
Step 8. Thin parts are the hardest. A simple ideal mask, built from how much of each 96 × 96 cell the dog covers and then enlarged and cut at zero the same way, overlaps the drawn dog with an IoU of 0.87. Legs and ears go first.

To see the limit, I built a simple ideal mask on the 96 × 96 grid: each cell’s score comes from how much of it the dog covers, then the map is enlarged and cut at zero the same way the model does it. Its IoU (intersection over union, the overlap divided by the combined area) with the drawn dog is 0.87, not 1.0. The body is fine; it loses on the thin legs and the ear tip. Tweaking how the cells are filled moves the score by about a point; it does not get near 1.0.

Mask DINO also paints on a quarter-resolution grid, so both share that limit. What RF-DETR gives up is the high-resolution backbone detail that helps fill that grid on fine structures; in exchange, it stays fast. The remedy is a larger model: RF-DETR-Seg 2XL works at 768 pixels with a 192 × 192 mask grid.

A mask cannot be sharper than the grid it is painted on.
Reading the answer

At the end, RF-DETR keeps the highest-scoring query-class pairs. Each kept query brings its own mask from the last decoder layer. The mask scores are enlarged to the size of the original photo, and every pixel with a score above zero and a sigmoid probability above 50% belongs to the mask. Box, class, and mask all come from the same query, so there is no clean-up step. One query can still appear twice if it is confident about two classes, with the same mask both times.

from rfdetr import RFDETRSegSmall

model = RFDETRSegSmall()
detections = model.predict(
    "https://media.roboflow.com/dog.jpg",
    threshold=0.5,
)
masks = detections.mask  # one boolean H × W mask per object

The result is a supervision Detections object with boxes, classes, confidences, and a mask array. An exported model returns per-query boxes, class scores, and mask scores at the quarter-resolution grid; picking the top answers, enlarging, and thresholding run after the model.

One recipe, several sizes

RF-DETR-Seg comes in six sizes, all built on the same DINOv2-S backbone. They differ mainly in input resolution and decoder depth.

Configurations as shipped in rfdetr 1.11.2. The paper’s Table 8 lists 300 queries for L; the released config uses 200.

Compared with the detection-only models, the segmentation models have deeper decoders and fewer queries: Seg Nano has 4 decoder layers where detection Nano has 2, and Seg Small has 4 where detection Small has 3. The paper suggests this “likely reflects a minimum viable segmentation head depth”, and explains the trade: “to offset its latency, RF-DETR-Seg reduces its total number of queries, yielding a thin, deep decoder”. The parameter count barely moves across sizes, from 33.6 million for N to 38.6 million for 2XL, because every size shares the same backbone.

How it compares

Here are the reported instance-segmentation numbers next to YOLO26-Seg, a recent Ultralytics generation, size for size. AP50:95 is COCO’s standard accuracy score: average precision, averaged over overlap thresholds from 0.50 to 0.95. Latency is measured on an NVIDIA T4 GPU with TensorRT at half precision (FP16), one image at a time.

RF-DETR-Seg is more accurate at every size. YOLO26-Seg is faster at four of five sizes and smaller at four of five.

RF-DETR-Seg is more accurate at every size, but the lead varies: 5.6 AP50:95 points at N, 1.3 at M, 2.0 at XL against X. YOLO26-Seg is faster at N, S, L, and X; RF-DETR-Seg is faster at M, 5.9 ms against 6.32 ms. YOLO26-Seg has fewer parameters up to L, while at the top RF-DETR-Seg XL has 38.1 million against 62.8 million for YOLO26-X-Seg.

Against the previous generation the gap is wider. The paper reports that “RF-DETR-Seg (nano) outperforms YOLOv11-Seg (x-large) on COCO while running 4 × as fast”: 40.3 against 40.1 AP50:95, at 3.4 ms against 13.7 ms.

Three caveats. First, these numbers were measured by the team that builds RF-DETR; treat them as a starting point for your own test. Second, the YOLO26-Seg rows come from the RF-DETR benchmarks page, not the paper. Third, the paper notes that “our latencies for YOLOs also include the conversion of protos into masks”, a step some published YOLO timings leave out, so compare latencies only when you know whether that step is included.

Accuracy per millisecond is the claim; your masks on your data are the test.
The whole story in eight steps

Strip away the details, and RF-DETR-Seg does two things at once. It finds each object with one question, and it paints that object’s pixels by mixing a shared pixel map with the question’s own weights. Here is the path from photo to mask, one step per animation:

  1. A box is a rough answer; a mask marks exactly which pixels belong to each object.
  2. The photo is cut into patches, and a pretrained backbone turns them into the memory, a grid of descriptions.
  3. A hundred learned questions each try to claim one object, and are trained not to repeat each other, so no clean-up step is needed.
  4. The memory is enlarged to a quarter of the input and refined into a pixel map, 256 numbers per pixel.
  5. Each query’s 256 weights mix the pixel map’s channels into its own mask.
  6. Every decoder layer paints a mask, each trained against the true outline; the last one is kept.
  7. Training compares masks at a few hundred points, most of them where the model is unsure.
  8. Thin parts of small objects are the hardest, because the grid is a quarter of the input.
RF-DETR-Seg end-to-end. Photo → patches → memory → four answers → pixel map → four score maps → four masks. The decoder's answers are carried along until the mix step uses them.

If your objects have complicated shapes, like bicycles, people, or animals, a box wastes most of its area on them, and this is the cheapest way to get the pixels right. If they are tiny, pick a larger size for a finer grid. If every millisecond counts, YOLO26-Seg is faster at most sizes; RF-DETR-Seg trades a little time for accuracy. And whatever you pick, test it on your own data.

The next post takes the same street and the same queries and adds keypoints: the cyclist’s joints and the dog’s pose.

Co-authored by Claude. The model sizes and how to run them are on the RF-DETR segmentation page.

Which object in your own images would lose the most to a box? Tell me in the comments, and if you want to try RF-DETR-Seg, the code is at github.com/roboflow/rf-detr.

items.title: Anthropic’s Margin is OpenAI’s Opportunity
items.summary: OpenAI’s efforts to undercut Anthropic on price are producing some results. For instance, in May, Anthropic models powered 57% of the coding work of hundreds of engineers at Rippling, an HR software firm, while OpenAI models handled 16% of that work. Since then, the situation has reversed: 52% of the coding work is now handled by OpenAI models and 18% with Anthropic ones, as the company sought to cut costs and OpenAI proved cheaper, CEO Parker Conrad said.

items.title: The AI data center boom has a ghost problem
items.summary: Halloween ghosts on a Silicon Valley lawn. Alistair Barr/Business Insider A version of this story originally appeared in the AI Insider newsletter. Sign up for Business Insider's weekly AI Insider newsletter here . The AI data center boom looks like it's running into serious trouble. Projects are being delayed, canceled, or abandoned. Electricity shortages are holding everything up. But there's a twist: A lot of these data centers were probably never going to get built in the first place. Bernstein Research analyzed thousands of planned US data centers and concluded that only about 35% of the announced capacity is likely to become reality. The industry has a wonderful name for some of the more dubious projects: " Bragawatts ." These are enormous data centers announced by companies that often have little experience building them. Some haven't secured electricity, construction permits, or even customers. Then there are the "ghost projects." Developers submit multiple requests for electricity connections, hoping at least one location works out. In Texas, these requests have reached more than five times the state's existing electricity supply. No wonder the grid looks overwhelmed. This doesn't mean the AI boom is fake. Far from it. My colleague Eugene Kim exclusively reported this week that even Amazon, one of the world's most experienced data center builders, is struggling to get enough electricity to power its expensive AI equipment . But there's a big difference between Amazon's very real problems and an inexperienced developer announcing a gigantic project that may never happen. The AI data center boom is real, and so are the challenges of building all these facilities. But the sheer number of speculative projects may be making those challenges look bigger than they truly are. Sign up for the AI Insider newsletter here . The AI data center boom looks like it's running into serious trouble. Projects are being delayed, canceled, or abandoned. Electricity shortages are holding everything up.

But there's a twist: A lot of these data centers were probably never going to get built in the first place.

Bernstein Research analyzed thousands of planned US data centers and concluded that only about 35% of the announced capacity is likely to become reality.

The industry has a wonderful name for some of the more dubious projects: "Bragawatts."

These are enormous data centers announced by companies that often have little experience building them. Some haven't secured electricity, construction permits, or even customers.

Then there are the "ghost projects." Developers submit multiple requests for electricity connections, hoping at least one location works out. In Texas, these requests have reached more than five times the state's existing electricity supply.

No wonder the grid looks overwhelmed.

This doesn't mean the AI boom is fake. Far from it.

My colleague Eugene Kim exclusively reported this week that even Amazon, one of the world's most experienced data center builders, is struggling to get enough electricity to power its expensive AI equipment.

But there's a big difference between Amazon's very real problems and an inexperienced developer announcing a gigantic project that may never happen.

The AI data center boom is real, and so are the challenges of building all these facilities. But the sheer number of speculative projects may be making those challenges look bigger than they truly are.

items.title: Building an agentic software factory? Start with the sensor.
items.summary: A gap has long existed between the shipping velocity of the best engineering teams and the rest of the bell curve. For most of the industry’s history, it was a multiple measured in deploys per week. Agents are turning that multiple into an exponent, and the dividing line is no longer tooling or talent. It is whether a team has rebuilt its delivery system into what the industry now calls a “software factory,” a largely autonomous system where intent goes in, agents plan, write, test, and ship the changes. People own the specifications and the gates. Anthropic put a number on the gap this month. In May the company merged around 2,500 code changes a day, and by September it merged more than 30,000 . Coding stopped being the bottleneck, they write. The bottleneck became the developer infrastructure built for human scale, and they now ask what continuous integration (CI) even means when thousands of changes merge while the tests are still running. “Agents are turning that multiple into an exponent, and the dividing line is no longer tooling or talent. It is whether a team has rebuilt its delivery system into what the industry now calls a ‘software factory.'” Getting there means rethinking the delivery lifecycle around one question: how does the factory know a change works before the next thousand land on top of it? Read as a control loop, intent is the setpoint, agents are the controller, and verification is the sensor. A controller that outruns its sensor does not go faster. It retries on stale information and ships the failures the sensor would have caught. The sensor decides how much of the factory can run on its own. What an agentic software factory is made of Addy Osmani’s definition is the one most people use: a software factory is many harnessed loops running at once, fed by a work queue and drained through a review gate into production , with humans owning the whole thing from above. Intent is the specs, tickets, and scenarios that say what done means. A queue holds the backlog. A harness constrains each agent with tools, context, and rules. Generation is the coding agents . Verification is the tests, scenario runs, and runtime checks that report whether a change works before it merges. A review gate is where a person or a policy lets a change merge. Integration and deploy move it to production, and production feedback carries telemetry and incidents back into the queue. Agents changed the controller, and the sensor has to change with it Agents change the lifecycle in two places. They add a generation step, so later stages receive changes at the rate agents write them, and they turn verification from a stage people wait at into a service agents call from inside their own loop. “A controller that outruns its sensor does not go faster. It retries on stale information and ships the failures the sensor would have caught.” Control engineers mount the sensor on the running system for a reason: it is the only reading that reflects what the system does. The traditional lifecycle got by with cheaper stand-ins at every stage, unit tests at commit, integration tests in CI, a shared staging environment before release and telemetry after, because reading the real system for every change was slow and expensive. Each stage traded fidelity for speed, and the trade held while people set the pace. A developer who spent two days on a change barely noticed that staging took four hours to report. An agent that writes the change in four minutes either waits, which wastes the speed, or keeps going with whatever it can see. What it can see depends on the environments and tests it can access, and for many teams that is unit tests and mocks. Dan Shapiro’s five levels of AI coding, read by what verifies the code at each one, are a ladder of sensors. At level 3, the agent writes, and you review diffs all day, which is where almost everyone tops out . At level 4, the tests are the sensor, and whether that is safe depends on what they run against. StrongDM’s two rules — that code must not be written by humans and must not be reviewed by humans — certainly received attention. What made them workable was its Digital Twin Universe, behavioral clones of its third-party dependencies that agents run thousands of scenarios against. That is the line between adding agents to a pipeline and running a factory. The rules are free to copy, but the sensor is the expensive part, and it is what gives people their place: on the intent and the slow loops like architecture, not as the per-change check for a controller a hundred times faster than they read. A sensor has three properties, and the factory needs all three Latency Latency is how long the sensor takes to report, and delay destabilizes the loop. Every action between a change and its signal rests on a state that no longer exists, so the agent retries on an unverified change and other agents build on that. Track time to signal: the minutes from a change being ready to a verified result in a production-like environment. Fidelity Fidelity is how closely the reading matches the real system, and it matters more than latency, because the loop trusts a biased sensor. Unit tests and mocks report what a change does against a model of its dependencies, and agents optimize for whatever the sensor rewards. StrongDM saw its agents return true to pass narrow tests, so it moved its scenarios outside the codebase as a holdout set. The number to track is escape rate, the share of failures found after merge. Bandwidth Bandwidth is how many readings the sensor can take at once, and it is the property agents strain first. Shared staging takes one reading at a time, so with fifty agents’ readings queued or mixed, failures stop being attributable to a change. The number is concurrent verification capacity. Autonomy follows the sensor, so measure the sensor A factory can run as much autonomy as its sensor can verify and no more, which Osmani calls back pressure. With only compilers and unit tests, the agent proposes, and a person verifies everything. With per-change checks in a production-like environment, the agent iterates in a loop until the change is verified, and a person reviews the intent and evidence. Anthropic’s engineers still review every major change to their codebase, but they examine evidence that the change does what was intended rather than reading every line. With held-out scenarios and fast rollback, defined classes of change can merge without review. “A factory can run as much autonomy as its sensor can verify and no more. The sensor, not the model, sets the level.” The sensor, not the model, sets the level. A better controller on a biased sensor reaches the wrong answer faster, and reviewing every change is also a sensor, with latency in hours and bandwidth of a few changes per reviewer per day. So measure the sensor, not the agents’ effort. Pull requests and tokens per engineer count how hard the agents work. Time to signal, escape rate, and concurrent verification capacity tell you which property is weak, and change failure rate and rework rate tell you whether the loop is stable. Start with the first three. Cloud-native systems make the sensor harder In a distributed system, behavior breaks across service boundaries. A field renamed in one service that another team’s service still reads. A consumer that assumes an ordering its topic does not guarantee. Each change is correct at its own boundary and wrong in combination, so a faithful sensor has to include the real services around a change. That is what makes all three properties hard to get at once: fidelity means real neighbors, and latency and bandwidth mean an environment with those neighbors for every change, in minutes. Most teams get two of the three. Verifying a batch of pull requests on a shared environment gets fidelity and nothing else. The environment is real, but it takes one reading at a time and reports hours after the change, outside any agent’s loop. Testing several changes in one run to save time makes a failure impossible to attribute, so the agent cannot act on a red result. Duplicating the full stack, or a large part of it, per change improves fidelity and isolation but adds latency and bandwidth costs. Provisioning takes tens of minutes, far longer than an agent’s attempt, and cost grows with every concurrent agent, so teams ration it to the changes that justify it. Behavioral twins work for third-party services with stable public behavior. Still, for 150 internal services, a clone is a second implementation that drifts while the real services already run in a cluster. At scale, a factory needs a way to give each agent, and each change, a realistic environment where the real services answer its calls, without the cost or latency of duplicating the stack. That sensor satisfies all three properties, and it is the model we built Signadot to enable. Rethinking the SDLC for agents starts with the sensor The gap between the teams merging 30,000 changes a day and the rest is not the agents, which everyone now has. It is a delivery system rebuilt around a sensor that reports in minutes, matches the real system, and runs for every change at once. On cloud-native systems , that sensor is the hardest part to build, and it decides whether more agents ship more software or only break more of it. For the full architecture, see our complete guide to software factories for cloud-native systems .

Anthropic’s engineers still review every major change to their codebase, but they examine evidence that the change does what was intended rather than reading every line. With held-out scenarios and fast rollback, defined classes of change can merge without review.

“A factory can run as much autonomy as its sensor can verify and no more. The sensor, not the model, sets the level.”

The sensor, not the model, sets the level. A better controller on a biased sensor reaches the wrong answer faster, and reviewing every change is also a sensor, with latency in hours and bandwidth of a few changes per reviewer per day.

So measure the sensor, not the agents’ effort. Pull requests and tokens per engineer count how hard the agents work. Time to signal, escape rate, and concurrent verification capacity tell you which property is weak, and change failure rate and rework rate tell you whether the loop is stable. Start with the first three.

Cloud-native systems make the sensor harder

In a distributed system, behavior breaks across service boundaries. A field renamed in one service that another team’s service still reads. A consumer that assumes an ordering its topic does not guarantee. Each change is correct at its own boundary and wrong in combination, so a faithful sensor has to include the real services around a change. That is what makes all three properties hard to get at once: fidelity means real neighbors, and latency and bandwidth mean an environment with those neighbors for every change, in minutes. Most teams get two of the three.

Verifying a batch of pull requests on a shared environment gets fidelity and nothing else. The environment is real, but it takes one reading at a time and reports hours after the change, outside any agent’s loop. Testing several changes in one run to save time makes a failure impossible to attribute, so the agent cannot act on a red result.

Duplicating the full stack, or a large part of it, per change improves fidelity and isolation but adds latency and bandwidth costs. Provisioning takes tens of minutes, far longer than an agent’s attempt, and cost grows with every concurrent agent, so teams ration it to the changes that justify it. Behavioral twins work for third-party services with stable public behavior. Still, for 150 internal services, a clone is a second implementation that drifts while the real services already run in a cluster.

At scale, a factory needs a way to give each agent, and each change, a realistic environment where the real services answer its calls, without the cost or latency of duplicating the stack. That sensor satisfies all three properties, and it is the model we built Signadot to enable.

Rethinking the SDLC for agents starts with the sensor

The gap between the teams merging 30,000 changes a day and the rest is not the agents, which everyone now has. It is a delivery system rebuilt around a sensor that reports in minutes, matches the real system, and runs for every change at once.

On cloud-native systems, that sensor is the hardest part to build, and it decides whether more agents ship more software or only break more of it. For the full architecture, see our complete guide to software factories for cloud-native systems.

items.title: Banks Preparing for Aftermath of Unprecedented Catastrophe Caused by AI
items.summary: Doomsaying about the coming AI apocalypse is no longer relegated to outbursts from a few tech billionaires . Now, the major American banks whose policies dictate the flow of capital throughout the world are starting to worry about rogue AI, preparing contingency plans for the “day after” a theoretical AI-driven catastrophe. That’s according to new reporting from Axios , which notes that banks are preparing for the worst as they experience a huge rise in AI agent activity on behalf of individual customers. The main worry seems to be an influx of financial activity driven by autonomous AI agents, which have been authorized to access bank accounts by their human users. In some cases, as Axios noted previously , those agents are making moves that haven’t explicitly been prompted by humans — a few even going so far as to contact call centers on behalf of their users, without being instructed to do so. That’s become a major liability for top banks like Morgan Stanley, Bank of America, JPMorgan, and Wells Fargo, which are scrambling to implement security procedures and policy updates to get ahead of the AI swarm. Failing to stay on top of emerging risks, some experts say, could result in financial catastrophe. As chief economist at the Apollo wealth management firm Torsten Slok explained in a late September brief , AI agents operating under instructions to “optimize the return” on their users’ money could mean banks “lose a large share of the cheap deposits they rely on to make loans, which would be a problem for the entire financial system.” As skeevy as that admission is, there’s plenty of truth in the fact that our for-profit banking system is simply not designed to handle that volume of consumer-friendly optimization. A casino whose slot machines paid out to every player wouldn’t stay in business very long, after all. Other finance gurus have pointed to the fact that AI agents might simply go haywire, regardless of what they’ve been instructed to do. “You’re assuming they’re going to act properly on your behalf and they may not,” JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon told a room full of economists and financial experts in Chicago earlier this month. “You can’t stop it. You just have to, like, manage the hell out of it.” More on AI safety: Godfathers of AI Say Models Are So Out of Control That They Need to Be Airgapped for the Safety of Us All

items.title: Inside the cyber flaw scramble that brought the AI threat to life
items.summary: Cybersecurity leaders talked with BI about the rise in demand for workers in the field. MASTER/Getty Images All hell broke loose this week after a security flaw in 70% of the world's websites was made public. It was supposed to be kept under wraps as a fix was deployed, but one researcher jumped the gun. Chainguard CEO Dan Lorenc told POLITICO why he decided to go public. The exposure was immense, with AI multiplying the risks — and yet time-tested global cybersecurity procedures appeared to be functioning. Then suddenly, it all broke down. The decision by a cybersecurity company on Wednesday to prematurely release information about a flaw in the popular PHP computer programming language left much of the web exposed to hackers, triggering a panic that brought to life months of warnings of how the AI-powered era could cause widespread damage. The flaws in PHP, discovered using AI tools through a monthslong process coordinated by OpenAI, caused cyber agencies across Europe, the US, the UK, Australia and Canada to post urgent warnings Wednesday. Numerous governments took websites offline as a precaution. While no major hacking damage was immediately apparent, the way the incident unfolded over 72 hours showed how easily cybersecurity processes can break down and the outsized consequences of cyber risks in the AI era. The man who set off the chain reaction with the early release — Chainguard's CEO Dan Lorenc — quickly apologized in a LinkedIn post. But on Thursday, in an interview with POLITICO, Lorenc said he'd shared the information ahead of time because the flaw was already being exploited. Though others disputed that, Lorenc said he believed he'd seen enough evidence to invalidate an embargo set up to allow time to find a fix for the flaws. While he disputed that his actions would have caused problems for other defenders, Lorenc said that the evidential threshold in these coordinated cyber defense systems is a "grey area." The revelation of the PHP flaw brings out into the open what cyber officials have been bracing for since the arrival of the most powerful tools of artificial intelligence, which not only can be used to discover vulnerabilities but also to exploit them at scale. The cybersecurity world's long-established protocols helped prevent disaster scenarios in which hackers would have successfully exploited the vulnerabilities to take control of numerous websites and access their data. But the scale and end-of-days potential of AI-driven cyber risks are now visible for the world to see. This "is what happens when AI turns up a flaw that's been hiding for years," said Eylam Milner, cofounder and chief technology officer at cybersecurity startup Echo. The vulnerabilities, he added, are "about as serious as it gets for the web." Origin story Understanding how this week's emergency unfolded offers a glimpse at how companies and authorities are working to stave off attacks — and how much risk they face going forward. The origins of the incident can be traced back as far as April, when leading frontier AI firm Anthropic unveiled Mythos, leading some in the cybersecurity world to worry that systems would quickly be overrun by advanced artificial intelligence, with potential for catastrophic events to ensue. But while researchers did find more flaws in computer systems in the months after Anthropic and other AI firms like OpenAI released those models, they had little impact in the real world. Even the Hugging Face incident, a widely discussed hack that saw OpenAI's autonomous AI agents go rogue during an internal security evaluation, related more to the level of control AI companies exert over their models than their power to break into systems worldwide. That changed this week after researchers unveiled the vulnerability in PHP, a coding language estimated to be integrated into some 70% of the web. The process by which information about flaws is released among cybersecurity officials and affiliated companies is crucial. Through a long-standing practice known as coordinated disclosure, researchers and companies that identify flaws can find a fix and share it confidentially with agencies and others before releasing it to the public, meaning they don't hand malicious hackers the gift of a hole without a fix. In the case of the PHP flaw, that process worked well, but not perfectly. Information about the bugs started to circulate ahead of the planned release time. Then, according to the PHP Foundation, Chainguard "unilaterally broke the embargo," which "disregarded weeks of work by many parties toward a coordinated disclosure." PHP Foundation executive director Elizabeth Barron told POLITICO by email that while it was "disappointed" with Chainguard, it hopes to "rebuild trust with them in the future to ensure we can continue to collaborate effectively." After the leak — which meant information about the bugs was in the open before the fix was ready — confusion quickly ensued, with government bodies and private companies choosing to temporarily shut down their websites rather than risk potentially damaging breaches to their data and the sites themselves. Early Thursday, Matthew Prince, the CEO of Cloudflare, an internet services company widely used by websites to block cyberattacks, which gives it a high level of visibility into what hackers are doing, said in a post on X that it had seen "millions" of attempts to exploit the flaw. Cloudflare saw thousands in the 10 hours before the flaw was publicly announced, then tens of thousands in the 45 minutes after the announcement, hundreds of thousands within two hours, and now millions, Prince said. Amazon's cloud division also said the flaw is "now being broadly exploited in the wild." One senior US government cyber official said that federal authorities have been overwhelmed — and not just by PHP. The same day the world was racing to address PHP, they were also dealing with bugs in node.js, a widely used JavaScript framework, Fortinet, GitHub and Oracle. "The fire department is fighting multiple fires at once," the official said, adding: "The good news is they're all one-story structures on fire, which the fire department deals with all day, every day." More to come Dauntingly, OpenAI said there's more on the way. "These bugs are among several significant vulnerabilities we've already found and are working to fix, and we expect similar findings to increase sharply in the coming months," the company said Wednesday in a statement. Matthijs van Amelsfort, head of the Dutch cybersecurity agency, said in an interview that the job of keeping computer systems safe has been transformed by the advancement of AI. "As soon as the frontier models came out, that's exactly what we said: This will be the trend," he said. "And actually that's happening now." Thomas Caspers, vice president of Germany's cyber agency BSI, concurred: "We expect that [to be] happening more and more during the coming months." AI also ramps up the risks once the flaws are out in the open. Cyber agencies' recommendation that organizations take their websites offline was "really a drastic measure," Caspers said. "We wouldn't have done that a few years ago or so." But because AI has made it quicker and easier to exploit flaws, "we had to do that," he said. At the same time, the use of advanced AI to detect the flaws may create a new level of protection against malicious hackers looking to take advantage of them. Caspers said that though his German agency has also seen attacks, it has not seen any successful use of the flaw by hackers. "It seems a little bit more complicated than expected to exploit," he said. Despite the fact that AI offers a new way to discover flaws, the work involved in keeping systems protected is more quotidian, with cyber agencies urging organizations to install the fix shared by the PHP Foundation, in a process known as patching. "There are three things that you have to do right now," said van Amelsfort from the Dutch agency. "And that's patch, patch, and patch." John Sakellariadis contributed to this report. items.title: Why Kubernetes autoscalers keep fighting each other (and why the solution must be autonomous)
items.summary: Ask an SRE a deceptively simple question: What is the right size for checkout-api , and how many replicas should it run right now? Their Helm values specify replicas: 3, cpu: 1000m , and memory: 2Gi . But the live cluster tells a different story: HPA has scaled the app to 11 replicas on CPU load; VPA insists it is over-provisioned, recommending cpu: 350m and memory: 3.1Gi ; KEDA demands 24 replicas due to an upstream Kafka lag spike; and Karpenter has provisioned two new nodes, sizing physical capacity strictly against declared requests rather than actual usage. “Five sources yield five contradictory answers. Each controller acts logically in isolation, but none sees the complete picture.” Five sources yield five contradictory answers. Each controller acts logically in isolation, but none sees the complete picture. This gap between isolated observations and actual workload needs represents a core architectural failure in modern Kubernetes operations. The breakdown of the Unix philosophy in elastic systems Kubernetes and its components were built on the Unix philosophy: build small, modular tools that do one thing well. For container orchestration, this principle seemed intuitive: HPA handles horizontal elasticity based on runtime resource utilization. VPA handles vertical container sizing based on historical consumption. KEDA bridges event sources to replica counts based on external queue lag. Karpenter and Cluster Autoscaler manage node capacity when pods are Pending. GitOps (Argo CD / Flux) enforces baseline cluster state from version control. In standard Unix environments, tools like grep and awk compose cleanly because they process immutable streams of text sequentially. One tool finishes and hands its output to the next. Autoscaling controllers do not operate sequentially. They execute concurrently, acting on the same target workload and mutating the same API fields: .spec.replicas, .resources.requests , and the underlying node pool. Each runs in an independent reconciliation loop , assuming exclusive control over workload sizing without visibility into adjacent tools. “Determining workload capacity is a single, coupled mathematical equation. Splitting it across decoupled controllers creates thrashing instead of modular efficiency.” Determining workload capacity is a single, coupled mathematical equation. Splitting it across decoupled controllers creates thrashing instead of modular efficiency. The four collisions: how autoscalers fight When independent control loops manipulate interdependent variables, feedback loops destabilize into four common failure modes. 1. The denominator collapse: HPA vs. VPA HPA calculates target replicas using pod CPU utilization as a percentage of declared requests: current metric = total actual usage / total declared requests Declared resource requests serve as the denominator. When VPA operates concurrently, it lowers CPU requests to eliminate waste. This shrinks the denominator. A minor traffic increase now pushes percentage utilization past HPA’s threshold, triggering an aggressive horizontal scale-out. As more pods split the traffic, per-pod usage drops, prompting VPA to shrink requests even further. The workload enters a death spiral: VPA continuously shrinks pod size while HPA creates an unmanageable fleet of microscopic containers. 2. Multi-writer race condition: native HPA vs. KEDA When teams combine queue-based scaling via KEDA with standard CPU-based HPA, two controllers target the same deployment’s /scale sub-resource. If an event queue spikes, KEDA scales the deployment up to drain the backlog. However, if those worker pods are I/O-heavy with low CPU usage, the standalone HPA evaluates the low utilization, concludes the app is over-provisioned, and scales it back down. The API server records alternating rescale events while actual processing throughput stalls. 3. GitOps drift ping-pong: declarative IaC vs. dynamic runtime GitOps engines enforce Git repositories as the source of truth. When HPA scales a deployment during a traffic spike, Argo CD flags the application as OutOfSync . If auto-sync is enabled, GitOps resets the live deployment back to its baseline, starving the application of capacity during peak demand. While engineers often configure GitOps to ignore replica differences, this breaks declarative infrastructure: Git no longer reflects production reality, and future rollouts risk quietly restoring outdated baselines. 4. The multiplier effect at the node layer Node autoscalers like Karpenter make placement decisions based strictly on declared container requests , not actual consumption. If a container requests 1000m CPU but consumes only 150m, the scheduler still reserves the entire core. Karpenter provisions physical instances to satisfy phantom demand, multiplying upstream sizing inefficiencies into massive cloud bills. Across production fleets, average cluster CPU utilization hovers around 8% despite heavy node provisioning. The path to a better autoscaler Every traditional autoscaler answers a narrow question: “What should my individual setting be?” But the real operational requirement is broader: What combination of replicas, resource requests, limits, and scaling thresholds satisfies latency SLOs at the lowest cost, and when should that configuration change? Horizontal and vertical sizing are interlinked variables of a single optimization problem. A true autoscaler cannot rely on reactive, single-metric heuristics. It must function as a unified control plane defined by five core capabilities: Unified signal ingestion: Evaluating CPU/memory metrics, queue depth, transaction rates, latency SLO compliance, node pricing, and IaC manifests simultaneously. Joint decision-making: Computing a single action vector that defines horizontal limits and vertical resource requests in tandem, rather than delegating replicas to one tool and pod sizing to another. Continuous GitOps synchronization: Submitting automated, reasoned pull requests against application repositories instead of forcing GitOps engines to ignore live cluster state, keeping version control aligned with real-world needs. Predictive and proactive capacity planning: Reactive scaling is inherently flawed because initializing new compute resources takes time. Traditional reactive controllers wait for load to breach arbitrary thresholds, causing latency spikes during sudden demand surges. A true autoscaler incorporates predictive algorithms to analyze historical consumption, detect daily or weekly seasonality, and forecast workload demand. It pre-warms application capacity and resizes resources before traffic arrives, transforming scaling from a panicked reflex into a smooth, scheduled operation. Explainable auditing: Providing clear operational rationale for every adjustment, giving SREs full transparency into trade-offs between cost savings, predicted demand, and latency boundaries. From reactive reflexes to true autonomy The cloud-native ecosystem routinely conflates “ automated” and “ autonomous .” Today’s autoscalers are automated : they act like biological reflexes, measure an isolated telemetry signal, and fire a predefined response. When an event occurs, HPA triggers, KEDA scales, or Karpenter provisions. But reflexes lack a central nervous system. When five independent reflexes fire simultaneously on the same limb, the system thrashes. “Today’s autoscalers are automated: they act like biological reflexes. But reflexes lack a central nervous system. When five independent reflexes fire simultaneously on the same limb, the system thrashes.” Autonomy requires a closed loop that observes the entire operating environment, understands the tradeoffs between performance and cost, and assumes end-to-end accountability for the outcome. The Unix philosophy remains the right blueprint for the execution layer: HPA, VPA, KEDA, and Karpenter should continue executing the specific API mutations they were designed to handle. What Kubernetes fundamentally lacks is the central intelligence layer that decides what those actuators should do. The next time your platform team debates whether to implement HPA or VPA, step back and ask a broader question: Who decides this workload’s size, and do they have the full picture? In modern clusters, nobody does. Solving Kubernetes rightsizing requires building a system that finally does.
items.summary_html:
Ask an SRE a deceptively simple question: What is the right size for checkout-api, and how many replicas should it run right now?

Their Helm values specify replicas: 3, cpu: 1000m, and memory: 2Gi. But the live cluster tells a different story: HPA has scaled the app to 11 replicas on CPU load; VPA insists it is over-provisioned, recommending cpu: 350m and memory: 3.1Gi; KEDA demands 24 replicas due to an upstream Kafka lag spike; and Karpenter has provisioned two new nodes, sizing physical capacity strictly against declared requests rather than actual usage.

“Five sources yield five contradictory answers. Each controller acts logically in isolation, but none sees the complete picture.”

Five sources yield five contradictory answers. Each controller acts logically in isolation, but none sees the complete picture. This gap between isolated observations and actual workload needs represents a core architectural failure in modern Kubernetes operations.

The breakdown of the Unix philosophy in elastic systems

Kubernetes and its components were built on the Unix philosophy: build small, modular tools that do one thing well. For container orchestration, this principle seemed intuitive:

  • HPA handles horizontal elasticity based on runtime resource utilization.
  • VPA handles vertical container sizing based on historical consumption.
  • KEDA bridges event sources to replica counts based on external queue lag.
  • Karpenter and Cluster Autoscaler manage node capacity when pods are Pending.
  • GitOps (Argo CD / Flux) enforces baseline cluster state from version control.

In standard Unix environments, tools like grep and awk compose cleanly because they process immutable streams of text sequentially. One tool finishes and hands its output to the next.

Autoscaling controllers do not operate sequentially. They execute concurrently, acting on the same target workload and mutating the same API fields: .spec.replicas, .resources.requests, and the underlying node pool. Each runs in an independent reconciliation loop, assuming exclusive control over workload sizing without visibility into adjacent tools.

“Determining workload capacity is a single, coupled mathematical equation. Splitting it across decoupled controllers creates thrashing instead of modular efficiency.”

Determining workload capacity is a single, coupled mathematical equation. Splitting it across decoupled controllers creates thrashing instead of modular efficiency.

The four collisions: how autoscalers fight

When independent control loops manipulate interdependent variables, feedback loops destabilize into four common failure modes.

1. The denominator collapse: HPA vs. VPA

HPA calculates target replicas using pod CPU utilization as a percentage of declared requests:

current metric = total actual usage / total declared requests

Declared resource requests serve as the denominator. When VPA operates concurrently, it lowers CPU requests to eliminate waste. This shrinks the denominator. A minor traffic increase now pushes percentage utilization past HPA’s threshold, triggering an aggressive horizontal scale-out. As more pods split the traffic, per-pod usage drops, prompting VPA to shrink requests even further. The workload enters a death spiral: VPA continuously shrinks pod size while HPA creates an unmanageable fleet of microscopic containers.

2. Multi-writer race condition: native HPA vs. KEDA

When teams combine queue-based scaling via KEDA with standard CPU-based HPA, two controllers target the same deployment’s /scale sub-resource. If an event queue spikes, KEDA scales the deployment up to drain the backlog. However, if those worker pods are I/O-heavy with low CPU usage, the standalone HPA evaluates the low utilization, concludes the app is over-provisioned, and scales it back down. The API server records alternating rescale events while actual processing throughput stalls.

3. GitOps drift ping-pong: declarative IaC vs. dynamic runtime

GitOps engines enforce Git repositories as the source of truth. When HPA scales a deployment during a traffic spike, Argo CD flags the application as OutOfSync. If auto-sync is enabled, GitOps resets the live deployment back to its baseline, starving the application of capacity during peak demand. While engineers often configure GitOps to ignore replica differences, this breaks declarative infrastructure: Git no longer reflects production reality, and future rollouts risk quietly restoring outdated baselines.

4. The multiplier effect at the node layer

Node autoscalers like Karpenter make placement decisions based strictly on declared container requests, not actual consumption. If a container requests 1000m CPU but consumes only 150m, the scheduler still reserves the entire core. Karpenter provisions physical instances to satisfy phantom demand, multiplying upstream sizing inefficiencies into massive cloud bills. Across production fleets, average cluster CPU utilization hovers around 8% despite heavy node provisioning.

The path to a better autoscaler

Every traditional autoscaler answers a narrow question: “What should my individual setting be?” But the real operational requirement is broader: What combination of replicas, resource requests, limits, and scaling thresholds satisfies latency SLOs at the lowest cost, and when should that configuration change?

Horizontal and vertical sizing are interlinked variables of a single optimization problem. A true autoscaler cannot rely on reactive, single-metric heuristics. It must function as a unified control plane defined by five core capabilities:

  1. Unified signal ingestion: Evaluating CPU/memory metrics, queue depth, transaction rates, latency SLO compliance, node pricing, and IaC manifests simultaneously.
  2. Joint decision-making: Computing a single action vector that defines horizontal limits and vertical resource requests in tandem, rather than delegating replicas to one tool and pod sizing to another.
  3. Continuous GitOps synchronization: Submitting automated, reasoned pull requests against application repositories instead of forcing GitOps engines to ignore live cluster state, keeping version control aligned with real-world needs.
  4. Predictive and proactive capacity planning: Reactive scaling is inherently flawed because initializing new compute resources takes time. Traditional reactive controllers wait for load to breach arbitrary thresholds, causing latency spikes during sudden demand surges. A true autoscaler incorporates predictive algorithms to analyze historical consumption, detect daily or weekly seasonality, and forecast workload demand. It pre-warms application capacity and resizes resources before traffic arrives, transforming scaling from a panicked reflex into a smooth, scheduled operation.
  5. Explainable auditing: Providing clear operational rationale for every adjustment, giving SREs full transparency into trade-offs between cost savings, predicted demand, and latency boundaries.
From reactive reflexes to true autonomy

The cloud-native ecosystem routinely conflates “automated” and “autonomous.”

Today’s autoscalers are automated: they act like biological reflexes, measure an isolated telemetry signal, and fire a predefined response. When an event occurs, HPA triggers, KEDA scales, or Karpenter provisions. But reflexes lack a central nervous system. When five independent reflexes fire simultaneously on the same limb, the system thrashes.

What Kubernetes fundamentally lacks is the central intelligence layer that decides what those actuators should do.

The next time your platform team debates whether to implement HPA or VPA, step back and ask a broader question: Who decides this workload’s size, and do they have the full picture?

In modern clusters, nobody does. Solving Kubernetes rightsizing requires building a system that finally does.
