items.title: Serverless Secure: Exploring AWS Continuum Through an Authorization Lab
items.summary: Moving an application to serverless removes a lot of infrastructure work. It does not remove the need to decide who can access each piece of data. A valid login can coexist with a serious authorization flaw. That makes a small notes application an interesting way to explore AWS Continuum: can security tooling connect a mistake in application code with its actual impact? This is a project idea I would like to explore, rather than a lab I have already built. I have not put it into practice yet because of the potential costs, particularly for Continuum’s code vulnerability analysis. The architecture and testing workflow below are a proposal; I do not have deployment results, confirmed Continuum findings, or remediation outcomes to share at this stage. A login is only the beginning Imagine two users, Alice and Bob. Each can create and read private notes. Alice signs in and requests GET /notes/alice-note-id . The API validates her token, and a Lambda function retrieves the requested note from DynamoDB. Now suppose Alice submits Bob’s note ID instead. If the function only looks up the supplied ID, it may return Bob’s note to Alice. Her token is valid, but the requested action is unauthorized. This is broken object-level authorization, often discussed as BOLA or IDOR. Using unpredictable IDs makes guessing harder; it does not replace an ownership check. Authentication answers “Who are you?” Authorization answers “May you access this resource?” Both checks matter. The proposed serverless architecture The proposed lab would use Amazon Cognito for user sign-in, an API Gateway HTTP API with a JWT authorizer, AWS Lambda for application logic, and DynamoDB for notes. Terraform would describe the infrastructure, and GitHub Actions could run checks and deploy changes. Cognito supplies the user identity. API Gateway validates the token. Lambda must then enforce access to the requested note using trusted identity claims from the validated request context. The intentionally vulnerable version would omit that final check. Its purpose would be to make one failure easy to understand and reproduce with synthetic data in an isolated account or environment. Where AWS Continuum fits AWS describes Continuum for code vulnerabilities as combining repository analysis with optional AWS environment context. It prioritizes issues, evaluates exploitability, and can reproduce some findings in a sandbox. Proposed fixes can arrive as pull requests for human review. The launch announcement makes clear that approval is required before a fix ships. [1] Continuum operates around the development and security workflow. It is not a request authorizer that the Lambda function calls whenever a user opens a note. For this lab, the question is whether its supported analysis can recognize the missing ownership check and provide useful evidence or remediation. That is an experiment, not a promised detection outcome. Application support, configuration, and the specific code path must be checked before making claims about coverage. What a meaningful experiment would show First, establish the behavior independently of any scanner: Alice can read her own note, and the vulnerable version also returns Bob’s note when she supplies its ID. Next, inspect the actual Continuum results. Record what it detects, the evidence it provides, and any limitations. An absent finding is also worth documenting; it does not make the application secure. Finally, review any proposed patch and rerun the authorization checks. The fixed version should allow Alice to read her notes, deny access to Bob’s, and reject unauthenticated requests. Equivalent checks belong on update, delete, and list operations too. A stronger data model can place notes under an owner-scoped partition key derived from the verified user identity. The client must never be allowed to choose the identity used for that scope. IAM permissions still matter, but a shared Lambda execution role does not automatically enforce each end user’s ownership rules. Can the lab be free? The application and the security service have separate cost models. Small application traffic may fit service allowances or eligible credits, depending on the account. DynamoDB’s free provisioned capacity allowance should not be confused with free on-demand requests. [3–7] Continuum also separates code vulnerability analysis from penetration testing. Its pricing page lists a two-month penetration-testing trial with up to 400 task-hours per trial month for eligible new customers of that capability. Code vulnerability analysis instead lists context and inference charges; the same page does not advertise an equivalent trial for it. [2] The penetration-testing trial therefore does not establish that repository scanning and generated remediation pull requests are free. Check account eligibility and the selected capability before enabling it. AWS Config collection, logging, and other supporting resources may add charges. Budget alerts help track spending but should not be treated as an immediate spending cutoff. What this lab is intended to teach The useful result is a documented comparison between observable application behavior, security-tool evidence, and a verified fix. Serverless changes who operates the infrastructure. Resource authorization remains an application design responsibility. If you try it, I would love your feedback For now, this remains an idea on paper because of the potential cost of running the full experiment. If you decide to build it, I would love to hear how it goes: whether Continuum identifies the authorization gap, how useful its evidence and suggested fix are, and what the experiment actually costs. Findings, limitations, and unexpected results would all be valuable feedback. References Pricing and availability checked on October 24, 2026; verify again before deploying. AWS Continuum launch announcement AWS Continuum pricing AWS Free Tier FAQs AWS Lambda pricing Amazon API Gateway pricing Amazon DynamoDB pricing Amazon Cognito pricing

items.title: An Ancient Virus Explains Why the Human Brain Is Special
items.summary: Welcome back to the Abstract! Here are the studies this week that invaded our brains, thought fast, swapped coffins, and hit the art gallery. First, an ancient viral pandemic that afflicted many of our primate relatives—but somehow missed humans—may help explain how we got so smart (relatively speaking). Then: mammal brains eat crow, an upcycled sarcophagus, and a trip to the starry Provençal summer of 1889. As always, for more of my work, check out my book First Contact: The Story of Our Obsession with Aliens , or subscribe to my personal newsletter The BeX Files . Your brain on viral content Gerdes, Patricia; Karlsson, Ofelia; Garza, Raquel; Atacho, Diahann A. M. et al. “Retroviral insertions contributed to the divergence of human and chimpanzee brains.” Science Advances. A virus that infected chimpanzees millions of years ago shaped the divergence of human and chimp brain development, shedding light on how our own species came to be more cognitively complex than our closest living relatives, according to a new study. Retroviruses are infectious agents that can invade the genomes of their hosts and insert copies of their own genetic material, producing long-term evolutionary effects. Researchers have now discovered a family of these endogenous retroviruses called PTERV1—which are abundant in chimpanzees, but absent in humans—that influence brain development. “Among primates, the human brain stands out as the largest and most complex due in part to an increase in cortical neurons and increase in synaptic connectivity,” said a team led by researchers from Lund University. “With a size roughly three times that of our closest living evolutionary relative, the chimpanzee, it has unique cognitive capabilities.” Sketches of gorilla, chimp, and human skulls. Image: kaiwei zhang “The underlying genetic divergences responsible for these differences are still poorly understood,” the researchers continued, noting that their new findings “reveal a mechanism by which endogenous retroviral insertions contributed to human-chimpanzee brain divergence.” The team discovered the mechanism using human and chimpanzee brain organoids, which are miniature clusters of neurons grown from stem cells that can model some aspects of brain development. The results revealed chimpanzee-specific PTERV1 insertions on chromosome 19 that silences a gene called LINC00662. In contrast, this gene is active during human brain development, and affects neuronal maturation, development, and outgrowth. “These PTERV1 insertions are thought to have originated from infections that occurred in the ancestors of African apes about 5 to 7 million years ago,” said the team. “PTERV1 elements are found in chimpanzees, bonobos, and gorillas…Notably, the absence of PTERV1 insertions from the human genome suggests that either the human and chimpanzee lineages did not occupy the same habitat at the time or that germline-competent cells of the human ancestor were resistant to this infection.” “In summary, this study describes how retroviral insertions contributed to the functional divergence of the human and chimpanzee brain, providing a mechanism by which retroviral infections influenced primate brain speciation,” they added. In other words, early humans appear to have dodged consequential pandemics that widely infected our primate brethren simply because they had a random immunity to it, or roamed different ranges. While retroviruses are far from the only factor in our cognitive development, it’s still eerie to think that our human brain—that brilliant lump you are using to read these words—is shaped by dumb luck. In other news… Another brain to crow about Schmidbauer, Philipp and Nieder, Andreas. “Ultrarapid decision-making in an avian brain.” Science. Speaking of interspecies brain-offs, it seems the birds have got us beat—at least when it comes to snap decisions. Scientists have discovered that carrion crows ( Corvus corone ) can make ultrafast choices in “approximately 235 milliseconds on average, which is roughly twice as fast as has been observed in monkeys or humans and without sacrificing accuracy,” according to a new study. Crow acing the test. Image: Andreas Nieder A pair of researchers observed two crows performing a common discrimination task in which dots on a screen move left, right, up, or down. The crows selected the predominant direction by pecking a target circle on a touchscreen, after which they were rewarded with promptly dispensed treats. The crows performed the task dozens of times at extremely high speeds, achieving an overall choice accuracy of 75 percent (crow 1) and 73 percent (crow 2). “Having diverged from mammals more than 360 million years ago, birds evolved a distinct nuclear pallium”—a part of the vertebrate forebrain—”that lacks the layered neocortex yet retains key organizational and computational principles characteristic of mammalian brains,” said study authors Philipp Schmidbauer and Andreas Nieder of the University of Tübingen. “These findings highlight the extraordinary efficiency of avian decisionmaking circuitry, possibly shaped by evolutionary pressures for rapid visuomotor control,” the team added. So if anyone ever calls you a birdbrain, the correct response is “thanks.” 🌘 Subscribe to 404 Media to get The Abstract , our newsletter about the most exciting and mind-boggling science news and studies of the week. Who is this sarcopha-guy? Rodwell, Warwick. “Westminster Abbey’s Roman Sarcophagus and its Afterlife.” Journal of the British Archaeological Association. Archaeologists may have finally discovered the mysterious identity of an ancient skeleton buried in a Roman-era sarcophagus that was first unearthed on the grounds of Westminster Abbey more than 200 years ago. Despite an inscription on the sarcophagus identifying the occupant as Valerius Amandinus—a wealthy Londoner who lived between 300 to 400 AD—the bones likely belong to a medieval monk named Ælfwig, born centuries later in the year 993. Interior of the sarcophagus, as found upon opening in 2016. Image: Rodwell, Warwick , 2026. “The burial was of a male, probably in his late forties, and was radiocarbon dated to around the turn of the 11th century,” said study author Rodwell Warwick of Westminster Abbey. “The corpse had been laid in a timber coffin and covered with lime; it was then placed inside the sarcophagus. It is argued that this was the prestigious burial of Abbot Ælfwig.” The sarcophagus was exhumed and moved to a northern courtyard during King Henry III’s reconstruction of the abbey in the mid-1200s, where it laid for about six centuries. On Easter Monday 1820, the coffin was “wantonly broke by workmen” according to a note from an unknown contemporary archivist. Any grave goods were likely plundered by this crew and the sarcophagus was hastily put back together and reburied with the bones all jumbled up inside. It was then re-discovered in 1869 with a note that the burial “‘had been subjected to violence by a previous examination.” It turns out anything is recyclable—even sarcophagi. The discovery that this Roman coffin at some point took on another tenant now raises the new question of how the earthly remains of Valerius Amandinus got evicted and where they ultimately wound up. “The Starry Night”—of July 22, 1889? Kim, Elijah Jeong-hyun et al. “The actual sky of Van Gogh’s Starry Night: a multidisciplinary reconstruction.” Scientific Reports. With its vibrant colors and psychedelic swirls, Vincent Van Gogh’s “The Starry Night” is one of the most beloved and recognizable paintings in art history. For years, experts and admirers have debated whether the mesmerizing skyscape, which van Gogh painted during an asylum stay in Provence, was a fantastical portrayal or if the artist included realistic renderings of astronomical phenomena. Now, a team has proposed that the celestial elements of the painting match with a specific night—July 22, 1889—when “the waning-crescent Moon, Venus, and the Hyades cluster gather within that narrow frame,” according to a new study. This date conflicts with the conventional timeline of van Gogh painting “The Starry Night” weeks earlier in June. “The question dividing fantasy from observation remained a matter of qualitative interpretation and was never treated in a physically decidable form,” said researchers led by Elijah Jeong-hyun Kim of Kyung Hee University. “The approach of this study shifts the burden of proof: if the celestial arrangement on the canvas matches a specific dawn sky, that match itself becomes what the imaginative reading must explain.” The Pepe Silvia meme meets “The Starry Night.” Image: Kim et al., Scientific Reports (2026) The team’s findings “suggest that the night sky in ‘The Starry Night’ originated from observation of a specific celestial arrangement, and call for reconsidering the June dating,” they continued. “This framework can extend to historical night paintings as a reproducible scientific art history.” I love a hyper-niche new subfield—let’s call this one “forensic astroartistry.” Regardless of the painting’s exact date of origin, it has inspired wonder and fascination for more than a century—including these new stellaria of long-lost summer nights. Thanks for reading! See you next week.

Welcome back to the Abstract! Here are the studies this week that invaded our brains, thought fast, swapped coffins, and hit the art gallery.

First, an ancient viral pandemic that afflicted many of our primate relatives—but somehow missed humans—may help explain how we got so smart (relatively speaking). Then: mammal brains eat crow, an upcycled sarcophagus, and a trip to the starry Provençal summer of 1889.

As always, for more of my work, check out my book First Contact: The Story of Our Obsession with Aliens, or subscribe to my personal newsletter The BeX Files. 

Your brain on viral content 

Gerdes, Patricia; Karlsson, Ofelia; Garza, Raquel; Atacho, Diahann A. M. et al. “Retroviral insertions contributed to the divergence of human and chimpanzee brains.” Science Advances.

A virus that infected chimpanzees millions of years ago shaped the divergence of human and chimp brain development, shedding light on how our own species came to be more cognitively complex than our closest living relatives, according to a new study. 

Retroviruses are infectious agents that can invade the genomes of their hosts and insert copies of their own genetic material, producing long-term evolutionary effects. Researchers have now discovered a family of these endogenous retroviruses called PTERV1—which are abundant in chimpanzees, but absent in humans—that influence brain development.   

“Among primates, the human brain stands out as the largest and most complex due in part to an increase in cortical neurons and increase in synaptic connectivity,” said a team led by researchers from Lund University. “With a size roughly three times that of our closest living evolutionary relative, the chimpanzee, it has unique cognitive capabilities.”

Sketches of gorilla, chimp, and human skulls. Image: kaiwei zhang

“The underlying genetic divergences responsible for these differences are still poorly understood,” the researchers continued, noting that their new findings “reveal a mechanism by which endogenous retroviral insertions contributed to human-chimpanzee brain divergence.”

The team discovered the mechanism using human and chimpanzee brain organoids, which are miniature clusters of neurons grown from stem cells that can model some aspects of brain development. The results revealed chimpanzee-specific PTERV1 insertions on chromosome 19 that silences a gene called LINC00662. In contrast, this gene is active during human brain development, and affects neuronal maturation, development, and outgrowth.  

“These PTERV1 insertions are thought to have originated from infections that occurred in the ancestors of African apes about 5 to 7 million years ago,” said the team. “PTERV1 elements are found in chimpanzees, bonobos, and gorillas…Notably, the absence of PTERV1 insertions from the human genome suggests that either the human and chimpanzee lineages did not occupy the same habitat at the time or that germline-competent cells of the human ancestor were resistant to this infection.”

“In summary, this study describes how retroviral insertions contributed to the functional divergence of the human and chimpanzee brain, providing a mechanism by which retroviral infections influenced primate brain speciation,” they added.

In other words, early humans appear to have dodged consequential pandemics that widely infected our primate brethren simply because they had a random immunity to it, or roamed different ranges. While retroviruses are far from the only factor in our cognitive development, it’s still eerie to think that our human brain—that brilliant lump you are using to read these words—is shaped by dumb luck.

In other news…

Another brain to crow about

Schmidbauer, Philipp and Nieder, Andreas. “Ultrarapid decision-making in an avian brain.” Science.

Speaking of interspecies brain-offs, it seems the birds have got us beat—at least when it comes to snap decisions. Scientists have discovered that carrion crows (Corvus corone) can make ultrafast choices in “approximately 235 milliseconds on average, which is roughly twice as fast as has been observed in monkeys or humans and without sacrificing accuracy,” according to a new study.

Crow acing the test. Image: Andreas Nieder

A pair of researchers observed two crows performing a common discrimination task in which dots on a screen move left, right, up, or down. The crows selected the predominant direction by pecking a target circle on a touchscreen, after which they were rewarded with promptly dispensed treats. The crows performed the task dozens of times at extremely high speeds, achieving an overall choice accuracy of 75 percent (crow 1) and 73 percent (crow 2).

“Having diverged from mammals more than 360 million years ago, birds evolved a distinct nuclear pallium”—a part of the vertebrate forebrain—”that lacks the layered neocortex yet retains key organizational and computational principles characteristic of mammalian brains,” said study authors Philipp Schmidbauer and Andreas Nieder of the University of Tübingen.   

“These findings highlight the extraordinary efficiency of avian decisionmaking circuitry, possibly shaped by evolutionary pressures for rapid visuomotor control,” the team added.

So if anyone ever calls you a birdbrain, the correct response is “thanks.” 

🌘
Subscribe to 404 Media to get The Abstract, our newsletter about the most exciting and mind-boggling science news and studies of the week.
Who is this sarcopha-guy?

Rodwell, Warwick. “Westminster Abbey’s Roman Sarcophagus and its Afterlife.” Journal of the British Archaeological Association.

Archaeologists may have finally discovered the mysterious identity of an ancient skeleton buried in a Roman-era sarcophagus that was first unearthed on the grounds of Westminster Abbey more than 200 years ago. 

Despite an inscription on the sarcophagus identifying the occupant as Valerius Amandinus—a wealthy Londoner who lived between 300 to 400 AD—the bones likely belong to a medieval monk named Ælfwig, born centuries later in the year 993. 

Interior of the sarcophagus, as found upon opening in 2016. Image: Rodwell, Warwick, 2026.

“The burial was of a male, probably in his late forties, and was radiocarbon dated to around the turn of the 11th century,” said study author Rodwell Warwick of Westminster Abbey. “The corpse had been laid in a timber coffin and covered with lime; it was then placed inside the sarcophagus. It is argued that this was the prestigious burial of Abbot Ælfwig.”

The sarcophagus was exhumed and moved to a northern courtyard during King Henry III’s reconstruction of the abbey in the mid-1200s, where it laid for about six centuries. On Easter Monday 1820, the coffin was “wantonly broke by workmen” according to a note from an unknown contemporary archivist. Any grave goods were likely plundered by this crew and the sarcophagus was hastily put back together and reburied with the bones all jumbled up inside. It was then re-discovered in 1869 with a note that the burial “‘had been subjected to violence by a previous examination.”

It turns out anything is recyclable—even sarcophagi. The discovery that this Roman coffin at some point took on another tenant now raises the new question of how the earthly remains of Valerius Amandinus got evicted and where they ultimately wound up. 

“The Starry Night”—of July 22, 1889?

Kim, Elijah Jeong-hyun et al. “The actual sky of Van Gogh’s Starry Night: a multidisciplinary reconstruction.” Scientific Reports.

With its vibrant colors and psychedelic swirls, Vincent Van Gogh’s “The Starry Night” is one of the most beloved and recognizable paintings in art history. For years, experts and admirers have debated whether the mesmerizing skyscape, which van Gogh painted during an asylum stay in Provence, was a fantastical portrayal or if the artist included realistic renderings of astronomical phenomena.

Now, a team has proposed that the celestial elements of the painting match with a specific night—July 22, 1889—when “the waning-crescent Moon, Venus, and the Hyades cluster gather within that narrow frame,” according to a new study. This date conflicts with the conventional timeline of van Gogh painting “The Starry Night” weeks earlier in June.

“The question dividing fantasy from observation remained a matter of qualitative interpretation and was never treated in a physically decidable form,” said researchers led by Elijah Jeong-hyun Kim of Kyung Hee University. “The approach of this study shifts the burden of proof: if the celestial arrangement on the canvas matches a specific dawn sky, that match itself becomes what the imaginative reading must explain.”

The Pepe Silvia meme meets “The Starry Night.” Image: Kim et al., Scientific Reports (2026)

The team’s findings “suggest that the night sky in ‘The Starry Night’ originated from observation of a specific celestial arrangement, and call for reconsidering the June dating,”  they continued. “This framework can extend to historical night paintings as a reproducible scientific art history.” 

I love a hyper-niche new subfield—let’s call this one “forensic astroartistry.” Regardless of the painting’s exact date of origin, it has inspired wonder and fascination for more than a century—including these new stellaria of long-lost summer nights.

Thanks for reading! See you next week.

items.title: Regression Testing in Agile for RAG Applications
items.summary: Here’s a sprint story that’s getting really common. The team building the company’s AI assistant tweaks the chunking strategy, because answers about long policy documents felt a bit thin. Demo day comes, the new answers look great, everyone’s happy. Then a week later support pings: the assistant now gets refund questions wrong. Questions it used to nail. Nobody touched the refund docs. Nobody touched the refund prompt. But retrieval-augmented generation has a lot of moving parts, and changing one of them can quietly shift behavior somewhere else entirely. That’s exactly the kind of thing regression testing in agile is supposed to catch. The twist is that RAG apps break in ways traditional regression suites were never designed to notice. Why RAG apps regress in sneaky ways A RAG app is really a chain of little decisions. Somebody decided how to slice the docs into chunks. Somebody picked an embedding model to turn those chunks into vectors. There’s a retriever deciding which chunks look relevant to a question, and only after all that does the LLM get to write anything. Every single one of those is fair game for a tweak in any given sprint. And they do get tweaked. A lot. Chunk size and overlap. The embedding model. How many chunks get retrieved. A new reranker. A prompt rewrite. A newer LLM version. Fresh documents getting ingested. Any one of those can improve answers on the questions the team was looking at, while making things worse for questions nobody checked. The tricky part is that nothing errors. No stack trace, no 500. The app just answers a little differently, and sometimes a little wrong. What a RAG regression actually looks like It helps to know what you’re hunting for. Most RAG regressions fall into a handful of buckets. The most common is retrieval drift. The right document used to land in the top results and now it doesn’t, so the model answers from the wrong context, or from none at all. Then there’s answer drift, where retrieval’s fine but the model now phrases things in a way that drops a key detail, or hedges where it used to be clear. Faithfulness can slip too, with the model adding claims the retrieved text doesn’t support. And don’t forget the boring ones. A prompt change alters the output format and the frontend can’t parse it anymore. Citations start pointing at the wrong source. The answer gets twice as long and latency creeps up. All very real, all very easy to miss in a demo. Splitting RAG regression testing into layers Here’s a lesson people tend to learn the hard way. Testing the whole chain with one kind of test is mostly an exercise in frustration. LLM output wobbles between runs, even with the temperature at zero, so end-to-end tests flake and nobody can tell why. You’ll have a much better time testing each layer in its own way. Retrieval: does the right context still show up? Start here, honestly. It’s the easiest layer to test properly, and it pays off the most. You need a golden set: a bunch of real questions, and for each one, a note of which documents or chunks really ought to come back. Then you just count. How often do those expected sources make it into the top results? That’s basically recall at your top-k cutoff, and it’s a number you can watch sprint over sprint. Retrieval tests are pretty deterministic as long as the index and embedding model don’t change, which makes them great regression checks. And when a team does swap the embedding model or re-chunk everything, comparing these scores before and after shows exactly which questions got worse. Generation: is the answer still right? This layer’s fuzzier. For each golden question, it helps to write down the key facts a good answer must include, rather than one exact expected answer. Then check whether new answers still include them, and whether they stay faithful to the retrieved context. Plenty of teams use an LLM as a judge here, scoring answers against a rubric. That works, with one caution. The judge is an LLM too, so it wobbles. Pin the judge model and its settings, treat its scores as a trend rather than gospel, and look at the actual answers whenever scores drop. Open-source evaluation libraries like Ragas can take care of a lot of this scoring for you. Contract: does the output still fit the app? This one’s plain old software testing, and it’s often skipped. If the frontend expects JSON with an answer field and a citations list, check that shape on every run. If citations should point at real document IDs, check that too. These tests are cheap, they’re deterministic, and they catch a surprising number of “it worked in the demo” bugs. Making the pipeline code testable on every pull request There’s a catch with all of the above. Running live evaluations calls real models and real vector stores, which is slow, costs money and gives slightly different results each time. You don’t want that on every pull request. But a lot of what changes in a sprint isn’t the model at all. It’s the code around it: the orchestration logic, how retrieved chunks get stitched into the prompt, how the response gets parsed, how citations get rendered. That code deserves fast, deterministic tests just like any other. The trick is to record a real run once, model calls and retrieval calls included, and replay those recorded responses in tests. Keploy, an open-source tool, does this by capturing an app’s traffic with eBPF at the kernel level, without code changes, and saving outbound calls as mocks. That covers HTTP calls to LLM APIs, plus queries to vector stores running on Postgres or Redis. Replayed, the pipeline gets identical model and retrieval responses every run, so if a test fails, it’s because the pipeline code changed, not because the model felt creative today. Fitting RAG regression testing into the sprint Here’s a rhythm that maps nicely onto how agile teams already work. On every pull request, run the fast, deterministic stuff: contract checks and replayed pipeline tests. They finish in seconds and catch code-level breakage before merge. Nightly or mid-sprint, run the retrieval checks against the golden set, especially if anyone touched chunking, embeddings or the index. Before sprint review, run the full live evaluation, with real retrieval, real model calls and scored answers, and compare everything to the previous sprint’s baseline. Any question whose score dropped gets a look before release. And then feed the golden set. Every time a user reports a bad answer, that question goes in, along with what a good answer needs. Over a few sprints the set grows into a pretty honest picture of what your users actually ask. Versioning what changes One habit makes all of this much easier: version every moving part. The prompt templates, the chunking settings, the embedding model, the index build, the LLM version. When a regression shows up, you want to look at a diff and see “this sprint we changed chunk overlap and bumped the model,” not guess. It also makes rollbacks sane. If a change made refund answers worse, you can revert just that part. Frequently asked questions How do agile teams do regression testing for RAG applications? They split it into layers. And output contracts get checked on every pull request. Fast deterministic tests run per PR, while full live evaluations run before each sprint review. How do you make tests for LLM and RAG apps deterministic? Record real model and retrieval responses once, then replay them in tests. That makes the pipeline code testable on every pull request without live model calls. Tools like Keploy record outbound calls to LLM APIs and vector stores as mocks, so replays return identical responses every run. items.title: Before you expand your GPU pool, measure the outcome
items.summary: For teams running AI workloads on Kubernetes, a fully allocated GPU pool and a growing batch-job queue might make expanding the pool seem like the obvious next step. But a growing queue could point to timing, serving capacity, or the choice of model and hardware. Before expanding a GPU pool, teams should define what success looks like, when it must finish, and what it costs to deliver. “An allocated GPU, a busy GPU, and a workload producing valuable results are not the same thing.” That starts with a distinction: an allocated GPU, a busy GPU, and a workload producing valuable results are not the same thing. Understanding how they relate can help teams use existing capacity more effectively before provisioning additional capacity they genuinely need. Start with the outcome and deadline Look at the workloads and the underlying use cases they support. A customer service chatbot may need around-the-clock inference capacity, while results from a model evaluation job might only be needed before the next internal release sync. Classifying workloads into broad categories like “inference” and “training” does not determine urgency. Some batch inference can wait, while a training job may have a firm deadline. KubeCon + CloudNativeCon is taking place in Salt Lake City from November 9 to 12. Register now ! For each workload, document its deadline, expected runtime, resource requirements, and whether interruption is acceptable. Also define what counts as a valuable output. An inference service should have a task-specific quality threshold and a latency objective. A completed request or valid JSON response alone does not show whether the workload met its objective. Keep start-time flexibility separate from interruption tolerance. A job that can wait to start may still need to run without interruption. Use scheduling flexibility before expanding the pool Suppose four compatible GPUs are available for batch work from noon until 5 p.m. Four independent evaluation jobs are ready at noon. Each needs two GPUs for one hour, and all results are due at 5 p.m. Starting all four jobs immediately requires eight GPUs. But running two at noon and two at 1 p.m. completes all four jobs by 2 p.m. using the four GPUs already available. Assuming runtimes and supporting resources remain unchanged, both schedules consume eight GPU-hours, excluding startup overhead. “Staggering reduces peak demand. The jobs still finish on time without expanding the pool.” Staggering reduces peak demand. The jobs still finish on time without expanding the pool. Before provisioning more GPUs to clear a queue, consider how much flexibility exists in start times. Tools like Kueue provide an admission control point, using configured quotas and policies to determine when work is admitted. Teams still need to decide how to represent and enforce deadlines and workload requirements. Flexible queueing can support capacity planning and reduce the need to start jobs early, only to preempt them later. Measure how much useful work the deployment can sustain Flexible scheduling can ease capacity constraints. But inference teams must also examine how well the model and serving configuration match that work. High GPU activity does not establish how much additional throughput is available. Nvidia’s profiling documentation explains that streaming multiprocessor activity can include warps waiting on memory. Serving metrics like running requests, waiting requests, and cache occupancy add context, while preemption counts help explain behavior. In vLLM, KV-cache usage measures the fraction of occupied cache blocks , but it doesn’t directly measure total serving capacity. “High GPU activity does not establish how much additional throughput is available.” Measure sustainable capacity with a representative load test. Keep the model, hardware, serving settings, and request mix constant. Then, increase the arrival rate and observe throughput, quality, and latency. The highest sustained rate that still meets the workload’s requirements, including error limits and selected latency percentiles, provides a useful capacity estimate. For interactive generation, include time to first token and subsequent token delivery, not just average completion time. DistServe shows why you should evaluate serving capacity against application-level objectives like latency. Compare production traffic with that tested capacity. Low cache occupancy may warrant further investigation, but claiming ten times more throughput requires a throughput test. Brief queues can represent temporary bursts, while persistent queues might require diagnosis. Neither on its own identifies the limiting resource. Connect OpenCost data to verified outcomes The FinOps community frames AI efficiency around cost and useful outcomes . For AI workloads , cost becomes more useful when it connects to the outcomes the infrastructure helps deliver. Kubernetes teams can make that relationship concrete by combining workload cost, serving behavior, and application results. Use OpenCost’s allocation API for workload costs at defined intervals, then join that data with serving telemetry and outcome records using workload identities and timestamps. OpenCost also provides opt-in inference cost tracking , including cost per million tokens. When calculating cost per outcome, include applicable GPU, CPU, memory, and other infrastructure costs, and document how shared and idle costs are assigned. Add relevant costs outside OpenCost separately without counting them twice. One useful metric is cost per verified outcome : total attributable cost divided by the number of results that meet the defined quality requirements and are delivered within the required time. Account for retries, failures, startup, and idle periods where they contribute to total cost. Count the final business result once. When correctness is estimated from sampled reviews, document the sampling method and uncertainty. OpenCost supplies the cost allocation details; the application supplies the outcome definition and evaluation evidence. Capacity still requires a separate measurement. OpenCost proposal 3915 explores bringing serving-engine telemetry into the cost model. The proposal remains a draft, rather than a released saturation or correctness score. Test whether the spare capacity earns its cost Consider an illustrative service receiving 1,000 tasks per hour with a 98% correctness requirement. A small model that achieves 90% is unsuitable, even if its GPU is cheap and fully occupied. A stronger model might produce 990 correct and timely results for $2 per hour while using only a fraction of its tested serving capacity. Its cost is about $2.02 per 1,000 qualifying outcomes, and that spare capacity may be an acceptable price for meeting quality requirements and absorbing bursty activity. The next test is whether a smaller GPU, fewer replicas, or a different batching setting can preserve those outcomes and the required reliability. If a tested configuration produces the same 990 qualifying results for $1.50, the cost falls to about $1.52 per 1,000 qualifying outcomes. Savings come from using fewer resources to deliver the same outcome. Increasing utilization on the original GPU without improving the outcome would provide no comparable value. “The target is a deployment that delivers the required outcomes at a defensible cost, with enough headroom to meet its requirements.” When two models both meet the minimum requirements, an additional quality improvement may justify a higher cost if it provides fewer consequential errors or requires less human review. Compare that value with actual demand. Cost per correct outcome is most useful when the outcomes being compared have similar value and error consequences. Change one major variable at a time, then compare the cost, verified outcomes, latency, and deadline attainment under representative demand. Preserve capacity for bursts and failures, and confirm that low activity corresponds to usable capacity. A GPU allocated exclusively to one Pod cannot be reassigned to another until it is released. Teams can then choose the change the evidence supports: delay flexible jobs, improve batching, resize a deployment, select a different model, or provision additional GPUs . The target is a deployment that delivers the required outcomes at a defensible cost, with enough headroom to meet its requirements.

items.title: A NATO drone maker says Ukraine's underground factories hold a lesson for the West. It's learning that firsthand.
items.summary: ORQA makes drones used by NATO militaries and parts used by Ukrainian manufacturers, and is now learning lessons about building in wartime. Reuters A NATO drone maker is partnering with a Ukrainian firm to manufacture drone parts underground. ORQA says the partnership offers lessons in keeping factories running during wartime. Western companies often overlook Ukraine's experience in manufacturing under attack, it says. A NATO drone maker is teaming up with Ukraine's defense industry and building drone parts underground. The company's CEO said it's seeking to learn lessons in wartime production that could prove critical for Western defense companies in a crisis. Croatian drone technology company ORQA and Ukrainian drone maker General Cherry are jointly developing and manufacturing interceptor drones, components, and other counter-drone systems in both countries. As part of the partnership, they are building an underground factory in Ukraine to make components. Working amid Ukraine's wartime risks teaches the company valuable lessons in manufacturing while under attack, ORQA CEO Srđan Kovačević told Business Insider. Producing components in Ukraine is also more efficient than making them in NATO and shipping them to the Ukrainian military, he said. Kovačević said his company is " learning from Ukraine ," where industry is "under constant threat." "They were also compelled to go underground, to go wide, to de-risk their assets in distribution," he said. "So I think that's the way forward for any critical capabilities." Ukrainian defense firms are splitting their manufacturing across multiple sites, frequently relocating, and moving some work underground to avoid being targeted by Russian attacks. It's less efficient, but more resilient to attacks. Some Western officials and companies warn that it's time for European industry to learn these practices amid concerns about Russian aggression. "Distributed systems are much more resilient to any disruption than concentrated systems, centralized systems," Kovačević said. "It's simply about not having a single point of failure." Ukraine has "this immensely valuable lived experience of building and scaling under fire," the ORQA CEO said, "that's being often abstracted and neglected by Western companies." That, however, is starting to change, he said. "I think the thinking is really shifting on the European side as well, that this distributed nature actually reinforces resilience even though there are economic downsides to it." Ukraine's General Cherry has experience building, innovating, and scaling while at risk of attack. AP Photo/Efrem Lukatsky, File Raivis Melnis, the defense minister of Latvia, told Business Insider that NATO companies work in a far more concentrated way than Ukrainian ones do, and "the question is whether we are ready to produce the systems in different locations, dispersed, and how we organize that." He wants Latvian and Ukrainian defense industries to work together in part so they can learn how Ukrainian companies maintain production during a war. Davyd Aloian, the deputy secretary of Ukraine's National Security and Defense Council, told Business Insider earlier this year that defense companies within parts of NATO should "definitely" start breaking up their production more. Some defense industry figures have voiced similar concerns about the state of production in the West. Karmo Saar, the head of sales for Estonian drone maker Krattworks, told Business Insider that in a war with Russia, if European companies don't disperse more, "I think we're going to be punished." Dispersing production is not without trade-offs, though. Achi, CEO of the Ukrainian-Estonian defense technology company and ground robot maker Ark Robotics, told Business Insider that such defensive steps are "necessary," but "not ideal." Operations would be easier with everything in one place. Choosing Ukraine despite the danger Some Ukrainian companies have begun setting up production in NATO countries, both to better share their expertise with partner nations and to operate without the risk of Russian attacks. But Kovačević, whose company makes drones as well as drone technology, including controllers, receivers, goggles, video equipment, and flight simulators, said that building in Ukraine comes with upsides. The company, which supplies 24 NATO allies, could have done all of its work with General Cherry in Croatia, but instead, they are spreading their joint work across both countries. Kovačević said building components in Europe and then importing them into Ukraine is "more inefficient than actually doing it in Ukraine." It's also more expensive, and Ukraine has shown its ability to produce in large volumes. Ukrainian companies like General Cherry are building at a scale and in conditions that their Western counterparts are typically not used to. AP Photo/Evgeniy Maloletka, File Localizing the supply chain also means that all parties can "exchange information more efficiently," including about what's happening and what's needed on the battlefield. He said he understands why some Ukrainian companies are building gear on NATO soil, but he sees value in partnering with General Cherry in Ukraine. He said the Ukrainian company, one of the country's largest drone makers, has "a high operational excellence in running their own manufacturing operations in a safe manner, even under constant threat." The partnership also offers lessons beyond manufacturing. He said that while the West "has a very deep technology expertise," it lacks "this lived experience of taking that technology and applying it to the operational reality of the 21st-century warfare." The goal is to both supply Ukraine and to equip NATO with weapons shaped by Ukraine's battlefield experience and expertise. In Croatia, the partners are establishing a joint serial-production facility for co-developed interceptor drones and other counter-drone systems destined for NATO, while in Ukraine, they intend to create drone components, including electronics and communications systems, which General Cherry says it will supply to "all our partners in Ukraine," not just use itself. Ukraine is already able to make the drones that the partnership will produce in Croatia, but "what they lack is the capacity to build components that go into those systems," Kovačević said, explaining the focus of the Ukrainian facility. He said the project won't disrupt Ukraine's existing supply chains. One of ORQA's priorities is to reduce reliance on Chinese products, and it wants to help Ukraine's industry do the same. "Now," he said, "it's time to merge the two and emerge better off on both sides of this partnership." Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: AI Billionaires Are Flooding Money Into Politics to Influence Elections, But It’s Backfiring
items.summary: Unreasonably wealthy AI plutocrats are pouring billions of dollars into US elections. Elon Musk alone has pumped more than $445 million into Republican campaigns ahead of the midterms, after spending a near-equal sum to get president Donald Trump elected in the last election cycle. Leading The Future, a Super PAC backed by OpenAI and Palantir cofounders and prominent tech venture capitalists including Marc Andreessen, has amassed $140 million to dole out to pro-AI candidates. But all that money doesn’t seem to be helping the AI industry’s interests, because its image is still in the toilet . A new analysis from Guardrails Action, an AI accountability advocacy group, found that voters in key battleground states still harbor mostly negative feelings towards the AI industry, with the tech being such a toxic topic that it’s potentially driving voters to cross the aisle. The survey, reported by Inc , questioned over 3,000 likely voters in Iowa, Michigan, and Ohio — states where close Senate races are unfolding — about their thoughts on AI. AI, the results showed, is a political landmine, with even a whiff of Big Tech money being potentially disastrous for a candidate’s image. Three quarters of the likely voters said that they would be less apt to vote for a candidate if they found out they had accepted a donation from an AI Super PAC . Some felt even more strongly than that. A quarter said they would switch parties to vote for a candidate who took a strong stance against AI companies and data center construction. “We found that the AI Super PACs were more toxic with voters than Wall Street, cryptocurrency or AIPAC,” Charles Blaettler, political director of Guardrails Alliance, a PAC that combats AI spending that the advocacy group is part of, told Inc . “The influence of AI money on elections and politics sits at this nexus of the anxieties that people are feeling about AI, and this increased disgust people have around corruption and special interest money and politics.” Ironically, this seems to be because voters are convinced by some of the noise coming out of the industry itself. Many luminaries in the industry have pushed doomy narratives about their tech destroying civilization, wiping out jobs, and possibly being conscious — while companies including Anthropic and OpenAI warn about their AIs going on rogue hacking sprees . More on AI: An Overwhelming Percent of Americans Now Want to Pause AI and Tax Billionaires

items.title: The rapid Ukraine war arms race means weapons makers can never truly consider a product finished
items.summary: TechEx gathers constant battlefield feedback about its drones' performance and makes regular changes based on soldiers' requests. Ukrinform/Ukrinform/Sipa USA The arms race is so intense that Ukrainian companies can never stop updating their products. One firm said a weapon could become obsolete in just three months without updates. Ukrainian firms work directly with soldiers to improve weapons faster than Western manufacturers. The fast-moving arms development race amid Russia's war against Ukraine means that the defense companies can't ever really consider a product finished or stop making regular updates, a leading Ukrainian drone maker told Business Insider. Ukraine's defense companies gather constant feedback from soldiers using their products in combat and make frequent updates, sometimes daily. Many companies and soldiers say that without these updates, their gear could become irrelevant on the battlefield within weeks. Oleg, an executive at major Ukrainian fiber-optic and interceptor drone maker TechEx, told Business Insider that "the most important thing is that you want this product to evolve over time. There will never be a moment when you just build a product, and it's just good." If a defense company "just stays with one single product, I think within three months, it will be outdated, and nobody will use it," he said, speaking on the condition that only his first name be used for safety purposes. TechEx's drones, he said, are updated weekly, sometimes with major modifications and other times with adjustments of just a few millimeters or grams. In this war, he said, "when you build a good product , the enemy builds the countermeasure." To stay in the fight, weapons makers must keep adapting. "You need to work constantly." Ukraine's Frontline Robotics, for example, told Business Insider that it gets feedback from soldiers 24/7 and makes small changes to its products up to 20 times a month, with major updates coming roughly every six months. Ukrainian soldiers assemble and repair drones close to the front lines, make upgrades, and give constant feedback and requests to their manufacturers. Carlo Bravo/Anadolu via Getty Images Ark Robotics, another Ukrainian company, said it may make about half a dozen different changes to a product over a few weeks. Companies are baking the ability for fast and regular updates into their design from the very beginning, making them modular and software-first so changes can be made remotely, quickly, and without needing to redesign or rebuild the entire product from scratch. The traditional model for Western weapons development is slower. A design is typically matured and tested before production, then is built in relatively stable batches for years, with changes made around scheduled upgrades rather than thinking about constant redesign. An analysis published by RUSI in December wrote that Western weapons systems "are treated as indivisible wholes, with procurement cycles often stretching over 10 to 20 years and upgrades requiring entire programme restructurings. This legacy approach treats innovation as a rare event rather than a continuous process." In Ukraine, companies and soldiers are allowed to directly communicate and innovate. Companies text, Whatsapp, and video call soldiers even when they are in the field to exchange constant feedback and requests. Ukraine's model is bottom-up and decentralized. Oleg said that TechEx's technical support department works with over 100 units to constantly support them and get battlefield feedback. Ukrainian companies often have employees who visit soldiers near the front lines, gather feedback, and help them make repairs or upgrades that can then be integrated back into the products. Soldiers often surprise Ukrainian companies with how they use or modify their gear, which in turn influences what they build and what features they add. TechEx updates its drones weekly, sometimes with small adjustments and sometimes with major changes. Pavlo Bahmut/Ukrinform/Sipa USA via Reuters Connect Western companies have long operated differently. Feedback from typically comes through a slower, formal chain rather than straight from the soldier who is using it. But many Western companies are starting to change their processes, particularly those with products in use in Ukraine . Earlier this year, US Air Force Gen. Alexus Grynkewich, who oversees NATO military operations as the Supreme Allied Commander Europe, told Business Insider that NATO wants to establish the same kind of battlefield feedback loop that Ukraine has, and that's something allies are working on. The drawback to constantly changing or redesigning weapons is that it makes it much harder to produce at scale. Achi, the CEO of the Ukrainian-Estonian robot, drone, and software company Ark Robotics, previously told Business Insider that when "talking about scale manufacturing, any change comes at a very high price," slowing down or even halting production. But change is essential. "You cannot afford not to be able to make changes," he said. That forces manufacturers to anticipate changing battlefield needs while trying to maintain production. Oleg said that European partners need to prepare for the reality of constant adaptation in weapons development, a warning echoed by other Ukrainian companies and officials. He cautioned that Russia is "really good at technology" and at developing countermeasures to even Ukraine's best weapons. "They're being underestimated by a lot of people." For Ukrainian weapons makers, that means there may never be a point when a product is truly finished. Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: Build Your Own Reasoning Model: A Full Video Course
items.summary: I have written a lot about reasoning models here over the last two years on Ahead of AI, including a recent article on mechanisms to control reasoning effort levels in contemporary LLMs . Reasoning models are still as relevant as ever. In fact, almost all current-generation LLMs today are reasoning models or offer a reasoning mode. For those who are interested in how reasoning models work, including inference scaling, reinforcement learning, and distillation, I wrote my recent Build Reasoning Model (From Scratch), which implements these from the ground up in PyTorch, which, in my experience, is still the best way to understand and learn how things really work. Now, in the last few months, I also sat down and recorded accompanying lectures I wanted to share with you. So, below, you will find eight reasoning model-from-scratch coding videos (11 hours of content). We start with a pre-trained LLM and implement methods to evaluate and improve it in Python and PyTorch. So, if you enjoyed my Coding LLMs from the Ground Up course last year, this is essentially the sequel (but you can also watch it without the prior course as a prerequisite). I’m currently taking a short break and will be back soon with more exciting LLM research roundups next month. In the meantime, I hope you enjoy coding along! How LLMs, reasoning models, and agents relate and fit together As a small side note, and since I often get asked how reasoning models relate to today’s AI agents, here’s a short section on this before getting started with the videos. A reasoning model is essentially an upgrade from a conventional LLM, that is, adding more post-training via reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (and optionally inference scaling techniques) to make it more capable of solving more challenging problems. Classically, reasoning models are developed for math and code, but the capabilities can generalize to other problem domains as well. A reasoning model then functions as the engine inside an agent harness, where the agent harness is a software or tooling framework around the LLM/reasoning model to tackle even more challenging problems (bigger coding tasks, travel booking, and all other sorts of personal assistant tasks). The task of the harness is sophisticated context management and giving the LLM access to tools. Figure 1: An engine analogy for conventional LLMs, reasoning models, and agent harnesses. Figure from my Components of a Coding Agent article. In this analogy depicted in the figure above, the model is the engine, and the agent harness adds the machinery that lets us use it for various things (as an upgrade from a simple chatbot interface). An agent can use either a conventional LLM or a reasoning model, but reasoning models are the more typical choice as they are more capable. (As mentioned above, most current-gen LLMs are reasoning models with variable reasoning effort settings.) So, the bottom line is that reasoning models, as the “engine,” remain an important part of understanding modern LLM agents. The resources accompanying these topics shown above are: The Build a Large Language Model (From Scratch) book and videos The Build A Reasoning Model (From Scratch) book (and videos below) The Components of a Coding Agent article on Substack The videos below focus on developing the reasoning model that can power such a system. Scope and prerequisites The reasoning-from-scratch videos focus on a small pre-trained Qwen3 model, where we implement the reasoning methods ourselves in Python and PyTorch. Starting with a pre-trained model lets us focus on the interesting part: evaluation, inference-time scaling, reinforcement learning, and distillation. Regarding the prerequisites, I recommend being comfortable with Python and PyTorch. I designed the reasoning materials as standalone content, so the previous Build A Large Language Model (From Scratch) content is recommended but not strictly required. Compute-resource-wise, you can work through the early text-generation and evaluation examples on a CPU. For the later experiments, especially training, a GPU makes the work much more practical. The first video covers the setup and some more recommendations; the repository also includes hardware and environment recommendations . Figure 2: An overview of the topics being covered. The companion book These videos accompany my book, Build a Reasoning Model (From Scratch) . If you like to read through the explanation in more detail and at your own pace, work through exercises, and so on, I recommend the book as a companion here. For the most in-depth learning experience, my suggestion is to read a chapter, work through its code alongside the corresponding video, and then try the exercises. The book is available from Manning and Amazon , and the print edition is in color! Figure 3: A random excerpt from the Build a Reasoning Model (From Scratch) print book. Thank you to everyone who has picked up a copy or recommended it to a friend. Your support helps me keep creating these materials. The videos As a last, quick side note before getting to the main videos below: For a shorter, more conceptual overview, I also recommend my AI Reasoning Models course on LinkedIn Learning (it should be free for 24h when accessing it via the link there, which shouldn’t then require a LinkedIn Premium subscription). The course is about 90 minutes and explains how reasoning models work, covering the main ideas behind inference-time scaling, reinforcement learning, and distillation. It’s a good optional preview if you’d like the main ideas without working through the full implementations below. To get to the main part of this article, here are the eight main lecture videos. 1. Motivation and code setup The first video starts with an explanation of the relationship between conventional LLMs, reasoning models, and agents. Next, the main topic of the video is setting up the coding environment. This includes installing the Python and PyTorch dependencies (with uv), among others. I also discuss hardware choices and common setup issues. Topics covered The relationship between conventional LLMs, reasoning models, and agent harnesses On the benefits of learning through code implementations The scope of this video series Installing Python dependencies Choosing hardware and checking CUDA or Apple Silicon support Using a remote GPU with VS Code and troubleshooting the environment Watch video 1 · Setup instructions 2. Loading a base model, text generation, and KV caching Before adding reasoning methods in the upcoming videos, we need a working base model. Instead of training it from scratch, since that would be a whole other book (see Build A Large Language Model (From Scratch) ), we start with a pre-trained model. Here, we load the pre-trained weights of a Qwen3 0.6B model. Then, we implement the text-generation process via a streaming text generator and add KV caching and model compilation to make text generation more efficient. These implementations give us the baseline and base components we will evaluate and improve in the following videos. Topics covered Encoding text as tokens and decoding it back into text Downloading Qwen3 weights and loading the model on the selected compute device Going over tensor shapes, logits, and next-token predictions Implementing greedy decoding and streaming text generation Handling end-of-sequence tokens and measuring generation speed Adding a KV cache to reuse attention keys and values Combining KV caching with torch.compile and comparing hardware performance Watch video 2 · Chapter 2 code 3. Building a verifier for evaluation and reinforcement learning In this lecture, we build a math-answer verifier step by step, from answer extraction to normalization and checking mathematical equivalence. We then use it to evaluate the model on MATH-500. We use this verifier to evaluate the base model’s performance on the MATH-500 evaluation dataset. However, the verifier also has a second job later in the series: providing the reward signal for reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). Topics covered Intro to verifiers and how they fit into LLM evaluation methods (other methods are covered in the book’s appendix) Reusing answer verification as a reward signal for RLVR (more on that in chapter 6) The verifier flow, including extracting final answers, normalizing answers and checking mathematical equivalence Building an answer grader and an evaluation loop for MATH-500 Comparing base and reasoning models on MATH-500 Watch video 3 · Chapter 3 code 4. Inference-time scaling: sampling and self-consistency Now we explore ways to improve answers while keeping the model weights fixed. But before implementing specific inference-scaling techniques, we first implement methods to generate diverse answers from the same prompt (this is standard practice in proprietary LLM chatbots, such as ChatGPT). Concretely, we implement temperature scaling, multinomial sampling, and top-p filtering to generate diverse responses.
