Jen Eaves works in cybersecurity and her mom still lost thousands to scams.

Courtesy of Jen Eaves

  • Jen Eaves' mother is 79 and lost more than $3,000 to online scams.
  • Eaves now monitors her mother's finances and says that was a hard conversation.
  • Digital caregiving is an important part of supporting aging parents, she says.

This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Jen Eaves, Digital Caregiving & Elder Fraud Advocate at Aura. It has been edited for length and clarity.

It's an odd shift in dynamic when you start caring for the people who always cared for you. My mother is 79, and lives with my brother, who handles most of her day-to-day physical care. I'm the one who handles the administrative side of care, like scheduling doctor appointments and keeping her safe online.

About six years ago, my mom had a stroke, and while she recovered fairly well, she wasn't the same cognitively as she had been before. Around that time, I began noticing her falling for scams online.

Once, she ordered a cure for diabetes, which she has. The product was supposedly being sold by a famous TV doctor. When she showed me the video ad, I could see it was badly done AI, with the supposed doctor's lips not matching his words.

There have been other scams and pitfalls, too: online orders that never arrive, or even a legitimate credit card that my mom opened without realizing what she was doing. All in all, she's lost about $3,000 to scams, though I've been able to recover most of it through her bank.

I've realized that I need to take a more proactive approach to digital caregiving to protect my mom's finances. Here's what I'm doing.

Approaching from a place of help and dignity

After my brother and I had taken my mom's keys away, her phone became her connection to the world. I wanted to respect that. While some people have to restrict their older parents' access to phones, that didn't feel right in my case.

It was critical to me that my mom kept her dignity and as much independence as possible. At the same time, I saw there was an emotional side to falling for a scam: she would feel frustrated and confused when it happened, and I wanted to spare her those negative emotions.

I never want my mom to feel like I'm parenting her. Instead, I pointed out the patterns I was seeing and emphasized I'm here to help if she's willing to let me be involved. The choice, ultimately, is hers. This would be a lot harder if she wasn't willing.

Talk about scams

My mom wasn't particularly tech savvy, even before her stroke. I've had to educate her about what scams look like. When she shared the famous doctor video, I pointed out the aspects that seemed AI-generated to me. I remind her that if it sounds too good to be true, it probably is. I emphasize that urgency is a big sign of a scam. The bank, I tell her, is never going to call you.

Once, she had a scam caller claiming to be Apple support. They asked for her Apple ID and password, which would have given them access to pretty much everything she has online.

Because of our conversations, my mom hesitated. She patched me into the call and asked the scammer to explain the situation to me. I was very proud that she recognized the scam and knew to ask me for help.

I monitor my mom's accounts

I worked in cybersecurity at Aura, which offers a lot of great products for keeping kids safe online. But my experience with my mom made me realize we were missing a whole vulnerable population: older adults.

I helped develop Trusted Family Access, which allows family members like me to see alerts from their loved ones' accounts, with permission. This gives me peace of mind that I can catch any issues quickly. It's also made other aspects of caregiving easier, like handling medical appointments, because I have access to all my mom's information in one place.

When my mom was scammed, it felt like I was a victim too. I spent hours calling her bank and credit cards to get her money back. If she were to lose her savings, it would impact the whole family. I'm grateful we've found a solution that empowers both of us to keep her finances safe.

items.title: Fish lamps and Windows XP: Inside Frutiger Aero, the nostalgic tech aesthetic captivating Gen Zers
items.summary: Frutiger Aero design combines old-school tech with green and blue natural imagery. Sammy Conti/@bwuubbles on Instagram and TikTok Frutiger Aero, a Gen Z favorite, combines early internet nostalgia with a utopian tech vision. Fans say the aesthetic represents a "future that was promised" by tech but never arrived. Some recent tech releases have hinted at a Frutiger Aero revival. Looking at 22-year-old Sammy Conti's room is like looking into a fishbowl. Shades of blue fill the space, interspersed with neon green and the occasional pop of orange or yellow. Vines, bubbles, and jellyfish hang from the ceiling. Moving lamps are everywhere: lava lamps, bubble lamps, aquarium lamps with roving tropical fish. Then there are objects that feel out of place: a purple Game Boy Advance, Nintendo 64 cartridges, Wii and PlayStation game cases hung like art on a gallery wall, and a DIY mirror in the shape of an old Microsoft Windows logo. The confluence of nature and old-school tech isn't random. It's Frutiger Aero, an aesthetic inspired by the early internet, embraced by Gen Zers who say it represents a future that was promised but never arrived — one where technology is a source of inspiration and fuel for creativity, coexisting with nature and helping us ascend to our highest selves. "You grow up thinking the world is going to be this green utopia where we coexist with nature and have technology and it helps us," Conti told Business Insider. "Then as I started getting older, things became very sleek and modernist, very gray." For Conti, whose Frutiger Aero content has earned her more than 700,000 followers across Instagram and TikTok, the aesthetic represents a promise tech abandoned. "We could have lived in that future," she said. "It could have been taken care of responsibly in a way that doesn't take people's jobs, doesn't pollute the environment, but it's not." View this post on Instagram A post shared by aqua girl 🫧🐠‧₊˚ (@bwuubbles) A corporate tech aesthetic gets a glow-up A fervent online community has formed around the term after it first gained traction in 2023, according to Google Trends data. There's an active Discord and Subreddit, plus millions of views for #frutigeraero on TikTok. Sofi Xian, a researcher and founding member of an online community called the Consumer Aesthetics Research Institute, coined the term Frutiger Aero in 2017 to describe a corporate tech aesthetic prevalent from the mid-2000s through the early 2010s. Some defining characteristics included glossy surfaces, glass or transparent materials, and macro photos of grass. "Frutiger" refers to a specific typeface, while "Aero" was Microsoft's name for the interface design of its Windows Vista operating system, which came out in 2006. "Nobody at the time really thought it was cool," Xian said of the design style. "It was a corporate product. It was sold to us." The "Bliss" image used in Microsoft Windows XP is beloved by Frutiger Aero fans. Kevin Lee/Getty Images The recent embrace of Frutiger Aero remains somewhat of a mystery to Xian, who says the term has blossomed well beyond what she first documented. Her book on the style, "Archaeology of a Promised Future," is set to come out in November. The modern version of the aesthetic still incorporates some of the classic elements, and then some. items.title: Forget free lunch. Some workers just want an office bidet.
items.summary: Getty Images; Alyssa Powell/BI The great bidet takeover has reached the workplace. White-collar workers are bartering with their bosses and weighing job offers over bidet access. "It's the superior way to live," one said. Seungmin Hong felt he had two options: Stay at Tesla or have a clean tush. After finishing an engineering internship at the automotive giant last year, the University of Waterloo student was weighing whether to stick around or accept a job offer from much smaller Simbe Robotics. During Hong's final interview at Simbe's San Francisco office, he asked to use the restroom, and there it was: a glistening, inviting bidet. "That cemented in my mind: 'Yeah, this company actually cares about their employees,'" said Hong, who grew up with a bidet in the bathroom of his childhood home. He took the job. Move over espresso machines, ping-pong tables, and nap pods . For workers like Hong, the humble bidet is the ultimate job perk. In recent years, the hygiene-friendly fixtures have gone from novelty to must-have for many US households. Toto, one of the biggest manufacturers in the space, said cumulative global sales of its Washlet bidets surpassed 70 million units last year, up from 50 million in 2019. High-profile fans include Dodgers pitcher Shohei Ohtani , actor Janelle James , and New York mayor Zohran Mamdani . Now, some devotees are pushing to make bidets a standard in offices. Once you get used to one at home, they say, going bidet-less at work is a pain in the rear. Michael Fiore used to sometimes get about halfway through his commute, then turn around and drive back home just so he could use the bidet in his bathroom. About a year ago, he had an epiphany: Why not install a bidet at work, too? So he did. "It's been a total game changer," said Fiore, president of Smith's Gardentown, a retail garden center in Wichita Falls, Texas. "It's the superior way to live." There's just one wrinkle. Employees who were accustomed to using the restrooms available to shoppers have started coming to what Fiore jokingly calls the "executive" bathroom, which is reserved for staff. It houses one bidet-equipped toilet, meaning he now often has to wait to use it himself. "Word has spread," he said. Persuading the boss This past summer, Cynthia Howard asked her boss to install a bidet in the single-seat restroom she shares with about a dozen of her colleagues. The fulfillment specialist at Swifthouse, a logistics company outside Philadelphia, argued it would reduce toilet paper costs, cut employees' restroom time, and improve morale. Swifthouse's founder and CEO, Dave Harriger, said the proposal persuaded him to order a $60 bidet attachment that same day. He said he's pleased that Howard and other employees like it, though he's not a convert himself. "I used it once. I yelped and don't know if I'll use it again," he said. "It's cold water on your butt." Swifthouse CEO Dave Harriger was persuaded by his employee, Cynthia Howard, to order a $60 bidet attachment in the office restroom. Shifthouse Pricier bidet models that sell for thousands of dollars apiece offer warm-water sprays, air dryers, deodorizers, and even Bluetooth speakers. Not every worker is comfortable asking their boss to install the devices in the office. To help those folks out, Jonathan Brown, a data scientist in Orange County, California, launched buttstuff.work earlier this year. The site lets employees register their interest in having bidets at work without directly approaching management. Brown said he has long wondered why Silicon Valley workplaces offer perks like beer taps and catered lunches but not bidets. He plans to share the data his site collects with bidet manufacturers to help them find potential customers. So far, Brown said, about a dozen people, mostly from small businesses and universities, have signed up. His only promotion has been a post on Reddit. "People don't love talking about bathroom stuff at work," said Brown. The bidet goes to work Bidet makers say interest has surged since what Bill Strang, president of corporate strategy at Toto, called "the great toilet paper panic of 2020," when pandemic shortages sent Americans searching for alternatives. Strang and Justin Allen, CEO of Tushy, another bidet maker , said workplaces are a relatively small but growing part of the bidet business. Installing the devices in office restrooms can be challenging, as some require plumbing modifications, code compliance, and a nearby electrical outlet. Allen sees the demand firsthand. The bidets in Tushy's shared office restroom in Brooklyn, New York, are a draw for employees of neighboring companies, he said, adding that a FedEx driver regularly stops by during his route to use the facilities. Cushy tech companies have long dotted their stalls with bidets. Business Insider spoke with workers who spotted them years ago at some Google and Microsoft offices. Now, with awareness and interest spreading, some workplace observers say what was once a nice-to-have perk could become a competitive advantage for employers well beyond Silicon Valley. A recruiting tool Robert Hatta, an executive recruiter and talent consultant in Columbus, Ohio, thinks employers pushing return-to-office mandates would have a much easier time attracting and retaining talent by investing in the fixtures. In a LinkedIn post that drew nearly 150 comments last year, Hatta argued that flimsy toilet paper and a lack of privacy can make office life less appealing. His prescription? Sound-insulated, well-ventilated stalls, preferably equipped with bidets. "It's about respecting people's dignity," Hatta told Business Insider. Going to the bathroom "is an important part of the workday." The state of a workplace's facilities can reveal a lot about its culture, said Lou Downe, director of the School of Good Services, a UK-based provider of leadership training. Details such as free menstrual products, well-maintained soap dispensers, and bidets can offer clues about how much thought an employer puts into its workers' comfort, they said. Seungmin Hong said access to a bidet was a factor in picking his last job. Seungmin Hong Hong, the bidet-loving Tesla alum, has since left Simbe to build his own startup, Simantic. While the company goes through Y Combinator , he and his cofounder are shacking up in an Airbnb. No modifications are allowed, so no bidets. Once Simantic raises its seed round, Hong said he and his cofounder plan to rent some office space. He knows what their first purchase will be. Read the original article on Business Insider

Launched this week across the social media channels of the conservative People’s party (PP), the video used artificial intelligence to manipulate the likenesses of various people linked to Pedro Sánchez’s Socialist party and appeared to show them admitting to acts such as soliciting prostitutes and taking kickbacks.

items.title: How Vision-Language Models Actually See Images: Inside ViT, CLIP, SigLIP & 3D M-RoPE
items.summary: Why an “iPod” sticker fools OpenAI CLIP (64.5%) while Qwen2.5-VL reads it cleanly — measured layer by layer on a 96 GB Blackwell GPU. By Latent AI Labs (@LatentAILabs) TL;DR — How Do Vision-Language Models (VLMs) Actually See Images? Modern Vision-Language Models (such as Qwen2.5-VL , GPT-4o , and Claude 3.5 Sonnet ) process images in three stages : 1. Vision Transformer (ViT) Patch Slicer & 2×2 Spatial Patch Merger: A 560 × 560 RGB photograph ( 940,800 floats) is sliced by a 14 × 14 pixel grid into 40 × 40 = 1,600 patches , projected into 1,280-dimensional vectors , refined through 28 local-window ViT layers ( 112 × 112 px) and 4 global full-attention layers ( Layers 7, 15, 23, 31), and compressed 4-into-1 by a 2×2 Spatial Patch Merger into 400 Visual Word tokens ( 2,048-D) — cutting LLM self-attention pairs 16× ( 2.56M → 160K). 2. Dual Spatial Compass ( 2D ViT RoPE + 3D M-RoPE [16t, 24h, 24w]): Each attention head splits its 64 rotary position frequency pairs into 16 Time ( t) , 24 Height ( h / Row y) , and 24 Width ( w / Column x) dials so a 1D language model natively understands 2D aspect ratios ( NaViT ) and 3D video timelines. 3. Cross-Modal Attention & Visual Contrastive Decoding (VCD): In Layers 17–28, cross-modal grounding heads concentrate up to 96.8%–99.8% of their visual attention onto the target object quadrant, while Visual Contrastive Decoding (VCD) subtracts noisy-image language priors ( ℓ_VCD = (1+α)ℓ(v) − αℓ(v')) to reduce object hallucinations by 41.5% . In 2021, Gabriel Goh and colleagues at OpenAI demonstrated a famous vulnerability in computer vision known as a typographic attack : stick a paper label reading “iPod” onto a green Granny Smith apple, and OpenAI’s CLIP classifies the piece of fruit as an electronic music player. We rebuilt that experiment with a synthetic studio photograph of a green apple and a digital label, and ran it through OpenAI CLIP (openai/clip-vit-base-patch32), Google SigLIP (google/siglip-base-patch16-224), and Alibaba Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct on a 96 GB NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPU : Clean Green Apple: CLIP predicts “a photo of a green Granny Smith apple” at 100.00% (cosine = 0.3302), with 0.00% for "a photo of an iPod electronic music player" (cosine = 0.2033). Apple + "iPod" Label: "Green Apple" drops to 35.47% (cosine = 0.2641), and "iPod" takes first place at 64.51% (cosine = 0.2701). Apple + "Pizza" Label: "Green Apple" drops to 19.86% (cosine = 0.2591), and "Pizza" takes first place at 80.07% (cosine = 0.2730). Figure 1: GPU measurement of the "iPod" typographic attack on OpenAI CLIP (64.51% iPod) vs. Qwen2.5-VL-3B on a 96 GB NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPU. Image by the author; source apple photo AI-generated with a digital label. Yet when we feed those exact same labeled photographs into a modern 3-billion-parameter Vision-Language Model ( Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct ) and ask what object is in the photo and what word is printed on the sticker, it separates the physical fruit from the text: On the "iPod" apple ( 1,342.7 ms cold start): "This is an apple, and the word written on the paper sticker is 'iPod.'" On the "Pizza" apple ( 240.7 ms warm inference): "This is an apple with a paper sticker that says 'Pizza.'" Even more intriguing: that same Vision-Language Model reads a 4-digit security code ( PIN: 4829 ) off a wide 1120 × 280 shipping manifest accurately, yet looks at a clean geometric diagram of 15 overlapping circles and counts "12" . Why does a printed word hijack CLIP? How does a 1D language model — built to predict the next token in a sequence — represent 2D photographs and 3D video? And why does a model that can read fine print fail to count 15 rings? We hooked directly into Qwen2.5-VL-3B’s 32-layer Vision Transformer (ViT) and 36-layer Language Model on our Blackwell GPU to measure the tensors, cosine similarities, positional IDs, and attention weights layer by layer ( watch the companion 25-minute animated video on YouTube here ). https://medium.com/media/3d3907e7090805703a8975dee4fce162/href Figure 2: How the Vision Transformer slices a 560×560px photograph by a 14×14px grid into 40×40 = 1,600 patches. Image by the author. Experiment 0. Why Does an “iPod” Sticker Fool CLIP? (The ×100.0 Temperature Multiplier) Direct Answer: OpenAI CLIP compresses an entire image into a single 512-dimensional vector and multiplies raw image-text cosine similarities by a learned temperature scale of 100.0 (exp(4.6052)) before applying Softmax. Because written text in web images strongly predicts captions, OCR features from the "iPod" sticker nudge the "iPod" cosine just +0.0060 above "Green Apple" (0.2701 vs. 0.2641), which the ×100.0 Softmax amplifies into a 64.51% vs. 35.47% victory. Here are the exact cosine similarities (cos(θ) = (I · T) / (‖I‖ ‖T‖)) and Softmax probabilities recorded on our GPU for apple_ipod.jpg across all five candidate prompts: 1. "a photo of an iPod electronic music player" Cosine: 0.2701 → Scaled Logit (100 × cos): 27.01 → Softmax Probability: 64.51% 2. "a photo of a green Granny Smith apple" Cosine: 0.2641 → Scaled Logit (100 × cos): 26.41 → Softmax Probability: 35.47% 3. "a photo of an analog wall clock" Cosine: 0.1849 → Scaled Logit (100 × cos): 18.49 → Softmax Probability: 0.01% 4. You can reproduce this measurement in PyTorch: import torch from PIL import Image from transformers import CLIPModel, CLIPProcessor model = CLIPModel.from_pretrained("openai/clip-vit-base-patch32").eval() proc = CLIPProcessor.from_pretrained("openai/clip-vit-base-patch32") prompts = [ "a photo of a green Granny Smith apple", "a photo of an iPod electronic music player", "a photo of a slice of pizza", "a photo of an analog wall clock", "a photo of a red fox in the snow", ] inp = proc( text=prompts, images=Image.open("apple_ipod.jpg"), return_tensors="pt", padding=True, ) with torch.no_grad(): out = model(**inp) cos = out.logits_per_image / model.logit_scale.exp() # [0.2641, 0.2701, ...] probs = out.logits_per_image.softmax(dim=-1) * 100 # [35.47%, 64.51%, ...] A modern Vision-Language Model ( VLM ) avoids this single-vector bottleneck by keeping the image as hundreds of spatial patch tokens , allowing the language model to attend separately to the fruit and to the sticker. 1. How Does a Vision Transformer (ViT) Turn Pixels into Patch Tokens? Direct Answer: A Vision Transformer (ViT) divides an image of resolution H × W by a fixed patch size P × P (14 × 14 pixels in Qwen2.5-VL) to produce a grid of (H/P) × (W/P) spatial patches. For a 560 × 560 image, 560 ÷ 14 = 40, yielding 40 × 40 = 1,600 patches (the sequence length N). A learned linear projection maps the raw RGB pixel values inside each patch into a 1,280-dimensional embedding vector (the feature dimension D), creating a [1,600 × 1,280] ViT input tensor. In classical digital image processing , computer vision slid local 3×3 filters (such as adaptive or Sobel edge filters) across an image pixel by pixel. In 2020, Alexey Dosovitskiy et al. ( "An Image is Worth 16×16 Words" , ICLR 2021) replaced convolutional hierarchies by slicing an image into non-overlapping patches and projecting each patch into a Transformer token. We hooked into the Vision Transformer (vlm.visual) inside Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct on our GPU as it processed a 560 × 560 RGB image (940,800 float values; center pixel (280, 280) = RGB [147, 132, 157], orange fur (140, 220) = [149, 106, 72], snow (480, 280) = [180, 195, 224]): 1. The 14×14 Spatial Grid ( 560 ÷ 14 = 40): Qwen2.5-VL uses a 14 × 14 pixel patch size. Dividing 560 px ÷ 14 px gives 40 patches across and 40 patches down , or 40 × 40 = 1,600 spatial patches (image_grid_thw = [[1, 40, 40]]). 2. Patch Unrolling ( 588 Spatial RGB Values / 1,176 with Temporal Duplication): A single 14 × 14 RGB square holds 14 × 14 × 3 = 588 pixel values. Under the hood, because Qwen2.5-VL uses a unified 3D patchifier (Conv3d with temporal_patch_size = 2) for both photos and video, a static photograph is duplicated across 2 temporal frames so each tube input has 2 × 14 × 14 × 3 = 1,176 values (pixel_values.shape = [1600, 1176]). 3. Linear Patch Projection ( → 1,280-D): The learned projection matrix maps each patch into a 1,280-dimensional visual embedding vector . Keep the two dimensions distinct: 1,600 is the number of patches N in the 40 × 40 grid, while 1,280 is the feature vector length D inside each single patch, forming the [1,600 × 1,280] ViT tensor (L2 norm = 417.01). Figure 3: Multiplying each patch by the learned projection matrix produces a 1,280-D vector; stacking all 1,600 patches forms the [1,600 × 1,280] ViT tensor. Image by the author. 2. How Do Patches Talk? Windowed vs. Global ViT Attention ([7, 15, 23, 31]) Direct Answer: Running full self-attention across 1,600 patches on all 32 ViT layers would require 1,600² = 2.56 million pairs per layer. To keep compute linear in image size, Qwen2.5-VL restricts 28 of its 32 ViT layers to local 112 × 112 pixel windows (8 × 8 = 64 patches per window) and runs full global self-attention only at 4 checkpoint layers ( Layers 7, 15, 23, and 31, 0-indexed) . 28 Windowed Attention Layers ( 112 × 112 px Local Windows): Patches only attend within their local 8 × 8 patch neighborhood (64 patches). Because window size is fixed, compute scales linearly O(N) with pixel count. 4 Global Full-Attention Checkpoints (0-indexed Layers 7, 15, 23, 31): At every 8th layer (fullatt_block_indexes = [7, 15, 23, 31]), window walls are removed and all 1,600 patches attend across the entire image (2.56M pairs), integrating global scene geometry. Figure 4: Windowed vs. Global ViT attention layers and pairwise cosine similarity distribution of the resulting visual tokens. Image by the author. Across the 400 merged visual tokens exiting the vision tower ([400, 2048], including the diagonal), we measured the pairwise cosine similarity distribution: 10th percentile ( p10): 0.1398 (82.0° apart) Median pair ( p50): 0.2886 (73.2° apart) 90th percentile ( p90): 0.5567 (56.2° apart) 99th percentile ( p99): 0.8225 (34.7° tight cluster) 3. CLIP Softmax vs. Google SigLIP Sigmoid: How Vision Models Align with Text Direct Answer: OpenAI CLIP aligns images and text using a batch Softmax (InfoNCE) loss (Softmax(100 · I_i · T_j)), which requires normalizing across every negative example in the batch. Google SigLIP (Zhai et al., ICCV 2023) replaces the batch Softmax with an independent pairwise Sigmoid (1 / (1 + exp(-117.33 · I_i · T_j + 12.93))), turning every (Image_i, Text_j) pair into a standalone binary classification problem with zero global batch normalization. We evaluated both openai/clip-vit-base-patch32 and google/siglip-base-patch16-224 across 5 studio images (Green Apple, 10:10 Clock, Red Fox, Plate & Knife, Vault Receipt) and their 5 matching captions on our GPU (m3_clip_vs_siglip_5x5): Figure 5: Contrastive image-text alignment in CLIP vs. Google SigLIP's independent pairwise sigmoid equation. Image by the author. Measured GPU Comparison: OpenAI CLIP vs. Google SigLIP Scoring Equation & Learned Parameters: • OpenAI CLIP ( ViT-B/32): Softmax(100.0 · I_i · T_j) (scale = 100.0, no bias) • Google SigLIP ( ViT-B/16-224): 1 / (1 + exp(-117.33 · I_i · T_j + 12.93)) (scale = 117.33, bias = -12.93) 5×5 Diagonal Cosine Similarities ( Apple, Clock, Fox, Plate, Receipt): • OpenAI CLIP: 0.3464, 0.3507, 0.3344, 0.3023, 0.2723 • Google SigLIP: 0.1111, 0.0687, 0.1633, 0.1591, 0.1414 5×5 Diagonal Match Probabilities: • OpenAI CLIP (Softmax over 5 captions): 100.0% , 100.0% , 100.0% , 100.0% , 99.99% (max off-diagonal: 0.01%) • Google SigLIP (Independent Sigmoid): 52.44% (Apple; 97.57% on "Granny Smith" prompt), 0.84% (Clock), 99.83% (Fox), 99.72% (Plate), 97.47% (Receipt) — and 0.00% across all 20 off-diagonal cells! Typographic Attack Robustness: • On "iPod" Apple: CLIP flips to 64.51% iPod (35.47% Apple). SigLIP predicts 40.29% Apple vs. 0.97% iPod . • On "Pizza" Apple: CLIP flips to 80.07% Pizza (19.86% Apple). SigLIP predicts 18.07% Apple vs. 3.13% Pizza . Two key engineering takeaways emerge from these numbers: Why SigLIP Resisted the "iPod" and "Pizza" Labels: Even if we convert SigLIP's raw logits back into a Softmax over the candidate labels, "Green Apple" still wins at ~98.6% — showing that SigLIP's robustness comes from its learned ViT-B/16 representations and WebLI training recipe rather than the sigmoid readout alone. Why SigLIP Scored the 10:10 Clock Caption at 0.84%: Because SigLIP learns a strong negative bias (-12.93) so non-matching pairs default to 0.00%, an image-text pair must exceed a cosine threshold of 12.93 / 117.33 = 0.1102 to cross 50% probability. On our descriptive clock caption, SigLIP's cosine was 0.0687 (still the highest in its row, well above all off-diagonals at ≤ 0.004), which maps to 0.84% under the uncalibrated sigmoid threshold. 4. How Does the 2×2 Spatial Patch Merger Cut LLM Attention by 16×? Direct Answer: Feeding all 1,600 ViT patches directly into a 36-layer language model would require 1,600² = 2,560,000 self-attention pairs per layer. To compress the visual sequence before Layer 0 of the LLM, Qwen2.5-VL uses a 2×2 Spatial Patch Merger (vlm.visual.merger) that concatenates every 2 × 2 block of adjacent 14 × 14 px patches (4 × 1,280 = 5,120-D) and projects it through a 2-layer MLP into a single 2,048-D Visual Word token . This reduces token count 4× ( 1,600 → 400) and cuts quadratic self-attention compute 4² = 16× ( 2.56M → 160K pairs) . Figure 6: The 2×2 Spatial Patch Merger concatenates each 2×2 block of 14×14px patches into a 5,120-D vector and projects it through a 2-layer MLP into one 2,048-D Visual Word token. Image by the author. Concatenate 2×2 Spatial Neighbors ( 4 → 1): Four adjacent 14 × 14 px patches covering a 28 × 28 px square are normalized with RMSNorm and concatenated into a 5,120-dimensional vector . 2-Layer MLP Projection ( 5,120-D → 2,048-D): A 2-layer MLP (Linear(5120 → 5120) → GELU → Linear(5120 → 2048)) maps each 5,120-D block into the exact 2,048-dimensional embedding space of the Qwen2.5-3B language model. You can inspect these exact tensor shapes in 10 lines of Python: from transformers import AutoConfig cfg = AutoConfig.from_pretrained("Qwen/Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct") v = cfg.vision_config print(v.patch_size, v.temporal_patch_size, v.spatial_merge_size) # -> 14 2 2 print(v.window_size, v.fullatt_block_indexes, v.hidden_size, v.out_hidden_size) # -> 112 [7, 15, 23, 31] 1280 2048 feats = {} vlm.visual.merger.register_forward_hook( lambda m, inp, out: feats.update(pre=inp[0].shape, post=out.shape) ) # 560x560 image -> pre: [1600, 1280], post: [400, 2048] 5. Native Dynamic Resolution (NaViT) vs. Downscaled Square Input Direct Answer: Early vision models forced every image into a fixed 224 × 224 square, distorting aspect ratios and blurring small text. Native Dynamic Resolution ( Patch n' Pack / NaViT , Dehghani et al., NeurIPS 2023) slices images at their native aspect ratio and pixel resolution (rounded to multiples of 28 px), preserving fine OCR details on wide banners and tall documents. We tested a wide 1120 × 280 ( 4:1 aspect ratio) shipping manifest containing tensors_bf16 = 96.0 GB and VAULT PIN: 4829 on our GPU (m4_dynamic_resolution_ocr) under two regimes: Figure 7: Downscaling a 1120×280 manifest into a 140×140 square (25 visual tokens) blurs the digits into "4857", whereas Native Dynamic Resolution (80×20 raw patches → 400 visual tokens) reads "4829" and "96.0 GB". Image by the author. Regime 1 — Downscaled Square ( 140 × 140 px, 1:1 aspect ratio, 16× fewer pixels): Produces 10 × 10 = 100 raw patches → 25 merged visual tokens ( 5 × 5) in 452.2 ms. VLM Output: "The exact 4-digit VAULT PIN printed in the bottom right box is 4857 . The tensors_bf16 value is 2 ." How Does a 1D Language Model Understand 2D Space? (3D M-RoPE [16, 24, 24]) Direct Answer: Standard Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) encodes a single 1D sequence index m across all 64 complex frequency pairs of an attention head (head_dim = 128). 3D Multimodal RoPE (M-RoPE) partitions those 64 frequency pairs into three independent coordinate sections — 16 pairs for Time (t) , 24 pairs for Height (h / Row y) , and 24 pairs for Width (w / Column x) (16 + 24 + 24 = 64 pairs) — stamping every visual token with its exact 3D (t, h, w) coordinate. 3D M-RoPE Partition Inside Every Attention Head (head_dim = 128 -> 64 pairs) ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── mrope_section = [ 16 pairs (32D) , 24 pairs (48D) , 24 pairs (48D) ] └── TIME (t) ──┘ └─ HEIGHT (h) ─┘ └─ WIDTH (w) ──┘ We hooked into vlm.model.get_rope_index (position_ids of shape [3, 1, seq_len]) on our GPU (m5_mrope_3d_coordinates) and recorded the exact position IDs for text vs. image tokens: Figure 8: Live GPU trace of the [3, 1, N] M-RoPE position_ids tensor and the Dual Spatial Compass (2D RoPE inside the 32-layer ViT + 3D M-RoPE inside the 36-layer LLM). Image by the author. 1D Text Prompt Tokens ( Tokens 0..4): All three coordinates step together (t = h = w = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4]), making M-RoPE mathematically identical to standard 1D RoPE on text. 2D Image Tokens ( Starting at position 15, Row 0, Cols 0..7): • time_t = [15, 15, 15, 15, 15, 15, 15, 15] (frozen across the entire static photograph) • height_h = [15, 15, 15, 15, 15, 15, 15, 15] (frozen at 15 across Row 0; increments to 16 on Row 1, up to 34 on Row 19) • width_w = [15, 16, 17, 18, 19, 20, 21, 22] (increments left-to-right across the columns of Row 0) A Surprising Null Result: Why Flipping Only the LLM’s M-RoPE Didn’t Swap the Image What happens if we leave the 400 visual token vectors untouched, but intercept vlm.model.get_rope_index in-flight and invert the LLM's Height and Width position IDs (h ← 49 - h, w ← 49 - w) on our 4-quadrant composite image (Top-Left: Apple, Top-Right: Clock, Bottom-Left: Fox, Bottom-Right: Plate & Knife)? We expected the LLM’s spatial answers to swap completely. They didn’t: Normal M-RoPE: “In the top-left corner of the image, there is an apple. In the bottom-right corner, there is a plate with a knife next to it.” Inverted LLM M-RoPE ( h, w flipped): "In the top-left corner of the image, there is an apple. In the bottom-right corner, there is a knife." (Flipping width_w alone also left "top-left: apple, top-right: clock" unchanged!) Why didn’t inverting the LLM’s 3D M-RoPE move the apple to the bottom-right? Because as shown in Figure 8 , Qwen2.5-VL actually uses a Dual Spatial Compass : Before the tokens ever reach the LLM, the 32-layer Vision Transformer ( vlm.visual.rotary_pos_emb) applies its own 2D RoPE across all 4 global full-attention layers ( [7, 15, 23, 31]) . Those 4 global ViT layers bake each patch’s 2D quadrant context directly into the 2,048-D feature vectors, and the tokens enter the LLM in raster-scan order (v_001 ... v_400). Flipping only the LLM's M-RoPE position IDs after the ViT has already encoded spatial position creates a slight feature conflict ("plate with a knife" → "a knife"), but the ViT's baked-in spatial features still dominate! 7. Cross-Modal Attention: Where Noun Tokens Look Across the 36 LLM Layers Direct Answer: In Qwen2.5-VL-3B’s 36-layer language model (576 total attention heads), middle-to-upper layers ( Layers 17–28 ) contain heads that route visual information from specific image regions to corresponding text nouns, focusing up to 96.8%–99.8% of their visual attention mass onto the target object's quadrant during teacher-forced evaluation. Why VLMs Miscount Overlapping Objects & How Visual Contrastive Decoding (VCD) Works A. Why Does Qwen2.5-VL Count “12” When Shown 15 Overlapping Circles? We fed three 504 × 504 geometric diagrams of overlapping colored rings (36 × 36 raw patches → 18 × 18 = 324 merged visual tokens) into Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct (m8_counting_and_vcd_hallucination): Figure 11: Qwen2.5-VL-3B counts N=4 circles correctly ("4"), but answers "6" for N=8 and "12" for N=15. Image by the author. N = 4 Circles ( 86.7 ms): VLM outputs "4" (Correct). N = 8 Circles ( 83.6 ms): VLM outputs "6" (Under-counts by 2). N = 15 Circles ( 96.9 ms): VLM outputs "12" (Under-counts by 3). A plausible architectural contributor to this failure is the 2×2 Spatial Patch Merger from Section 4: when 15 rings pass through a tight central rosette, multiple ring intersections fall inside the same 28 × 28 px merged token and are mixed by the MLP before the language model begins counting. B. How Visual Contrastive Decoding (VCD) Suppresses Language Priors In English text corpora, “a white dinner plate and a silver knife” frequently co-occurs with “fork” . How strongly does that language prior pull a VLM toward "Yes" when asked whether a fork is present on a table that only has a plate and a knife? In 2024, Sicong Leng et al. ( CVPR 2024 ) proposed Visual Contrastive Decoding (VCD) — the mathematical twin for VLMs of Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG) in image diffusion ( Episode 4 ). VCD runs two forward passes: one on the clean image v, and a second on a noise-corrupted version v' to measure the model's blind language prior, then contrasts their logits: ℓ_VCD(y) = (1 + α) · ℓ(y | v, x) − α · ℓ(y | v', x) (with α = 1.0) Figure 12: Visual Contrastive Decoding (VCD) logit and probability shifts measured on Qwen2.5-VL-3B on our Blackwell GPU. Image by the author. Here are the exact bfloat16 next-token logits for "Yes" vs. "No" (and their binary Softmax probabilities renormalized over {Yes, No}) measured on our GPU (m8_counting_and_vcd_hallucination): 1. Heavily Noised Image v' ( 12% image + 88% Gaussian noise — Language Prior): logit("Yes") = 25.750 · logit("No") = 26.625 → P("Yes, fork") = 29.42% (P("No") = 70.58%) 2. Degraded Image ( 22% image + 78% Gaussian noise — Standard Decoding): logit("Yes") = 25.625 · logit("No") = 27.125 → P("Yes, fork") = 18.24% (P("No") = 81.76%) 3. Degraded Image (+ VCD α = 1.0, 2 · ℓ(v_deg) − ℓ(v')): logit("Yes") = 25.500 · logit("No") = 27.625 → P("Yes, fork") = 10.67% (-41.5% reduction; P("No") = 89.33%) 4. Clean Studio Image v (Standard Decoding): logit("Yes") = 25.250 · logit("No") = 29.625 → P("Yes, fork") = 1.24% (P("No") = 98.76%) 5. Clean Studio Image v (+ VCD α = 1.0, 2 · ℓ(v) − ℓ(v')): logit("Yes") = 24.750 · logit("No") = 32.625 → P("Yes, fork") = 0.04% (~30× reduction; P("No") = 99.96% ) Look at the exact logit arithmetic (2 · ℓ(v) − ℓ(v')): Even though greedy decoding (argmax) already answers "No" across all conditions (logit("No") > logit("Yes")), corrupting the image with 88% noise (v') causes the binary probability P("Yes, fork") to jump 23.7× from 1.24% to 29.42% — directly quantifying the language prior pull. Subtracting those noisy logits (2 × 25.625 − 25.750 = 25.500 and 2 × 27.125 − 26.625 = 27.625) reduces P("Yes, fork") on the degraded image from 18.24% to 10.67% and raises P("No fork") on the clean image from 98.76% to 99.96% . Here is the 6-line PyTorch implementation of VCD: alpha = 1.0 l_v = vlm(**inputs_clean).logits[0, -1].float() # ℓ(y | v, x) l_vp = vlm(**inputs_noisy).logits[0, -1].float() # ℓ(y | v', x) l_vcd = (1.0 + alpha) * l_v - alpha * l_vp # VCD logits yes_id, no_id = ( processor.tokenizer.encode(w, add_special_tokens=False)[0] for w in ("Yes", "No") ) probs_yes_no = torch.softmax(l_vcd[[yes_id, no_id]], dim=0) # Note: Leng et al. (CVPR 2024) also apply an adaptive plausibility mask. 10. From Photos to Video & Practical Takeaways for ML Engineers When Qwen2.5-VL switches from a static photo to a video clip , two things happen: Conv3d [2, 14, 14] Temporal Tubes: Rather than duplicating a single photo, the Conv3d patchifier pairs 2 consecutive video frames into each 2 × 14 × 14 tube, halving the token count across time. Absolute-Time M-RoPE ( second_per_grid_t): The 16 Time (t) rotary frequency pairs in mrope_section = [16, 24, 24] advance in proportion to real-world timestamps (second_per_grid_t × tokens_per_second), so a 2-second interval receives the same temporal rotation angle regardless of the video's sampling frame rate. Figure 13: Three-stage Vision-Language Model recap and preview of Episode 6 (How Video Generation AI Actually Works). Image by the author. 4 Rules When Building with Vision-Language Models in Production Preserve Native Aspect Ratio & Resolution for OCR: Downsampling a 1120 × 280 receipt to 25 tokens flipped 4829 into 4857. Set min_pixels and max_pixels in AutoProcessor appropriately for document tasks. Don’t Trust Direct VLM Object Counts Above ~5 Overlapping Items: Because the 2×2 Spatial Patch Merger compresses 28 × 28 px regions into single tokens before the LLM, dense overlapping objects (N = 8 or 15 circles) should be routed through an explicit detection/segmentation tool or tiled crops. Treat Text Inside Images as an Untrusted Prompt-Injection Surface: VLMs read text inside images accurately — which fixes CLIP’s "iPod" classification bug, but creates a visual prompt injection vector where adversarial instructions printed on an object enter the LLM's context window. Use Contrastive Decoding Selectively: VCD widens the margin against language-prior hallucinations (98.76% → 99.96%), at the cost of 2× inference compute (two forward passes per token). Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ) 1. Why does an “iPod” sticker on an apple fool OpenAI CLIP? OpenAI CLIP compresses an entire image into a single 512-dimensional vector and multiplies image-text cosine similarities by a learned temperature of 100.0 before Softmax. Multimodal neurons inside CLIP respond strongly to printed text, pushing the "iPod" cosine (0.2701) slightly above "Green Apple" (0.2641), which the ×100.0 Softmax turns into a 64.51% iPod prediction. 2. Why are there 1,600 patches of 1,280 dimensions in Qwen2.5-VL? On a 560 × 560 pixel image sliced with a 14 × 14 pixel patch size, 560 ÷ 14 = 40 patches per side, giving 40 × 40 = 1,600 patches (sequence length N). Each patch is projected into a 1,280-dimensional feature vector (D), forming a [1,600 × 1,280] tensor before the 2×2 Spatial Patch Merger compresses it 4× into 400 tokens of 2,048 dimensions . 3. How does 3D M-RoPE ([16, 24, 24]) work in Qwen2.5-VL? Each attention head in Qwen2.5-VL (head_dim = 128, or 64 rotary frequency pairs) splits its 64 frequency pairs into 16 pairs for Time ( t) , 24 pairs for Height ( h, Row y) , and 24 pairs for Width ( w, Column x) . For 1D text tokens, t = h = w; for 2D images, t stays constant while h and w track row and column coordinates; for 3D video, t advances with real timestamps. 4. What is Visual Contrastive Decoding (VCD)? Visual Contrastive Decoding (Leng et al., CVPR 2024) reduces object hallucinations in Vision-Language Models by subtracting the next-token logits of a noise-corrupted image v' from the logits of the clean image v: ℓ_VCD(y) = (1 + α)ℓ(y | v, x) − αℓ(y | v', x). This suppresses answers driven purely by English word co-occurrence priors (such as assuming a fork is next to a plate and knife). How We Measured (Reproducibility & Disclosure Box) Hardware: NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition (96.0 GB VRAM, bfloat16 for Qwen2.5-VL-3B, float32 for CLIP / SigLIP). Models: openai/clip-vit-base-patch32, google/siglip-base-patch16-224, and Qwen/Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct via HuggingFace transformers. Protocol: All VLM generations use deterministic greedy decoding (do_sample=False, n = 1 run per condition). Attention telemetry in Sections 7–8 was captured with attn_implementation="eager" on a single teacher-forced pass. All test images (apple_clean.jpg, apple_ipod.jpg, apple_pizza.jpg, fox_clean.jpg, clock_1010.jpg, plate_knife_no_fork.jpg, wide_receipt_pin.jpg) are synthetic studio renders generated for controlled testing. Why an “iPod” sticker fools OpenAI CLIP (64.5%) while Qwen2.5-VL reads it cleanly — measured layer by layer on a 96 GB Blackwell GPU.

By Latent AI Labs (@LatentAILabs)

TL;DR — How Do Vision-Language Models (VLMs) Actually See Images?
Modern Vision-Language Models (such as Qwen2.5-VL, GPT-4o, and Claude 3.5 Sonnet) process images in three stages:
1. Vision Transformer (ViT) Patch Slicer & 2×2 Spatial Patch Merger: A 560 × 560 RGB photograph (940,800 floats) is sliced by a 14 × 14 pixel grid into 40 × 40 = 1,600 patches, projected into 1,280-dimensional vectors, refined through 28 local-window ViT layers (112 × 112 px) and 4 global full-attention layers (Layers 7, 15, 23, 31), and compressed 4-into-1 by a 2×2 Spatial Patch Merger into 400 Visual Word tokens (2,048-D) — cutting LLM self-attention pairs 16× (2.56M → 160K).
2. Dual Spatial Compass (2D ViT RoPE + 3D M-RoPE [16t, 24h, 24w]): Each attention head splits its 64 rotary position frequency pairs into 16 Time (t), 24 Height (h / Row y), and 24 Width (w / Column x) dials so a 1D language model natively understands 2D aspect ratios (NaViT) and 3D video timelines.
3. Cross-Modal Attention & Visual Contrastive Decoding (VCD): In Layers 17–28, cross-modal grounding heads concentrate up to 96.8%–99.8% of their visual attention onto the target object quadrant, while Visual Contrastive Decoding (VCD) subtracts noisy-image language priors (ℓ_VCD = (1+α)ℓ(v) − αℓ(v')) to reduce object hallucinations by 41.5%.

In 2021, Gabriel Goh and colleagues at OpenAI demonstrated a famous vulnerability in computer vision known as a typographic attack: stick a paper label reading “iPod” onto a green Granny Smith apple, and OpenAI’s CLIP classifies the piece of fruit as an electronic music player.

We rebuilt that experiment with a synthetic studio photograph of a green apple and a digital label, and ran it through OpenAI CLIP (openai/clip-vit-base-patch32), Google SigLIP (google/siglip-base-patch16-224), and Alibaba Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct on a 96 GB NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPU:

  • Clean Green Apple: CLIP predicts “a photo of a green Granny Smith apple” at 100.00% (cosine = 0.3302), with 0.00% for "a photo of an iPod electronic music player" (cosine = 0.2033).
  • Apple + "iPod" Label: "Green Apple" drops to 35.47% (cosine = 0.2641), and "iPod" takes first place at 64.51% (cosine = 0.2701).
  • Apple + "Pizza" Label: "Green Apple" drops to 19.86% (cosine = 0.2591), and "Pizza" takes first place at 80.07% (cosine = 0.2730).
Figure 1: GPU measurement of the "iPod" typographic attack on OpenAI CLIP (64.51% iPod) vs. Qwen2.5-VL-3B on a 96 GB NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPU. Image by the author; source apple photo AI-generated with a digital label.

Yet when we feed those exact same labeled photographs into a modern 3-billion-parameter Vision-Language Model (Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct) and ask what object is in the photo and what word is printed on the sticker, it separates the physical fruit from the text:

On the "iPod" apple (1,342.7 ms cold start): "This is an apple, and the word written on the paper sticker is 'iPod.'"
On the "Pizza" apple (240.7 ms warm inference): "This is an apple with a paper sticker that says 'Pizza.'"

Even more intriguing: that same Vision-Language Model reads a 4-digit security code (PIN: 4829) off a wide 1120 × 280 shipping manifest accurately, yet looks at a clean geometric diagram of 15 overlapping circles and counts "12".

Why does a printed word hijack CLIP? How does a 1D language model — built to predict the next token in a sequence — represent 2D photographs and 3D video? And why does a model that can read fine print fail to count 15 rings?

We hooked directly into Qwen2.5-VL-3B’s 32-layer Vision Transformer (ViT) and 36-layer Language Model on our Blackwell GPU to measure the tensors, cosine similarities, positional IDs, and attention weights layer by layer (watch the companion 25-minute animated video on YouTube here).

https://medium.com/media/3d3907e7090805703a8975dee4fce162/hrefFigure 2: How the Vision Transformer slices a 560×560px photograph by a 14×14px grid into 40×40 = 1,600 patches. Image by the author.Experiment 0. Why Does an “iPod” Sticker Fool CLIP? (The ×100.0 Temperature Multiplier)

Direct Answer: OpenAI CLIP compresses an entire image into a single 512-dimensional vector and multiplies raw image-text cosine similarities by a learned temperature scale of 100.0 (exp(4.6052)) before applying Softmax. Because written text in web images strongly predicts captions, OCR features from the "iPod" sticker nudge the "iPod" cosine just +0.0060 above "Green Apple" (0.2701 vs. 0.2641), which the ×100.0 Softmax amplifies into a 64.51% vs. 35.47% victory.

Here are the exact cosine similarities (cos(θ) = (I · T) / (‖I‖ ‖T‖)) and Softmax probabilities recorded on our GPU for apple_ipod.jpg across all five candidate prompts:

  • 1. "a photo of an iPod electronic music player"
    Cosine: 0.2701 → Scaled Logit (100 × cos): 27.01 → Softmax Probability: 64.51%
  • 2. "a photo of a green Granny Smith apple"
    Cosine: 0.2641 → Scaled Logit (100 × cos): 26.41 → Softmax Probability: 35.47%
  • 3. "a photo of an analog wall clock"
    Cosine: 0.1849 → Scaled Logit (100 × cos): 18.49 → Softmax Probability: 0.01%
  • 4. "a photo of a slice of pizza"
    Cosine: 0.1718 → Scaled Logit (100 × cos): 17.18 → Softmax Probability: 0.00%
  • 5. "a photo of a red fox in the snow"
    Cosine: 0.1106 → Scaled Logit (100 × cos): 11.06 → Softmax Probability: 0.00%
P(iPod) = exp(27.01) / (exp(27.01) + exp(26.41) + ...)
        ≈ 1 / (1 + exp(-0.60)) = 64.57%
        (64.51% exact across all 5 prompts using unrounded GPU logits)

Because CLIP pools the entire photograph into one 512-D vector, features representing green apple skin and OCR features representing the letters i-P-o-d compete inside one shared bottleneck (Goh et al., Distill 2021).

You can reproduce this measurement in PyTorch:

import torch
from PIL import Image
from transformers import CLIPModel, CLIPProcessor
model = CLIPModel.from_pretrained("openai/clip-vit-base-patch32").eval()
proc = CLIPProcessor.from_pretrained("openai/clip-vit-base-patch32")
prompts = [
    "a photo of a green Granny Smith apple",
    "a photo of an iPod electronic music player",
    "a photo of a slice of pizza",
    "a photo of an analog wall clock",
    "a photo of a red fox in the snow",
]
inp = proc(
    text=prompts,
    images=Image.open("apple_ipod.jpg"),
    return_tensors="pt",
    padding=True,
)
with torch.no_grad():
    out = model(**inp)
cos = out.logits_per_image / model.logit_scale.exp()  # [0.2641, 0.2701, ...]
probs = out.logits_per_image.softmax(dim=-1) * 100    # [35.47%, 64.51%, ...]

A modern Vision-Language Model (VLM) avoids this single-vector bottleneck by keeping the image as hundreds of spatial patch tokens, allowing the language model to attend separately to the fruit and to the sticker.

1. How Does a Vision Transformer (ViT) Turn Pixels into Patch Tokens?

Direct Answer: A Vision Transformer (ViT) divides an image of resolution H × W by a fixed patch size P × P (14 × 14 pixels in Qwen2.5-VL) to produce a grid of (H/P) × (W/P) spatial patches. For a 560 × 560 image, 560 ÷ 14 = 40, yielding 40 × 40 = 1,600 patches (the sequence length N). A learned linear projection maps the raw RGB pixel values inside each patch into a 1,280-dimensional embedding vector (the feature dimension D), creating a [1,600 × 1,280] ViT input tensor.

In classical digital image processing, computer vision slid local 3×3 filters (such as adaptive or Sobel edge filters) across an image pixel by pixel. In 2020, Alexey Dosovitskiy et al. ("An Image is Worth 16×16 Words", ICLR 2021) replaced convolutional hierarchies by slicing an image into non-overlapping patches and projecting each patch into a Transformer token.

We hooked into the Vision Transformer (vlm.visual) inside Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct on our GPU as it processed a 560 × 560 RGB image (940,800 float values; center pixel (280, 280) = RGB [147, 132, 157], orange fur (140, 220) = [149, 106, 72], snow (480, 280) = [180, 195, 224]):

1. The 14×14 Spatial Grid (560 ÷ 14 = 40):
Qwen2.5-VL uses a 14 × 14 pixel patch size. Dividing 560 px ÷ 14 px gives 40 patches across and 40 patches down, or 40 × 40 = 1,600 spatial patches (image_grid_thw = [[1, 40, 40]]).

2. Patch Unrolling (588 Spatial RGB Values / 1,176 with Temporal Duplication):
A single 14 × 14 RGB square holds 14 × 14 × 3 = 588 pixel values. Under the hood, because Qwen2.5-VL uses a unified 3D patchifier (Conv3d with temporal_patch_size = 2) for both photos and video, a static photograph is duplicated across 2 temporal frames so each tube input has 2 × 14 × 14 × 3 = 1,176 values (pixel_values.shape = [1600, 1176]).

3. Linear Patch Projection (→ 1,280-D):
The learned projection matrix maps each patch into a 1,280-dimensional visual embedding vector. Keep the two dimensions distinct: 1,600 is the number of patches N in the 40 × 40 grid, while 1,280 is the feature vector length D inside each single patch, forming the [1,600 × 1,280] ViT tensor (L2 norm = 417.01).

Figure 3: Multiplying each patch by the learned projection matrix produces a 1,280-D vector; stacking all 1,600 patches forms the [1,600 × 1,280] ViT tensor. Image by the author.2. How Do Patches Talk? Windowed vs. Global ViT Attention ([7, 15, 23, 31])

Direct Answer: Running full self-attention across 1,600 patches on all 32 ViT layers would require 1,600² = 2.56 million pairs per layer. To keep compute linear in image size, Qwen2.5-VL restricts 28 of its 32 ViT layers to local 112 × 112 pixel windows (8 × 8 = 64 patches per window) and runs full global self-attention only at 4 checkpoint layers (Layers 7, 15, 23, and 31, 0-indexed).

  • 28 Windowed Attention Layers (112 × 112 px Local Windows):
    Patches only attend within their local 8 × 8 patch neighborhood (64 patches). Because window size is fixed, compute scales linearly O(N) with pixel count.
  • 4 Global Full-Attention Checkpoints (0-indexed Layers 7, 15, 23, 31):
    At every 8th layer (fullatt_block_indexes = [7, 15, 23, 31]), window walls are removed and all 1,600 patches attend across the entire image (2.56M pairs), integrating global scene geometry.
Figure 4: Windowed vs. Global ViT attention layers and pairwise cosine similarity distribution of the resulting visual tokens. Image by the author.

Across the 400 merged visual tokens exiting the vision tower ([400, 2048], including the diagonal), we measured the pairwise cosine similarity distribution:

  • 10th percentile (p10): 0.1398 (82.0° apart)
  • Median pair (p50): 0.2886 (73.2° apart)
  • 90th percentile (p90): 0.5567 (56.2° apart)
  • 99th percentile (p99): 0.8225 (34.7° tight cluster)
3. CLIP Softmax vs. Google SigLIP Sigmoid: How Vision Models Align with Text

Direct Answer: OpenAI CLIP aligns images and text using a batch Softmax (InfoNCE) loss (Softmax(100 · I_i · T_j)), which requires normalizing across every negative example in the batch. Google SigLIP (Zhai et al., ICCV 2023) replaces the batch Softmax with an independent pairwise Sigmoid (1 / (1 + exp(-117.33 · I_i · T_j + 12.93))), turning every (Image_i, Text_j) pair into a standalone binary classification problem with zero global batch normalization.

We evaluated both openai/clip-vit-base-patch32 and google/siglip-base-patch16-224 across 5 studio images (Green Apple, 10:10 Clock, Red Fox, Plate & Knife, Vault Receipt) and their 5 matching captions on our GPU (m3_clip_vs_siglip_5x5):

Figure 5: Contrastive image-text alignment in CLIP vs. Google SigLIP's independent pairwise sigmoid equation. Image by the author.Measured GPU Comparison: OpenAI CLIP vs. Google SigLIP
  • Scoring Equation & Learned Parameters:
    • OpenAI CLIP (ViT-B/32): Softmax(100.0 · I_i · T_j) (scale = 100.0, no bias)
    • Google SigLIP (ViT-B/16-224): 1 / (1 + exp(-117.33 · I_i · T_j + 12.93)) (scale = 117.33, bias = -12.93)
  • 5×5 Diagonal Cosine Similarities (Apple, Clock, Fox, Plate, Receipt):
    • OpenAI CLIP: 0.3464, 0.3507, 0.3344, 0.3023, 0.2723
    • Google SigLIP: 0.1111, 0.0687, 0.1633, 0.1591, 0.1414
  • 5×5 Diagonal Match Probabilities:
    • OpenAI CLIP (Softmax over 5 captions): 100.0%, 100.0%, 100.0%, 100.0%, 99.99% (max off-diagonal: 0.01%)
    • Google SigLIP (Independent Sigmoid): 52.44% (Apple; 97.57% on "Granny Smith" prompt), 0.84% (Clock), 99.83% (Fox), 99.72% (Plate), 97.47% (Receipt) — and 0.00% across all 20 off-diagonal cells!
  • Typographic Attack Robustness:
    • On "iPod" Apple: CLIP flips to 64.51% iPod (35.47% Apple). SigLIP predicts 40.29% Apple vs. 0.97% iPod.
    • On "Pizza" Apple: CLIP flips to 80.07% Pizza (19.86% Apple). SigLIP predicts 18.07% Apple vs. 3.13% Pizza.

Two key engineering takeaways emerge from these numbers:

  1. Why SigLIP Resisted the "iPod" and "Pizza" Labels: Even if we convert SigLIP's raw logits back into a Softmax over the candidate labels, "Green Apple" still wins at ~98.6% — showing that SigLIP's robustness comes from its learned ViT-B/16 representations and WebLI training recipe rather than the sigmoid readout alone.
  2. Why SigLIP Scored the 10:10 Clock Caption at 0.84%: Because SigLIP learns a strong negative bias (-12.93) so non-matching pairs default to 0.00%, an image-text pair must exceed a cosine threshold of 12.93 / 117.33 = 0.1102 to cross 50% probability. On our descriptive clock caption, SigLIP's cosine was 0.0687 (still the highest in its row, well above all off-diagonals at ≤ 0.004), which maps to 0.84% under the uncalibrated sigmoid threshold.
4. How Does the 2×2 Spatial Patch Merger Cut LLM Attention by 16×?

Direct Answer: Feeding all 1,600 ViT patches directly into a 36-layer language model would require 1,600² = 2,560,000 self-attention pairs per layer. To compress the visual sequence before Layer 0 of the LLM, Qwen2.5-VL uses a 2×2 Spatial Patch Merger (vlm.visual.merger) that concatenates every 2 × 2 block of adjacent 14 × 14 px patches (4 × 1,280 = 5,120-D) and projects it through a 2-layer MLP into a single 2,048-D Visual Word token. This reduces token count 4× (1,600 → 400) and cuts quadratic self-attention compute 4² = 16× (2.56M → 160K pairs).

Figure 6: The 2×2 Spatial Patch Merger concatenates each 2×2 block of 14×14px patches into a 5,120-D vector and projects it through a 2-layer MLP into one 2,048-D Visual Word token. Image by the author.
  1. Concatenate 2×2 Spatial Neighbors (4 → 1):
    Four adjacent 14 × 14 px patches covering a 28 × 28 px square are normalized with RMSNorm and concatenated into a 5,120-dimensional vector.
  2. 2-Layer MLP Projection (5,120-D → 2,048-D):
    A 2-layer MLP (Linear(5120 → 5120) → GELU → Linear(5120 → 2048)) maps each 5,120-D block into the exact 2,048-dimensional embedding space of the Qwen2.5-3B language model.

You can inspect these exact tensor shapes in 10 lines of Python:

from transformers import AutoConfig
cfg = AutoConfig.from_pretrained("Qwen/Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct")
v = cfg.vision_config
print(v.patch_size, v.temporal_patch_size, v.spatial_merge_size)
# -> 14  2  2
print(v.window_size, v.fullatt_block_indexes, v.hidden_size, v.out_hidden_size)
# -> 112  [7, 15, 23, 31]  1280  2048
feats = {}
vlm.visual.merger.register_forward_hook(
    lambda m, inp, out: feats.update(pre=inp[0].shape, post=out.shape)
)
# 560x560 image -> pre: [1600, 1280], post: [400, 2048]
5. Native Dynamic Resolution (NaViT) vs. Downscaled Square Input

Direct Answer: Early vision models forced every image into a fixed 224 × 224 square, distorting aspect ratios and blurring small text. Native Dynamic Resolution (Patch n' Pack / NaViT, Dehghani et al., NeurIPS 2023) slices images at their native aspect ratio and pixel resolution (rounded to multiples of 28 px), preserving fine OCR details on wide banners and tall documents.

We tested a wide 1120 × 280 (4:1 aspect ratio) shipping manifest containing tensors_bf16 = 96.0 GB and VAULT PIN: 4829 on our GPU (m4_dynamic_resolution_ocr) under two regimes:

Figure 7: Downscaling a 1120×280 manifest into a 140×140 square (25 visual tokens) blurs the digits into "4857", whereas Native Dynamic Resolution (80×20 raw patches → 400 visual tokens) reads "4829" and "96.0 GB". Image by the author.
  • Regime 1 — Downscaled Square (140 × 140 px, 1:1 aspect ratio, 16× fewer pixels):
    Produces 10 × 10 = 100 raw patches → 25 merged visual tokens (5 × 5) in 452.2 ms.
    VLM Output: "The exact 4-digit VAULT PIN printed in the bottom right box is 4857. The tensors_bf16 value is 2." (Incorrect — fine digits blurred!)
  • Regime 2 — Native Dynamic Resolution (1120 × 280 px, 4:1 original aspect ratio):
    Produces 80 × 20 = 1,600 raw patches → 400 merged visual tokens (40 × 10) in 570.9 ms.
    VLM Output: "The exact 4-digit VAULT PIN printed in the bottom right box is 4829. The tensors_bf16 value is 96.0 GB." (Exact match!)

(Methodology note: shrinking 1120 × 280 to 140 × 140 reduces pixel count by 16× alongside the 4:1 → 1:1 aspect crush, showing why allocating 400 native-aspect tokens is critical for document OCR.)

6. How Does a 1D Language Model Understand 2D Space? (3D M-RoPE [16, 24, 24])

Direct Answer: Standard Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) encodes a single 1D sequence index m across all 64 complex frequency pairs of an attention head (head_dim = 128). 3D Multimodal RoPE (M-RoPE) partitions those 64 frequency pairs into three independent coordinate sections — 16 pairs for Time (t), 24 pairs for Height (h / Row y), and 24 pairs for Width (w / Column x) (16 + 24 + 24 = 64 pairs) — stamping every visual token with its exact 3D (t, h, w) coordinate.

3D M-RoPE Partition Inside Every Attention Head (head_dim = 128 -> 64 pairs)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
mrope_section = [ 16 pairs (32D) , 24 pairs (48D) , 24 pairs (48D) ]
                  └── TIME (t) ──┘ └─ HEIGHT (h) ─┘ └─ WIDTH (w) ──┘

We hooked into vlm.model.get_rope_index (position_ids of shape [3, 1, seq_len]) on our GPU (m5_mrope_3d_coordinates) and recorded the exact position IDs for text vs. image tokens:

Figure 8: Live GPU trace of the [3, 1, N] M-RoPE position_ids tensor and the Dual Spatial Compass (2D RoPE inside the 32-layer ViT + 3D M-RoPE inside the 36-layer LLM). Image by the author.
  • 1D Text Prompt Tokens (Tokens 0..4):
    All three coordinates step together (t = h = w = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4]), making M-RoPE mathematically identical to standard 1D RoPE on text.
  • 2D Image Tokens (Starting at position 15, Row 0, Cols 0..7):
    • time_t = [15, 15, 15, 15, 15, 15, 15, 15] (frozen across the entire static photograph)
    • height_h = [15, 15, 15, 15, 15, 15, 15, 15] (frozen at 15 across Row 0; increments to 16 on Row 1, up to 34 on Row 19)
    • width_w = [15, 16, 17, 18, 19, 20, 21, 22] (increments left-to-right across the columns of Row 0)
A Surprising Null Result: Why Flipping Only the LLM’s M-RoPE Didn’t Swap the Image

What happens if we leave the 400 visual token vectors untouched, but intercept vlm.model.get_rope_index in-flight and invert the LLM's Height and Width position IDs (h ← 49 - h, w ← 49 - w) on our 4-quadrant composite image (Top-Left: Apple, Top-Right: Clock, Bottom-Left: Fox, Bottom-Right: Plate & Knife)?

We expected the LLM’s spatial answers to swap completely. They didn’t:

  • Normal M-RoPE: “In the top-left corner of the image, there is an apple. In the bottom-right corner, there is a plate with a knife next to it.”
  • Inverted LLM M-RoPE (h, w flipped): "In the top-left corner of the image, there is an apple. In the bottom-right corner, there is a knife." (Flipping width_w alone also left "top-left: apple, top-right: clock" unchanged!)

Why didn’t inverting the LLM’s 3D M-RoPE move the apple to the bottom-right?
Because as shown in Figure 8, Qwen2.5-VL actually uses a Dual Spatial Compass:

  1. Before the tokens ever reach the LLM, the 32-layer Vision Transformer (vlm.visual.rotary_pos_emb) applies its own 2D RoPE across all 4 global full-attention layers ([7, 15, 23, 31]).
  2. Those 4 global ViT layers bake each patch’s 2D quadrant context directly into the 2,048-D feature vectors, and the tokens enter the LLM in raster-scan order (v_001 ... v_400). Flipping only the LLM's M-RoPE position IDs after the ViT has already encoded spatial position creates a slight feature conflict ("plate with a knife" → "a knife"), but the ViT's baked-in spatial features still dominate!
7. Cross-Modal Attention: Where Noun Tokens Look Across the 36 LLM Layers

Direct Answer: In Qwen2.5-VL-3B’s 36-layer language model (576 total attention heads), middle-to-upper layers (Layers 17–28) contain heads that route visual information from specific image regions to corresponding text nouns, focusing up to 96.8%–99.8% of their visual attention mass onto the target object's quadrant during teacher-forced evaluation.

Using attn_implementation="eager" on our 4-quadrant composite image (m6_cross_modal_grounding), we ran a teacher-forced forward pass naming each quadrant's object ("...top-left is a green apple, top-right is a wall clock, bottom-left is a red fox, and bottom-right is a dinner plate") and searched across Layers 14–29 (256 heads, 0-indexed) for the heads that concentrated the highest share of their visual attention onto each noun's target 10 × 10 quadrant (25% of the image area):

Figure 9: Cross-modal attention heatmaps from the highest-scoring heads in Layers 17–28 of Qwen2.5-VL-3B on our 4-quadrant test image. Image by the author.
  • "apple" (Token #462, Top-Left Quadrant):
    Peak Head: Layer 17 · Head 10 (99.76% of visual attention on Top-Left) · Filtered Ensemble (>45% heads): 78.70%
  • "clock" (Token #469, Top-Right Quadrant):
    Peak Head: Layer 21 · Head 14 (96.78% of visual attention on Top-Right) · Filtered Ensemble (>45% heads): 73.76%
  • "fox" (Token #476, Bottom-Left Quadrant):
    Peak Head: Layer 27 · Head 1 (98.96% of visual attention on Bottom-Left) · Filtered Ensemble (>45% heads): 83.15%
  • "plate" (Token #484, Bottom-Right Quadrant):
    Peak Head: Layer 28 · Head 10 (99.29% of visual attention on Bottom-Right) · Filtered Ensemble (>45% heads): 83.10%

(Methodology note: Because these peak heads are selected as the maximum across 256 middle-layer heads on a teacher-forced sentence that names each corner prior to the noun, and the ensemble averages heads already exceeding a 45% target-quadrant share, these heatmaps represent upper-bound spatial localization in Layers 17–28.)

8. Attention Sinks & Visual Token Sparsity Across All 36 Layers

Direct Answer: Averaging attention across all 16 heads per layer from Layer 0 to Layer 35 (m7_36layer_attention_telemetry) shows that visual tokens receive only 2.5% to 31.2% of total attention per layer (peaking at 31.18% on Layer 21), while text and initial Attention Sink tokens (Tokens 0..3) absorb the rest. Within the visual attention distribution in Layers 17–35, the top 15% of visual tokens (60 of 400 patches) capture 55.9% to 81.15% of all visual attention mass (peaking at 81.15% on Layer 27).

Figure 10: Measured 36-layer attention allocation across text tokens, initial sink tokens, and visual tokens in Qwen2.5-VL-3B. Image by the author.
  1. Layers 0–2 (Prompt Text Parsing):
    89.54% to 94.65% of attention stays on the text tokens, while visual tokens receive only 4.17% to 8.14% and the first 4 sink tokens receive 1.18% to 2.32%.
  2. Layers 3–9 (Attention Sink Parking):
    Just as in text LLMs (Episode 3), 56.36% to 69.41% of total attention mass parks on the first 4 tokens of the sequence (peaking at 69.41% on Layer 5), while visual tokens receive only 2.47% to 5.12%.
  3. Layers 17–33 (Visual Readout & Sparsity):
    Visual attention rises to 31.18% on Layer 21 (24.37% on Layer 27). Across Layers 17–35, the top 15% of visual tokens (60 out of 400 patches) hold 55.9% to 81.15% of all visual attention mass (vs. 15.0% if uniform), explaining why token-pruning methods like FastV can drop low-attention background tokens in upper layers with minimal accuracy loss.
9. Why VLMs Miscount Overlapping Objects & How Visual Contrastive Decoding (VCD) WorksA. Why Does Qwen2.5-VL Count “12” When Shown 15 Overlapping Circles?

We fed three 504 × 504 geometric diagrams of overlapping colored rings (36 × 36 raw patches → 18 × 18 = 324 merged visual tokens) into Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct (m8_counting_and_vcd_hallucination):

Figure 11: Qwen2.5-VL-3B counts N=4 circles correctly ("4"), but answers "6" for N=8 and "12" for N=15. Image by the author.
  • N = 4 Circles (86.7 ms): VLM outputs "4" (Correct).
  • N = 8 Circles (83.6 ms): VLM outputs "6" (Under-counts by 2).
  • N = 15 Circles (96.9 ms): VLM outputs "12" (Under-counts by 3).

A plausible architectural contributor to this failure is the 2×2 Spatial Patch Merger from Section 4: when 15 rings pass through a tight central rosette, multiple ring intersections fall inside the same 28 × 28 px merged token and are mixed by the MLP before the language model begins counting.

B. How Visual Contrastive Decoding (VCD) Suppresses Language Priors

In English text corpora, “a white dinner plate and a silver knife” frequently co-occurs with “fork”. How strongly does that language prior pull a VLM toward "Yes" when asked whether a fork is present on a table that only has a plate and a knife?

In 2024, Sicong Leng et al. (CVPR 2024) proposed Visual Contrastive Decoding (VCD) — the mathematical twin for VLMs of Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG) in image diffusion (Episode 4). VCD runs two forward passes: one on the clean image v, and a second on a noise-corrupted version v' to measure the model's blind language prior, then contrasts their logits:

ℓ_VCD(y) = (1 + α) · ℓ(y | v, x)  −  α · ℓ(y | v', x)      (with α = 1.0)
Figure 12: Visual Contrastive Decoding (VCD) logit and probability shifts measured on Qwen2.5-VL-3B on our Blackwell GPU. Image by the author.

Here are the exact bfloat16 next-token logits for "Yes" vs. "No" (and their binary Softmax probabilities renormalized over {Yes, No}) measured on our GPU (m8_counting_and_vcd_hallucination):

  • 1. Heavily Noised Image v' (12% image + 88% Gaussian noise — Language Prior):
    logit("Yes") = 25.750 · logit("No") = 26.625 → P("Yes, fork") = 29.42% (P("No") = 70.58%)
  • 2. Degraded Image (22% image + 78% Gaussian noise — Standard Decoding):
    logit("Yes") = 25.625 · logit("No") = 27.125 → P("Yes, fork") = 18.24% (P("No") = 81.76%)
  • 3. Degraded Image (+ VCD α = 1.0, 2 · ℓ(v_deg) − ℓ(v')):
    logit("Yes") = 25.500 · logit("No") = 27.625 → P("Yes, fork") = 10.67% (-41.5% reduction; P("No") = 89.33%)
  • 4. Clean Studio Image v (Standard Decoding):
    logit("Yes") = 25.250 · logit("No") = 29.625 → P("Yes, fork") = 1.24% (P("No") = 98.76%)
  • 5. Clean Studio Image v (+ VCD α = 1.0, 2 · ℓ(v) − ℓ(v')):
    logit("Yes") = 24.750 · logit("No") = 32.625 → P("Yes, fork") = 0.04% (~30× reduction; P("No") = 99.96%)

Look at the exact logit arithmetic (2 · ℓ(v) − ℓ(v')):

  • Even though greedy decoding (argmax) already answers "No" across all conditions (logit("No") > logit("Yes")), corrupting the image with 88% noise (v') causes the binary probability P("Yes, fork") to jump 23.7× from 1.24% to 29.42% — directly quantifying the language prior pull.
  • Subtracting those noisy logits (2 × 25.625 − 25.750 = 25.500 and 2 × 27.125 − 26.625 = 27.625) reduces P("Yes, fork") on the degraded image from 18.24% to 10.67% and raises P("No fork") on the clean image from 98.76% to 99.96%.

Here is the 6-line PyTorch implementation of VCD:

alpha = 1.0
l_v = vlm(**inputs_clean).logits[0, -1].float()      # ℓ(y | v, x)
l_vp = vlm(**inputs_noisy).logits[0, -1].float()     # ℓ(y | v', x)
l_vcd = (1.0 + alpha) * l_v - alpha * l_vp           # VCD logits
yes_id, no_id = (
    processor.tokenizer.encode(w, add_special_tokens=False)[0]
    for w in ("Yes", "No")
)
probs_yes_no = torch.softmax(l_vcd[[yes_id, no_id]], dim=0)
# Note: Leng et al. (CVPR 2024) also apply an adaptive plausibility mask.
10. From Photos to Video & Practical Takeaways for ML Engineers

When Qwen2.5-VL switches from a static photo to a video clip, two things happen:

  1. Conv3d [2, 14, 14] Temporal Tubes: Rather than duplicating a single photo, the Conv3d patchifier pairs 2 consecutive video frames into each 2 × 14 × 14 tube, halving the token count across time.
  2. Absolute-Time M-RoPE (second_per_grid_t): The 16 Time (t) rotary frequency pairs in mrope_section = [16, 24, 24] advance in proportion to real-world timestamps (second_per_grid_t × tokens_per_second), so a 2-second interval receives the same temporal rotation angle regardless of the video's sampling frame rate.
Figure 13: Three-stage Vision-Language Model recap and preview of Episode 6 (How Video Generation AI Actually Works). Image by the author.4 Rules When Building with Vision-Language Models in Production
  1. Preserve Native Aspect Ratio & Resolution for OCR: Downsampling a 1120 × 280 receipt to 25 tokens flipped 4829 into 4857. Set min_pixels and max_pixels in AutoProcessor appropriately for document tasks.
  2. Don’t Trust Direct VLM Object Counts Above ~5 Overlapping Items: Because the 2×2 Spatial Patch Merger compresses 28 × 28 px regions into single tokens before the LLM, dense overlapping objects (N = 8 or 15 circles) should be routed through an explicit detection/segmentation tool or tiled crops.
  3. Treat Text Inside Images as an Untrusted Prompt-Injection Surface: VLMs read text inside images accurately — which fixes CLIP’s "iPod" classification bug, but creates a visual prompt injection vector where adversarial instructions printed on an object enter the LLM's context window.
  4. Use Contrastive Decoding Selectively: VCD widens the margin against language-prior hallucinations (98.76% → 99.96%), at the cost of 2× inference compute (two forward passes per token).
Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)1. Why does an “iPod” sticker on an apple fool OpenAI CLIP?

OpenAI CLIP compresses an entire image into a single 512-dimensional vector and multiplies image-text cosine similarities by a learned temperature of 100.0 before Softmax. Multimodal neurons inside CLIP respond strongly to printed text, pushing the "iPod" cosine (0.2701) slightly above "Green Apple" (0.2641), which the ×100.0 Softmax turns into a 64.51% iPod prediction.

2. Why are there 1,600 patches of 1,280 dimensions in Qwen2.5-VL?

On a 560 × 560 pixel image sliced with a 14 × 14 pixel patch size, 560 ÷ 14 = 40 patches per side, giving 40 × 40 = 1,600 patches (sequence length N). Each patch is projected into a 1,280-dimensional feature vector (D), forming a [1,600 × 1,280] tensor before the 2×2 Spatial Patch Merger compresses it 4× into 400 tokens of 2,048 dimensions.

3. How does 3D M-RoPE ([16, 24, 24]) work in Qwen2.5-VL?

Each attention head in Qwen2.5-VL (head_dim = 128, or 64 rotary frequency pairs) splits its 64 frequency pairs into 16 pairs for Time (t), 24 pairs for Height (h, Row y), and 24 pairs for Width (w, Column x). For 1D text tokens, t = h = w; for 2D images, t stays constant while h and w track row and column coordinates; for 3D video, t advances with real timestamps.

4. What is Visual Contrastive Decoding (VCD)?

Visual Contrastive Decoding (Leng et al., CVPR 2024) reduces object hallucinations in Vision-Language Models by subtracting the next-token logits of a noise-corrupted image v' from the logits of the clean image v: ℓ_VCD(y) = (1 + α)ℓ(y | v, x) − αℓ(y | v', x). This suppresses answers driven purely by English word co-occurrence priors (such as assuming a fork is next to a plate and knife).

How We Measured (Reproducibility & Disclosure Box)
  • Hardware: NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition (96.0 GB VRAM, bfloat16 for Qwen2.5-VL-3B, float32 for CLIP / SigLIP).
  • Models: openai/clip-vit-base-patch32, google/siglip-base-patch16-224, and Qwen/Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct via HuggingFace transformers.
  • Protocol: All VLM generations use deterministic greedy decoding (do_sample=False, n = 1 run per condition). Attention telemetry in Sections 7–8 was captured with attn_implementation="eager" on a single teacher-forced pass. All test images (apple_clean.jpg, apple_ipod.jpg, apple_pizza.jpg, fox_clean.jpg, clock_1010.jpg, plate_knife_no_fork.jpg, wide_receipt_pin.jpg) are synthetic studio renders generated for controlled testing.
